notes.title: — I —
notes.html_source:
As we can see from the title of the novel, Ulysses is structured around allusions to the Odyssey by Homer. Joyce used the Greek epic poem as a backbone for his work.

Note: This list uses the following scheme:

Number of the Ulysses book. “Name of the book”: Book of the Odyssey to which it corresponds.

Part I of Ulysses is known as the “Telemachiad”; it corresponds to books 1-4 of the Odyssey (often called the “Telemachiad” also):

  1. “Telemachus”: Book one.

  2. “Nestor”: Book three.

  3. “Proteus”: In book four we find the episode of Proteus.

The second part of the Ulysses, Wanderings of Odysseus, has this scheme:

  1. “Calypso”: Book five.

  2. “Lotus Eaters”: Refers to the ninth book.

  3. “Hades”: Book eleven.

  4. “Aeolus”: First part of book ten.

  5. “Lystrygonians”: Book ten again, but the latest part this time.

  6. “Scylla and Charybdis”: Parts of the book twelve.

  7. “Wandering Rocks”: There’s not a real parallel in the Odyssey; it’s the alternative path for Odysseus mentioned by Circe in book twelve, but it was just a possibility, not something that really happened.

  8. “Sirens”:Book twelve.

  9. “Cyclops” Ninth book again.

  10. “Nausicaa”: Books six and seven.

  11. “Oxen of the Sun”: Book twelve.

  12. “Circe”: She appears as an enchantress in the tenth book in a role of prophet and helper for Ulysses' crew, especially in book twelve.

Part III of the novel, named Nostos (Return), corresponds to the second half of the Odyssey, books 13 to 24.

  1. “Eumaeus”: Books fourteen, fifteen and sixteen.

  2. “Ithaca”: Books seventeen through twenty-three, the return to his palace (seventeen), the slaying of the suitors (book twenty-two), the death sentence for the maid who helped them (twenty-two), and the return to his bed with Penelope (twenty-three).

  3. “Penelope”: No parallel book in the Odyssey gives Penelope’s sustained perspective or voice. In this last part of the poem there won’t be any punctuation.

notes.title: Stately, plump Buck Mulligan came from the stairhead, bearing a bowl of lather on which a mirror and a razor lay crossed. A yellow dressinggown, ungirdled, was sustained gently behind him on the mild morning air. He held the bowl aloft and intoned:
notes.html_source:
Buck Mulligan is modelled after Oliver St. John Gogarty, a fellow Irish poet.

This opening scene is a parody of the Catholic Mass suggested here by the “stately” manner of Buck’s entry, which follows that of a priest or clergyman, and again with the “cross(ing)” of the mirror and the razor. The bowl in the scene, “held aloft” ceremoniously, stands in for the chalice of communion that contains the blood of Christ.

It’s significant that the first word of Joyce’s novel, ‘Stately’ contains its last, ‘Yes’. This is a story of return, and as we depart, we have the shadow of our destination in mind.

The yellow dressinggown: 16 June is the feast day of St. John Francis Regis (1597-1640), the appropriate vestments for a Mass would be white and gold. Within the church the colour yellow suggests degradation, jealousy, treason and deceit. As such Judas is often portrayed in a garment of yellow.

The ungirdled gown is in contrast of the priests vow of chastity and the “razor” refers to slaughter, with Mulligan, the priest, acting as a butcher.

notes.title: Introibo ad altare Dei.
notes.html_source:
Latin for:

“I will go up to the altar of God.” – from Psalms 43:4

The line makes explicit that the opening scene is a parody of Roman Catholic mass.

Also hints at a parody of ‘the Odyssey’ which, as epics conventionally did, opens with an invocation of the Muse, the daughter of Zeus.

notes.title: Stephen Dedalus,
notes.html_source:
Stephen Dedalus is, to put it very bluntly and broadly, Joyce’s artistic representation of his self. He is the protagonist of Joyce’s previous novel, A Portrait of The Artist as a Young Man, a bildungsroman which draws heavily on Joyce’s own formative experiences.

In Stephen Hero, an early version of what became Portrait, Stephen’s surname is spelled “Daedalus” in more precise allusion to Daedalus, the architect in Greek myth who was contracted by King Minos to build the Labyrinth in which he would imprison his wife’s son the Minotaur.

Stephen appears in Ulysses as the character who correlates to Telemachus. He harnesses, tentatively, aspects of Hamlet. He is the protagonist of the first three chapters.

More fancifully, we might view Stephen as an autobiographical reference for the being who builds the labyrinth (Ulysses the novel) for King Minos (Joyce himself?) to imprison an unconquerable beast– what the beast is would require an overreaching level of speculation.

notes.title: Made rapid crosses in the air
notes.html_source: The sign of the cross, a ubiquitous Roman Catholic gesture used to convey a blessing or a prayer of supplication, involves moving your right hand vertically then horizontally in a shape recalling the Cross of Jesus’s crucifixion. While clergy and laypeople alike often perform a solo gesture with hand close to their own chest and head, a Catholic priest may perform the gesture with their arm extended outward to “bless” another person in front of them, as Mulligan does to Stephen here as part of his mock priest shtick.

notes.html_source:
“Equine” means horse-like– we might today say “horse-faced”.

PROPOSED SUGGESTION: We might well, but we probably wouldn’t say “his face was horse-faced in its length”.

notes.title: Buck Mulligan
notes.html_source:
Joyce based this character on his acquaintance, Oliver St. John Gogarty. Joyce’s Trieste Notebook from 1909 contains an entry on Gogarty, complete with phrases which would go on to appear in Ulysses. For instance, the sentence

The Omphalos was to be the temple of a neo-paganism.

Would turn up in

To ourselves… new paganism… omphalos.

a bit later in this chapter.

Both men had suffered a falling out, hence Joyce’s critical depiction. Gogarty was a poet, an author, a politician, but above all else a conversationalist. Joyce’s opinion on whether or not he was successful at any of those occupations is fairly clear from the text.

PROPOSED SUGGESTION: Gogarty was also importantly a doctor (and Joyce himself spent some time as a medical student in Paris); at the time of the setting of Ulysses, Buck Mulligan is a medical student.

notes.title: For this, O dearly beloved, is the genuine Christine: body and soul and blood and ouns. Slow music, please. Shut your eyes, gents. One moment. A little trouble about those white corpuscles. Silence, all.
notes.html_source:
Continuing his self-aware perversion of the Eucharist, Buck Mulligan here parodies Christ’s words at the Last Supper:

“And as they were eating, Jesus took bread, and blessed it, and brake it, and gave it to the disciples, and said, Take, eat; this is my body.

And he took the cup, and gave thanks, and gave it to them, saying, Drink ye all of it;

For this is my blood of the new testament, which is shed for many for the remission of sins.“ (Matthew 26: 26-28)

By using the feminine “Christine” rather than “Christian” Mulligan is imputing a sexuality to the holy matter: Christ as woman. He is further mocking the Christ figure to poke fun at Stephen’s intellectualism and former religious seriousness. Femininity will play a role throughout the novel as the magnetic force behind Ulysses' journey in Homer’s Odyssey as well as Bloom’s “search” for Molly. Joyce is planting metaphorical seeds that will bear fruit later. The careful reader can rejoice in these complexities with each additional reading.

As Mulligan holds aloft the chalice containing (or about to contain) God’s blood, he acknowledges that some of the flecks of shaving foam are experiencing difficulty in their effort to become “white corpuscles,” the antigen-destroying part of the holy substance. When medical students encounter miracles, they like to get their facts straight.

Alludes to the Black Mass in which a woman’s body plays the part of the altar.

notes.title: Chrysostomos
notes.html_source:
Greek for “golden-mouthed.” A pun on Buck’s fillings which also refers to two early orators, Dio Chrysostomos (c.50-c.117) and St. John Chrysostomos (c.345-407). See this article from the Joyce Foundation for an in-depth explantion.

It is, arguably, the first glimpse of Stephen’s thoughts within the narrative.

Joyce experienced many religions in Trieste – a cultural, historic, linguistic and religious melting pot. Greek orthodox ceremonies were seen by him on the city which he perceived as mock Christian – ‘ Another result of this process of estrangement may have been to bring Joyce to look on the Greek Orthodox mass as a something of a mockery of a Latin one, a mockery he would later find useful when writing the opening of “Telemachus” (McCourt, J, The Years of Bloom, p60).

notes.title: Two strong shrill whistles answered through the calm.
notes.html_source:
A shrill noise would be piercing and high pitched; the whistles would break through “the calm” atmosphere and disrupt it.

From the top of the tower, Buck can see across the port. He sees the steam come from the ship’s whistle and he whistles first, then they hear the ship’s reply–another indication of how clever and self-aware Buck is.

No one knows the exact source of these whistles, but one possibility is the mailboat (whose whistle was deep not shrill).

The three whistles, Buck’s and two replies, is a mockery of the sacring bell. The sacring bell, also known as the sanctus bell, is the bell which rings when the Host is elevated at the celebration of High Mass.

notes.title: He skipped off the gunrest and looked gravely at his watcher, gathering about his legs the loose folds of his gown
notes.html_source:
The generally heroic description of Buck Mulligan and the general anti-heroic description of Stephen is part of the gender mesh of Ulysses.

“In designing Ulysses Joyce first identified what the socially conditioned reader is most likely to want and expect from male and female characters of different ages, and then he provides his readers with characters of different ages, and then provides his readers with characters who frustrate and implicitly challenge that desire (Vicki Mahaffey, ”Ulysses and the End of Gender", in Margot Norris (ed.), A Companion to James Joyce’s “Ulysses” (p. 153).

PROPOSED SUGGESTION: Gender and Ulysses is fascinating, but how does this particular moment relate to questions of gender? The flowing gown? The “watcher”? “Heroic” as a traditionally masculine trait? And … “not being heroic” feminine? To be honest, without having read Mahaffey’s essay through, I’m sceptical of the assertion that Joyce began his characters programatically to invert or disrupt cultural expectations of gender. There are plenty of ways to approach gender in Ulysses, and this seems way oversimplified. But again, I haven’t read the essay in question, and I’m sure it has a broader vision than that.

What do you actually mean by “heroic” and “non-heroic”, and what exactly is it about either characters' presentations that invites these adjectives? Do you mean Mulligan has a “mock-heroic” air? Are you making a reference to the Odyssey as it underpins Ulysses? Do you simply mean “heroic” as “like a hero”? The word “heroic” is far too complicated to just leave hanging like this, imo.

notes.title: Your absurd name,
notes.html_source:
This whole consideration of Stephen’s name may allude to the first chapter of A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man, where “Nasty Roche” asks Stephen, “What kind of name is that?” Stephen was unable to answer, and here, Mulligan considers its derivation and “The mockery of it”.

Buck Mulligan may be specifically referring to Stephen’s first name, being the name of the first Christian Martyr, but more likely he is concerned by the incongruous nature of an Irishman having the name of a mythological Ancient Greek—by the same token, this might be wry self-comment on Joyce’s outlandish choice of name for his protagonist and alter-ego.

Stephen’s name also ties in with the conflict and commingling of Hebraism and Hellenism (very roughly, Jewishness and Ancient Greekness) throughout the novel.

notes.title: Malachi Mulligan, two dactyls
notes.html_source:
“Two Dactyls” refers to the meter that is used to pronounce his name. A dactyl is a unit of poetic meter that has one stressed syllable followed by two unstressed syllables.

It should be noted that Malachi, (a Hebrew name) means “The Messenger”, and is the name of the last prophet the Old Testament.

The dominant rhythm of Homer’s Odyssey is also a hexameter (six metrical feet to the line), and the dactyl is the dominant type of metrical foot employed.

notes.title: Athens
notes.html_source:
While making fun of their Greek-influenced names he suggest a trip to Athens: the largest city and capital of Greece both Ancient and modern.

For Stephen and for Joyce, the significance of going or not going to Athens reflects the fact that Joyce, although a polyglot and in general a virtuoisic linguist, never really learned Ancient Greek. (Slightly later in this chapter, Mulligan tells Stephen that he should learn the language, and that maybe Mulligan should be the one to teach him.) This is also perhaps an oblique comment on the fact that Ulysses is a modern update of the Odyssey, and also of the fact that Joyce’s immersion in Homer could be seen, at certain stages, as not particularly deep. Joyce’s original fascination with Ulysses (Odysseus) and the Odyssey was bound up not with the original text but with Charles Lamb’s retellings of it in The Adventures of Ulysses—themselves a modern update on the original Homeric poem.

notes.title: The aunt
notes.html_source: Referred to again soon after, this is Malachi’s wealthy and pious Aunt Ursula who disapproves of Stephen. Some researchers have identified this unseen character with Oliver St. John Gogarty’s real life aunt, Anne “Annie” Henry Oliver. Annie occasionally lived in the home of her sister Margaret Gogarty (née Oliver) and Margaret’s children, including Oliver St. John, after Margaret’s husband Henry died in 1891. She seemed to have played a role in managing the household and raising Margaret’s children, which matches the descriptions in this chapter of Mulligan’s aunt hiring the servants in his house, lending him money, and lecturing Mulligan about his company.

notes.title: How long
notes.html_source:
“How long is Haines going to stay in this tower?”: Stephen views Haines not as a visiting English scholar rooming with Mulligan and him, but as an invading force occupying his home. How long indeed?

The contemporary occupation of Ireland/the Martello tower finds ancient correspondence in the occupation of Penelope’s home by the unwelcome suitors, who move in and refuse to be dislodged for the duration of Odysseus’s absence.

notes.title: Kinch, the knife-blade
notes.html_source:
Mulligan’s nickname for Dedalus is “Kinch.” Kinch is a form of Kinchin, which means child.

This meaning is significant in the context of this chapter and its predecessor book Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man. Stephen did his best to free himself from his roots and his parents and emigrated to Paris, but due to the death of his mother he returned and therefore is confronted with his dependence on his parents (and his roots).

“Knife-blade” lends some aggression to the name Kinch. It is not unlikely that Mulligan alludes to the fact that Stephen tries to behave as independently from his parents as possible, thereby hurting them (cf. the passage where Mulligan says that Stephen refused to pray at his mother’s deathbed).

notes.title: He was raving all night about a black panther
notes.html_source:
Haines, the English house guest, suffers from night terrors – having the night before raved after dreaming of a black panther. Later in the novel the black panther becomes for Bloom a symbol carrying overtones of divinity.

Likely an allusion to the three animals mentioned in the opening of Dante’s Divine Comedy. In the first canto (Canto I, 30-36) Dante the pilgrim is lost in a remote area when:

And lo! almost where the ascent began,
A panther light and swift exceedingly,
Which with a spotted skin was covered o'er!

And never moved she from before my face,
Nay, rather did impede so much my way,
That many times I to return had turned.

(Longfellow trans.)

Although Longfellow translates “panther”, the animal mentioned here, “una lonza” is actually a leopard; throughout the first Canto Dante also encounters a lion and a she-wolf. Respectively, they are thought to be symbols of lust, pride and avarice.

PROPOSED SUGGESTION: Many folk suggest Dante’s Panther is an allegory for Florence and worldly pleasures, and Dante’s anger at their failure to revolt. Given Haines is English is this an allegory for Ireland-England relations and the Irish Rising? He will shoot him if he doesn’t stop?
The ‘blacks’ are clarified below and the following note illustrates this sourced from
http://www.poetryintranslation.com/PITBR/Italian/DantnotesInf.htm#_Toc64100649

Salvation of Italy

There are various interpretations of Dante’s imagery, for example that the leopard (panther) represents Florence and worldly pleasure, lust or envy; the lion the Royal House of France, and ambition or pride; the she-wolf the Papacy, and avarice. Lust, pride and avarice are the three roots of sin. The imagery of the three animals may come from Jeremiah (v.6). The she-wolf, the Papacy, made many alliances.

The Greyhound (Veltro) has been suggested to be Can Grande della Scala, born in Verona, between Feltro in Venetia and Montefeltro in Romagna, the great Ghibelline leader. Dante’s later patron, he may have been regarded by Dante as the deliverer who would restore Imperial power, reinstitute Roman law, eliminate avarice, bring peace, and establish a reformed order of things.

Dante, whose father Aldighiero was a Guelf, and supporter of the papacy, traced his ancestry back to Cacciaguida, a crusader under Emperor Conrad III, and identified with the Romans who had allied Florence to Imperial Rome. He was of the populo vecchio, the populus, the old inhabitants, not the plebs, from Fiesole etc. Dante’s opposition however to the dishonesty and corruption of the Papacy under Boniface VIII aligned him with the Ghibelline pro-Imperial cause, and opposed him to the pro-Papacy Guelfs. The Florentine families also split between the local Bianchi (white) and Neri (black) factions. Dante’s family belonged to the Bianchi. Ultimately the Bianchi combined with the old half-suppressed Ghibelline party, and the Neri aligned with the Papacy, claiming to represent the old Guelph traditions of Florence.

Dante’s personal ideals when fully developed were for an apolitical Church, and an earthly Empire, both enfranchised by God, supreme in their own spheres, one of spiritual and the other temporal power. He was therefore opposed to the Guelf principles of his father (the Ultramontanism of Gregory VII and Innocent III), and to the democracy and plutocracy of Florence. He was equally opposed to the supremacy of State over Church asserted by the Emperors Henry IV and Frederick II, by Henry II of England, and Philip the Fair of France. Dante therefore found himself ‘a party of one’ caught in the cross-currents of his time, supporting an autocratic view of the Imperial State, and a desire for a reformed, spiritual Papacy.

An alternative candidate for ‘the Greyhound’ is Uguccione della Faggiuola, head of the Ghibelline forces at Lucca in 1315 when the Guelphs were driven out, and at the siege of Montecatini (within ten miles of Florence) where he gained a decisive victory. However Uguccione was eclipsed by 1316.

PROPOSED SUGGESTION: This is generally accepted to have a biographical source: the real-life counterpart to Haines (Samuel Chenevix Trench) had a dream about a black panther in this very Martello tower, and in his distress fired a pistol at the wall.

Have any other Joyce commentators suggested this is a Dante allusion? It might well be, all this stuff is interesting, but it does kind of run away from Ulysses without really fleshing out the connection … It’s an annotation on Dante way more than it is anything else …

PROPOSED SUGGESTION: I agree with jayclay about the discussion of Dante being irrelevant.

PROPOSED SUGGESTION: @DavidDevalle Thanks for replying to this! I’d more or less forgotten I’d left this suggestion—and thanks for pointing me to Mary Reynolds. I’ve managed to read the p. 36 you specified, but (without having read the rest of her book, and admittedly not being myself very familiar with Dante; I’m sure I’ve got a partial view of the whole thing) the ‘panther’ referenced by that page is the phrase ‘black panther vampire’, which Stephen utters as a kind of epithet for Bloom in the ‘Circe’ episode. The reverberations and recurrences of the ‘black panther’ motif or symbol no doubt stem from its appearance in ‘Telemachus’, but I’m not convinced that the first appearance of the panther was even an allusion to Dante. Would Joyce or Stephen, both accomplished in Italian (Joyce had certainly read the Commedia in Italian before 1904), think of it as Dante’s panther instead of what it is in Italian: a leopard? Possibly, if Longfellow was what stuck in his mind, I suppose. When Reynolds mentions when, as you say, ‘Leopold recognises’ the Yeats poem which references Dante, she actually writes that Bloom ‘recogniz[es] a reference to poetry though he does not know whose’. And when she discusses the ‘black panther vampire’, the connection to Dante is not made via the ‘panther’ or ‘leopard’; she writes of this as ‘reflecting Dante’s plea for help against “the beast that turned me back.”’ This ‘beast’ isn’t the first of the animals Dante encounters (not a panther or a leopard)—it’s a she-wolf. I’m grateful to have been directed to the Reynolds, but as far as I can see she doesn’t claim that the panther in Telemachus is meant to reflect Dante’s ‘panther’; instead, she suggests that Stephen has panthers on the brain in such a way that later brings out references to Dante, which are tied to the opening of Canto 1 but not to the actual appearance in it of any panther.

I wasn’t trying to suggest that ‘Joyce didn’t know that about the panther’. (Didn’t know what? Its symbolic connection to Florence?) I was addressing the scope of this particular annotation. As I can see, it identifies an allusion to Dante (well and good), and suggests some significance of this panther (or leopard) to Dante, while making a connection between ‘the worldly pleasures of Florence’ and the English response to the Rising and as colonisers in general (well and good, and I feel a very valid point)—but then the rest of it just discusses Dante’s life and his relationship with the church and state, without trying to draw a parallel to Joyce. Maybe the parallels are supposed to be obvious, but I don’t really see them and I think many others won’t either.

So by ‘fleshing out the connection’, I meant: I wasn’t convinced that the discussion of Dante and nothing but Dante added a great deal to the annotation on this particular moment. This is too long for a genius annotation, and I think many would be confused as to how the Dante info relates to this specific description of Haines’s dream.

I’m aware that this was probably originally added as a suggestion, and I think it was a mistake to have integrated it without editing it. This annotation is now very choppy and not in line with how annotations here should be. The biographical info on Dante would have been fine as an illuminating comment below the annotation, but not as the bulk of it.

And I wasn’t claiming a biographical connection with ‘Introibo ad altare Dei’ but very specifically with Haines’s dream (I didn’t mention the parody of Catholic Mass at all): as I wrote,

the real-life counterpart to Haines (Samuel Chenevix Trench) had a dream about a black panther in this very Martello tower, and in his distress fired a pistol at the wall.

And I’m not sure what you meant by the following:

Mulligan murmuring “Introibo ad altare Dei” is no doubt biographical but that does not mean the first scene parody of the Catholic Mass and Joyce’s intent concerning Stephen’s sin about his mother is contextualised and interwoven with the Hellenic and Hebraic context of the journey evoking such as Thalatta.

Did you mean to write, ‘that does not mean the first scene parody […] isn’t contextualised and interwoven […]’? I would agree that the fact that something is biographical doesn’t mean it doesn’t have wider significance and complexity. I think biographical details are often minor points—they can help anchor us while we’re reading, but don’t often constitute an interpretation. My bringing up the point of a biographical parallel was to try to add an interesting (and documented) detail to this annotation, not to try to dismiss the more interesting suggestions surrounding allusions and symbolic significance.

Anyway, I hope we’re not talking at cross-purposes, and I hope what I’ve written is halfway intelligible. Forgive me if I seem to have addressed things that you didn’t write or don’t agree with—as I said above, the fact that this annotation is clogged up with unedited proposed suggestions is the main reason why it’s overlong and even confusing; and it would take some time to figure out which contributions belong to whom. I really do appreciate that you took the time to address what I wrote. :)

notes.title: The bard’s noserag! A new art colour for our Irish poets: snotgreen. You can almost taste it, can’t you?
notes.html_source:
Mulligan’s epithet for Stephen—“the bard”—is both mocking and admiring: he acknowledges the young Dedalus’s talents as writer and poet while also suggesting that he acts above his station. “Bard” is a term most often attached to Shakespeare, but it also suggests a kind of travelling poet (appropriate for Joyce the exile) as well as a poet of national importance. Here, then, Mulligan suggests that Dedalus—and Joyce by extension—is, despite his youth and pretensions, a representative writer for Ireland with the weight of the country on his shoulders.

The colour green has long been highly symbolic in relation to Ireland. Mulligan’s compound “snotgreen” recalls—as noted below—Homer’s famous phrase “winedark sea”, tying Joyce to Homer as well as Shakespeare. The snot also evokes the candour Joyce habitually displayed when writing about bodily practices: snot will indeed play a role again, notably in the third chapter, “Proteus”. By suggesting that “snotgreen” might be “a new art colour for our Irish poets”, Mulligan also indicates some of the flavours and textures of modernist art, and the down-to-earthiness of Irish writers in particular. The handkerchief becomes a kind of canvas in this moment, with Stephen’s bodily effluence representing the art he has sent forth from himself.

It’s also appropriate that Mulligan would claim that this is a colour that “you can almost taste”.

notes.title: Hyperborean
notes.html_source:
In Greek mythology the hyperboreans were a mythical people who lived far to the north of Thrace. Also used by Friedrich Nietzsche to describe the Ubermensch or Superman.

Hyperborea was also held by the ancient Greeks to be Apollo’s winter home, where he was venerated among its people. Also noting that Apollo was recognized as the God of truth, prophecy, and light (among other things), this furthers Mulligan’s character by aligning it with said aspects. (see §2 for Apollo’s association with Hyperborea)

notes.title: But to think of your mother begging you with her last breath to kneel down and pray for her. And you refused.
notes.html_source:
When Mulligan says, “The aunt thinks you killed your mother,” and then charges, “You could have knelt down, damn it, Kinch, when your dying mother asked you,” he resembles his model Oliver Gogarty, who casually declared to all his acquaintances “that Joyce was ‘mad,’ and ‘had killed his mother by telling her what he thought’” (Ellmann, 173). But Mulligan overstates the facts, assuming that they were similar to those surrounding Joyce’s mother’s death in August 1903,

Ellmann writes of Mary Joyce’s illness, “Her fear of death put her in mind of her son’s impiety, and on the days following Easter she tried to persuade him to make his confession and take communion. Joyce, however, was inflexible; he feared, as he had Stephen Dedalus say later, ‘the chemical action’ which would be set up in his soul ‘by a false homage to a symbol behind which are massed twenty centuries of authority and veneration.’ His mother wept, and vomited green bile into a basin, but he did not yield. His aunt Josephine Murray argued with him” (129, emphasis added). Four months later, in Mrs. Joyce’s final hours, “she lay in a coma, and the family knelt about her bed, praying and lamenting. Her brother John Murray, observing that neither Stanislaus nor James was kneeling, peremptorily ordered them to do so. Neither obeyed” (136, emphasis added).

Joyce may have refused to compromise his spiritual integrity by making false declarations of faith, but he was not so priggishly self-righteous as to attempt to ruin other people’s spiritual consolations. After his mother’s death, he comforted his nine-year-old sister Mabel, sitting beside her on the stairs with “his arm around her, saying, ‘You must not cry like that because there is no reason to cry. Mother is in heaven. She is far happier now than she has ever been on earth, but if she sees you crying it will spoil her happiness. You must remember that when you feel like crying. You can pray for her if you wish, Mother would like that. But don’t cry any more’” (Ellmann, 136). The Stephen Dedalus of Telemachus was as sensitive to his mother’s suffering as Joyce was to Mabel’s: “Silent with awe and pity I went to her bedside. She was crying in her wretched bed.”

Given such complex family dynamics, the accusation made by Gogarty and Mulligan seems callous and shallow. Joyce felt there was some, but only some, truth to the charge. At the end of August 1904 he wrote to his wife, Nora, “My mother was slowly killed, I think, by my father’s ill-treatment, by years of trouble, and by my cynical frankness of conduct. When I looked on her face as she lay in her coffin—a face grey and wasted with cancer—I understood that I was looking on the face of a victim and I cursed the system which had made her a victim” (Ellmann, 169). But he did not back down from his principled stand about kneeling in prayer. In the following paragraph of the same letter he wrote, “Six years ago I left the Catholic Church, hating it most fervently… . I made secret war upon it when I was a student and declined to accept the positions it offered me… . Now I make open war upon it by what I write and say and do.”

Ulysses appears to heighten and focus the guilt Joyce felt, maximizing its narrative importance as much as the treatment of the black panther episode minimizes the narrative importance of those events. The dream which Stephen had of his mother after death seems to him a kind of malevolent ghostly visitation. His anguish at the ghost’s implicit demand that he kneel down in prayer attains a shattering climax in Circe.

notes.title: Lathered again
notes.html_source:
Joyce often chooses this slightly unexpected word order in Ulysses. (E.g. “wiped again his razorblade” below.) A more usual syntax would be “lathered his farther cheek again.” The version that stands connects the verb with the idea of repetition before the verb’s object.

One effect of Joyce’s choice is to render the action intrinsically repetitive, rather than incidentally so. That is, the verb becomes “to lather again.” This tells us something about Mulligan’s actions–this is a routine–and perhaps also, if this carries Stephen’s perspective, Stephen’s sense of boredom at watching Mulligan’s show.

Stephen’s point of view certainly seems to be in play throughout this section; his mind concerned with repetition. We have the unhappy replays of his mother’s death, as well as the ‘return’ of his mother in Stephen’s dream.

The syntactical choice also, of course, draws our attention to the broader structure of the novel, which is based on repetition: the text repeats The Odyssey, so that many of the individuals and their actions are versions of something that has happened before. All of these people and their behaviour is intrinsically ‘again’ in Joyce’s system.

Anthony Burgess’s book Joysprick spends some time discussing this specific syntactical habit in Joyce’s prose.

notes.title: Farther
notes.html_source:
A striking choice over the more usual ‘further’, suggesting Mulligan has taken on the role of Stephen’s father – a position currently vacant due to Simon Dedalus’s neglect.

PROPOSED SUGGESTION: ‘Further’ and ‘farther’ have different meanings. ‘Farther’ would be the appropriate word in this case, regardless of whether it sounds closer to the word ‘father.’

I’m not aware of two different meanings. I understand that there’s a tendency to use one for physical and the other for non-physical instances in the US, but not in British English, which Joyce uses. Is there another difference that you’re referring to? 

PROPOSED SUGGESTION: There is some dispute over the difference between “further” and “father” both in British and American usage, but there’s never really been any firmly established rule (unsurprisingly). There are conventions, though: American usage does tend towards using “farther” for physical distances, while “further”—to borrow a very questionable construction from the movie Finding Forrester—“is a definition of degree”. It ultimately doesn’t matter, at least for your own use of the words.

See this stirring but still essentially ludicrous movie clip

Also, clogging up these Ulysses annotations with PROPOSED SUGGESTIONS, instead of finding a way to maintain delicately coherent annotations, with suggestions below (which might not necessarily deserve being incorporated even if they are useful and illuminating)—it’s pretty frustrating, and makes sensible judicious edits somewhat difficult, if not impossible.

Still, I think the jarring echo of “father” is very much intended, even if I wouldn’t stretch it to a suggestion of fatherhood for Mulligan over Stephen. Not every association needs to grow into a beautiful butterfly conclusion. Not saying that this tate particularly strained to do that, though; I’m just waffling.

notes.title: Stephen, an elbow rested on the jagged granite, leaned his palm against his brow and gazed at the fraying edge of his shiny black coat-sleeve.
notes.html_source:
Possibly the first line of the book which expresses Stephen’s abject state explicitly.

The verbs here play a crucial role in drawing a parallel between his current state of mind and his actions.

He rests his elbow on ‘jagged granite’— something that doesn’t provide comfort but, quite to the contrary, makes him feel more restless, ostensibly from lack of finding anything better suited. Comfort is not Stephen’s priority at the moment.

The ‘fraying’ edge of his coat sleeve could perhaps be an ominous symbol for his own emotional decay: he and his sleeve both are, it could be said, tattered.

The particular quality of the damage to Stephen’s coat is of interest. Frayed edges come from abrasion, as on jagged granite, while shininess comes from pressure, as when resting. Together they give the impression that Stephen’s pose here is a long-held one. As such, they not only communicate Stephen’s poverty but his stasis. As we are shown, Stephen has become ‘stuck’: in his aesthetic pursuits and in Dublin itself.

notes.title: Laughter seized all his strong wellknit trunk.
notes.html_source:
Kenner (Kenner, H. Joyce’s Voices, p71) describes the emergence of two narrative voices in Ulysses. One ‘is moving characters about and reporting their doings,in fluent unemphatic novelese, barely to be distinguished from a neutral idiom save by occasional “great searching eyes,” and occasional “strong wellknit trunk”……. . And while the first voice attends to the chapter’s housekeeping, a second narrative voice is uttering passages like the following

Woodshadows floated silently by through the morning peace from the stairhead seaward where he gazed. Inshore and farther out the mirror of water whitened, spurned by lightshod hurrying feet. White breast of the dim sea. The twining stresses, two by two. A hand plucking the harpstrings, merging their twining chords. Wavewhite wedded words shimmering on the dim tide.

They are written as Stephen is alone on the parapet in Telemachus. This second narrator does not explicitly indicate the words are those of Stephen’s, ‘but the sentences that brush them in absorb Stephen-words and Stephen-rhythms, moving us imperceptibly into Stephen’s thoughts’.

notes.title: It is a symbol of Irish art. The cracked looking-glass of a servant
notes.html_source:
Or rather, the art of the colonized and subjugated Irish.

The “cracked looking-glass” is an image from Oscar Wilde’s essay “The Decay of Lying.” Stephen adds to the image by reducing it to the status of servant’s possession, as he feels Ireland has been.

Joyce favoured being part of all nations rather than one and putting art before a nation (Cheng,V. Joyce, Race, and Empire, p66).

notes.title: Parried again. He fears the lancet of my art as I fear that of his. The cold steelpen.
notes.html_source:
There is possibly an echo of the fencing scene from Hamlet in the word “parried”.

More generally, however, this plays with a common metaphor of seeing the writer’s pen as a kind of weapon. Stephen’s interior monologue here recognises that Mulligan’s moments of kindness and conciliation are not necessarily genuine, but in fact indicate an anxiety about his eventual representation in the later writings of Stephen Dedalus. If you take Mulligan as a definite counterpart to Oliver St John Gogarty, it seems that this anxiety was warranted. Joyce’s art is concentrated in his “cold steelpen”, an object that suggests the dispassionate recording of what really happened (the coldness, the cold eye) while also being something that could cut and injure as a dagger.

The lancet of Mulligan’s art might well be the surgical instruments he uses as a medical student, which perhaps make Stephen wary. There are doubtless many other suggestions for what Mulligan’s own lancet might be in this case, however.

Stephen has complained to Mulligan about their visitor, Haines, and Mulligan has threatened some violence against him if he acts up again. This has led Stephen to a sequence of thoughts about Mulligan’s real or imagined hazing of someone named Clive Kempthorpe, involving at least the threat of castration with shears: “debagged”.

While some might not think it means that, you might be appalled when you study the text further:

With slit ribbons of his shirt whipping the air, he hops and hobbles round the table, with trousers down at heels, chased by Ades of Magdalen with the tailor’s shears. A scared calf’s face gilded with marmalade.

In this descriptive scene of terror, Buck talks about shredding Haines' shirt with shears and dropping his pants to his ankles as he chases after him with the shears; his face being covered with sweat because he is fearful of his life.

PROPOSED SUGGESTION: “Debagged” = having your trousers removed by force.

PROPOSED SUGGESTION: I think the hazing being described here is by English boys in a prep school against Clive Kempthorpe. The mention of “moneyed” voices and pale faces would suggest that. Also the “giddy ox” along side the term debugging would suggest threat of castration.

PROPOSED SUGGESTION: Not a prep school: Magdalen is an Oxford College

PROPOSED SUGGESTION: I might also mention the very similar debagging scene at the beginning of Evelyn Waugh’s ‘Decline & Fall’ and add that Oxbridge Colleges have quadrangles. When Joyce refers to Mathew Arnold he may be thinking of Arnold’s poem ‘The Scholar Gypsy’ about an Oxford student who deserts his studies to follow the gypsies.

notes.title: I remember only ideas and sensations.
notes.html_source: As he does frequently, Mulligan dodges responsibility for his hurtful remarks by relying on philosophical jargon. In this remark Buck echoes two 18th-century philosophers: the English empiricist John Locke and the Irish idealist Bishop George Berkeley. Both of them wrote that all knowledge (and thus all memory, as Buck would have it) comes only from man’s physical sensation of external stimuli, and subsequently the ideas formed in our mind based on those sensations. Stephen will ponder these philosophies at the beginning of chapter 3, “Proteus”.

notes.title: The Mater
notes.html_source: The Mater Misericordiae University Hospital, often shortened to just “The Mater”, is a large hospital on Eccles Street in the north of Dublin (near Leopold Bloom’s house at 7 Eccles Street). Mulligan evidently trains there sometimes as a medical student (although he attends the University of Dublin’s Trinity College, whereas Mater Misricordiae is associated with the separate University College Dublin). The name “Mater Misericordiae” is Latin for “Mother of Mercy”, an epithet of the Virgin Mary. The hospital was the site of a hospice ward, which leads Buck (like several characters will do later in the book) to associate it with death. Calling it “The Mater” (literally “The Mother”) and associating it with death lends an irony to Buck’s dismissal about Stephen and his dead mother.

notes.title: Because you have the cursed jesuit strain in you, only it’s injected the wrong way.
notes.html_source: Stephen, like the real James Joyce, had much of his schooling at institutions run by the Society of Jesus, a Catholic order better known as the Jesuits: first at the Clongowes primary school and then at Belvedere College secondary school. Stephen was strongly influenced by his Jesuit education which combines rigorous Aristotelian scholasticism with strict Catholic zeal, as is depicted in Joyce’s previous novel A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man. Stephen can’t help thinking in a Jesuit-influenced way even years after he left the church and renounced the Catholic concept of God. Hence Buck claiming that Stephen still has the “jesuit strain” in him, only it goes “the wrong way”: Stephen uses Catholic reasoning to formulate his opposition to Catholicism. Many of his thoughts throughout the book reference thinkers who are key parts of a Jesuit curriculum: Aristotle, St. Thomas Aquinas, and Jesuits founder St. Ignatius of Loyola (whom Mulligan encourages Stephen to “chuck” a few lines later). Stephen’s anxieties sometimes turn to Catholic conceptions of hellfire and damnation; in chapter 10, “Wandering Rocks”, Mulligan suggests this comes from his education by Jesuits who “drove his wits astray [by] visions of hell”, which is why “he can never be a poet”.

notes.title: I am not thinking of the offence to my mother
notes.html_source:
Though Stephen claims he is not thinking of “the offence” (not kneeling to pray with his mother at her deathbed) he in fact is and will throughout the day.

Stephen’s rejection of his mother’s dying wish to go through the simple motions of the Catholic orthodoxy is at the center of his longing for personal freedom.

There is a parallel to the story of Satan’s disobedience of God as well as Eve’s rebellion against God. Therefore the Fall of the Angels (when Satan was cast out of heaven) and the Fall of Man (Adam and Eve’s banishment from Eden) provide a cosmic background for Stephens story – he is banished from his father’s house and from Martello tower and must seek his way as an artist and a man.

notes.title: —Of the offence to me, Stephen answered.
notes.html_source:
What does Stephen mean by this, and why is it coming out now? On the simplest level, Stephen is perhaps as offended by Mulligan referring to him as

“only Dedalus”
as he is about his mother being
“beastly dead.”
Further, if Mulligan respected Stephen, or saw him as a social equal, he wouldn’t have said that. It’s another small detail that shows you how Mulligan’s interest in Stephen is insincere. I think Stephen also is offended because his mother’s death is such a huge presence in his present life–he might like to escape his fixation on it, but as we’ve already seen, the experience still haunts him.

#On a Deeper Level

Stephen is also showing Mulligan that he is unmoved by the verbal assault he was attacked with; that he has no intent of dropping his grudge. Stephen knows that behind Mulligan’s bluster is a strong desire to be adored and respected.

Buck Mulligan swung round on his heel.
 
 —O, an impossible person! he exclaimed.
 
 He walked off quickly round the parapet. Stephen stood at his post, gazing over the calm sea towards the headland. Sea and headland now grew dim. Pulses were beating in his eyes, veiling their sight, and he felt the fever of his cheeks.
notes.html_source: This is a perfect moment to go back to the Odyssey, where Athena appears to young Telemachus to tell him that he must leave his house, which is filled with usurpers, and to go out into the world to find out what happened to his father. Homer doesn’t really discuss it, but it seems Telemachus could have chosen to attach himself to one or more of his mother’s suitors and he could have allowed himself to become coopted by them. It would have been tempting to do so; it would be similarly tempting for Stephen to sign on with Mulligan’s vision of Ireland’s cultural future. But he can’t, and in this reading, it seems clear that what has happened overnight is that Stephen has realized that Mulligan really has no vision of his own, but has been preying on others the whole time.

Upon love’s bitter mystery

notes.html_source:
In telling Stephen to quit his “moody brooding,” he triggers in Stephen’s mind a memory of the days at the end of his mother’s life. Instead of praying with his mother at the time of her death, Stephen sings the W. B. Yeats poem “Who Goes with Fergus.”

It’s another example of the “Uncle Charles Principle” where a voice that is ostensibly the narrator’s takes on the personality and knowledge of an individual character.

notes.title: Woodshadows floated silently by through the morning peace from the stairhead seaward where he gazed. Inshore and farther out the mirror of water whitened, spurned by lightshod hurrying feet. White breast of the dim sea. The twining stresses, two by two. A hand plucking the harpstrings, merging their twining chords. Wavewhite wedded words shimmering on the dim tide.
notes.html_source:
Stephen is beginning to work on a poem. His mind has left the conflict with Mulligan and has begun to shape, to try to capture in words, a visual impression of the happenstance.

The reference to “lightshod hurrying feet” sounds like a reference to the god Mercury, who, in the Odyssey, is described several times as running over the surface of the ocean with his winged sandals, on his way to deliver messages to mortals.

In the Odyssey this god would have been called Hermes, who in Book 1 at the behest of Athena is dispatched to prompt Calypso to release Odysseus, while she herself goes to Ithaca to stir Telemachus into action. Hermes, like Athena, precipitates change, and here Joyce has combined this Homeric allusion with an image that in itself also suggests change — “the mirror of water whitened”.

notes.title: Her secrets: old featherfans, tasselled dancecards, powdered with musk, a gaud of amber beads in her locked drawer. A birdcage hung in the sunny window of her house when she was a girl.
notes.html_source:
Stephen is remembering his mother as a young girl, long before he was born, with her stereotypical fascinations common with little girls.
Her past is a secret she has left behind now.

This perspective induces him to imagine her life without him, before the insurmountable task of motherhood, one which inevitably makes a person accountable for another human being, was bestowed upon her. Stephen is most probably using anecdotes to get a more vivid picture of his mother in her independent days, something more tangible to relate to without prejudiced compassion.

notes.html_source:
The Pantomime of Turko the Terrible was a popular Christmas pantomime (a form of musical comedy), first of the famous Gaiety pantomimes that have been performed at the Gaiety Theatre in Dublin since the 1870s. It was described as follows in an article in The Irish Playgoer in 1899:

It was at Christmas 1873 that the first pantomime was tried at the Gaiety and the famous Turko the Terrible–a pantomime never excelled in Dublin–was the work selected. Mr. Edwin Hamilton was accountable for the words of the songs and the one sung by King Turko in the throne room while anticipating the delights to be derived from his magic rose, where he thinks, ‘Invisibility is just the thing for me,/I am the boy that can enjoy/Invisibility’ was the most successful in the whole book. Mr. E. W. Royce enacted the title role as only his lively self at that time could."

notes.title: Ghoul! Chewer of corpses!
notes.html_source:
The word “ghoul” comes from Arabian mythology (Arabic: غُول, or ghūl) where it is a demon or monster that does precisely what Stephen says: eats corpses. It often takes the forms of animals, especially the hyena, or the form of the dead person whose body it ate last. Arabian ghoul imagery reappears a few times in chapter 15, “Circe”: a dog eats the remains of Paddy Dignam (whose funeral we saw in chapter 6, “Hades”) and takes the form of his partially “ghouleaten” body; then later Stephen has a vision of his mother rising from the grave, which he once again declares is “The ghoul!”, “The corpsechewer!” and “Hyena!”

The concept of the Ghoul was introduced to western culture via translations of One Thousand and One Nights (aka “Arabian Nights”), which are alluded to many times throughout Ulysses.

notes.title: Druidy druids
notes.html_source: Druids were the priesthood in the pre-Christian pagan religion of Celtic Ireland and Britain. They are referred to several times in the book, usually by Mulligan, as a byword for traditional Gaelic culture which at the time was in the process of being reconstructed by proponents of the Celtic Revival such as W.B. Yeats. This movement believed that a return to Gaelic pagan traditions could be used to inspire pride in indigenous Irish culture, and thus help the cause of Irish independence. However very little of the Druids' beliefs can be known for certain since they left no written records, but their legacy remains in physical artifacts, most famously Stonehenge in England. Buck Mulligan seems skeptical of the Celtic Revival, later in the chapter characterizing the movement’s books as “ten pages of notes about the folk and the fishgods of Dundrum”.

notes.title: Warm sunshine merrying over the sea
notes.html_source:
Joyce inserted many parallels between Stephen’s first three chapters and Bloom’s first three. One of them is meteorological. The sunlight that greets Stephen on the first page of Telemachus greets Bloom when he leaves his home in pursuit of meat, and several pages later both men experience a cloud obscuring the sun—an adumbration of the dramatic thunderstorm that will visit Dublin later in the day. The eclipse is only brief, and with the return of the sun the mood of both men brightens.

Nearly seven pages into Telemachus, “A cloud began to cover the sun slowly, shadowing the bay behind him in deeper green.” A little more than six pages into Calypso, “A cloud began to cover the sun, slowly, wholly. Grey. Far.” Given the distance between the two men (between five and ten miles), they cannot be seeing the same eclipse at precisely the same instant. But given the close locations of these passages in each episode, it seems likely that they are seeing the same eclipse. The sense of simultaneity is reinforced by what happens next. Some forty lines after a cloud begins to obscure the sun in Telemachus, Stephen “heard warm running sunlight” on the morning air. Some twenty-five lines after the cloud begins to cover the sun in Calypso, “Quick warm sunlight came running from Berkeley Road, swiftly in slim sandals, along the brightening footpath” to greet Bloom. In both cases, the sun’s reappearance coincides with a move away from depressing thoughts.

notes.title: Paris fads
notes.html_source: As we learn about more in chapter 3, “Proteus”, Stephen moved to Paris after his undergraduate studies. Joyce’s previous novel, A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man, ends with Stephen Dedalus dramatically announcing his move to Paris, hoping to find a world of spiritual and artistic freedom there he felt absent in Ireland. In Ulysses we learn Stephen, like Joyce in real life, only lived in Paris a short while before returning to Ireland when his mother was dying. Stephen found his life and his accomplishments in Paris very disappointing, but his thoughts frequently return to it throughout Ulysses. Mulligan here insinuates that drinking tea without milk, in the French style, is a habit Stephen picked up in Paris.

notes.title: The blessings of God on you! Buck Mulligan cried, jumping up from his chair.
notes.html_source:
Throughout this chapter, one may observe Mulligan often using such expressions as, “The blessings of God on you”, or another with “a miracle!” He also displays his fluency in Catholic matters, through such instances as “In nomina Patris et Spiritus Sancti”, or “Lead him not into temptation, which may also lead one to believe that he is aware of the fourth commandment—which states that “thou shalt not take the Lord thy God in vain"—though he proceeds to bestow "the blessings of God” to a woman bringing milk for his beverage.

Mulligan does, however, display a great deal of enthusiasm to the milk’s arrival, “jumping from his chair”, but might easily be perceived as quite the blasphemer by the Holy Roman Catholic and Apostolic Church from the nature of many of his expressions.

He also displays his capacity to societal indifference, with one instance being his noting Stephen’s mother’s death, “ O, it’s only Dedalus whose mother is beastly dead”, and his reaction to Stephen bringing that point up, “A flush which made him seem younger and more engaging rose to Buck Mulligan’s cheek”, from which he proceeds to rebuke Stephen for his prolonged grieving. This indifference is seen elsewhere in Mulligan’s manner.

Can you recall, brother, is mother Grogan’s tea and water pot spoken of in the Mabinogion or is it in the Upanishads?
 
 —I doubt it, said Stephen gravely.
 
 —Do you now? Buck Mulligan said in the same tone. Your reasons, pray?
 
 —I fancy, Stephen said as he ate, it did not exist in or out of the Mabinogion. Mother Grogan was, one imagines, a kinswoman of Mary Ann.
notes.html_source:
The Mabinogion is a collection of ancient folklore and considered the earliest prose literature in Britain. While it contains many celtic legends, it is entirely a Welsh rather than Irish text. As well, the Upanishads are a collection of ancient Vedic religious text that contain early theologic concepts of Hinduism. In placing a contemporary Irish character in these texts (Mother Grogan), Mulligan effectively gives Haines the impression that these texts unrelated to Ireland are entirely important and interconnected to the culture, and not regarded with esteem only by theosophists like William Butler Yeats, a prominent Irish poet of the Revivalist movement, whom he mocks earlier.

Furthermore, in recognizing these two texts, one being Britain’s leading colony at the time (India) and the other a nation incorporated into Britain (Wales), Mulligan mocks Haines rather pointedly.

Stephen, however, ends Mulligan’s charade with his own cheeky reply by mentioning that Mother Grogan is related to Mary Ann, a character in another contemporary Irish song.

notes.html_source:
This is adapted from “The Song of the Cheerful (but slightly Sarcastic) Jesus” by Oliver St. John Gogarty, who was the inspiration for the character Buck Mulligan. Here is the full version:

I’m the queerest young fellow that ever was heard.
My mother’s a Jew; my father’s a Bird
With Joseph the Joiner I cannot agree
So ‘Here’s to Disciples and Calvary.’

If anyone thinks that I amn’t divine,
He gets no free drinks when I’m making the wine
But have to drink water and wish it were plain
That I make when the wine becomes water again.

My methods are new and are causing surprise:
To make the blind see I throw dust in their eyes
To signify merely there must be a cod
If the Commons will enter the Kingdom of God

Now you know I don’t swim and you know I don’t skate
I came down to the ferry one day and was late.
So I walked on the water and all cried, in faith!
For a Jewman it’s better than having to bathe.

Whenever I enter in triumph and pass
You will find that my triumph is due to an ass
(And public support is a grand sinecure
When you once get the public to pity the poor.)

Then give up your cabin and ask them for bread
And they’ll give you a stone habitation instead
With fine grounds to walk in and raincoat to wear
And the Sheep will be naked before you’ll go bare.

The more men are wretched the more you will rule
But thunder out ‘Sinner’ to each bloody fool;
For the Kingdom of God (that’s within you) begins
When you once make a fellow acknowledge he sins.

Rebellion anticipates timely by ‘Hope,’
And stories of Judas and Peter the Pope
And you’ll find that you’ll never be left in the lurch
By children of Sorrows and Mother the Church

Goodbye, now, goodbye, you are sure to be fed
You will come on My Grave when I rise from the Dead
What’s bred in the bone cannot fail me to fly
And Olivet’s breezy—Goodbye now Goodbye.

notes.title:
—If anyone thinks that I amn’t divine
 He’ll get no free drinks when I’m making the wine
 But have to drink water and wish it were plain
 That I make when the wine becomes water again.
notes.html_source:
In the opening verses of John 2, Jesus turns water into wine for a wedding feast in Cana—the first of his many miracles, and the most Irish of the lot. Mulligan’s Joking Jesus unhospitably demands faith as the price of admission to such alcoholic miracles: those who think “that I amn’t divine” will “get no free drinks.”

In addition to threatening nonbelievers with the pains of sobriety, Joking Jesus rather fantastically condemns them, by a pun that has Mulligan has already put into the mouth of Mother Grogan, to drink urine. They will “have to drink water,” but since to “make water” is to urinate and since Jesus seems to be making all the drinks in the place, the water they drink will be the stuff “That i make when the wine becomes water again.” They may “wish it were plain"—i.e., Guinness' stout, as in the Irish phrase "a pint of plain"—but this water is done with being miraculously converted.

notes.title: Photius and the brood of mockers of whom Mulligan was one, and Arius, warring his life long upon the consubstantiality of the Son with the Father, and Valentine, spurning Christ’s terrene body, and the subtle African heresiarch Sabellius who held that the Father was Himself His own Son.
notes.html_source:
A list of early heretics.

Photius, while not a heretic in the usual sense, was deposed by the Fourth [Roman Catholic] Council of Constantinople (869-870) from his position as Patriarch of Constantinople, the head of the Eastern (today, Eastern Orthodox) Church. This was in part because he was a layman when he was appointed to the Patriarchate. This was the first council that was not recognized by both East and West, and an early indicator of the approaching 1054 schism.

Arius (256-336) believed that Jesus Christ was not of the same essence of God, and was only the first creation of the Father. His promulgation of this teaching was the impetus for the calling of the Council of Nicaea in 325, the very first ecumenical council.

Valentine, more commonly called Valentinus, lived from c.100-c.160, and was a Christian gnostic theologian who believed that the material world was evil, and to some extent denied the incarnation of Christ.

Sabellius (3rd century) was a Christian priest who taught that God was not three persons, but three manifestations of the same person.

Arius, Valentinus, and Sabellius all held anti-Trinitarian views that were rejected and condemned by orthodox Christianity.

notes.title: The Ship, Buck Mulligan cried. Half twelve.
notes.html_source:
Telemachus ships out of Ithaca at the end of Book 2 of The Odyssey, to inquire about his father on the mainland. On his return at the end of Book 4, Antinous and nineteen other suitors lie in ambush for him behind an island that he must pass. Athena helps him to escape the deadly trap.

Similarly, Stephen will evade his antagonist. Instead of meeting Mulligan at “The Ship,” the downtown tavern that has figured in their conversation earlier in their chapter, at the appointed time of “Half twelve” (i.e., 12:30), he sends him a taunting telegram from only a short distance away. We learn of this development in Scylla and Charybdis, when Mulligan finds Stephen in the library (Stephen thinks, “Hast thou found me, O mine enemy?”). Mulligan reads the telegram with delight, and asks, “Where did you launch it from?”

notes.title:
Liliata rutilantium.
 Turma circumdet.
 Iubilantium te virginum
notes.html_source:
Liliata rutilantium te confessorum turma circumdet: iubilantium te virginum chorus excipiat, translates as:

May the troop of confessors, glowing like lilies, surround you. May the choir of virgins, jubilant, take you in.

The source of these words is in the Prayers for the Dying in the Catholic Layman’s Missal.

The Missal contains instructions on the acceptable use of the prayer: “In the absence of a priest, these prayers for commending a dying person to God, may be read by any responsible person, man or woman.” The prayer was chanted, then, by one or more of the family members who “prayed on their knees” while gathered around the bedside of Stephen’s dying mother, as Stephen recalls in Telemachus the first time he thinks of the Latin lines. Stephen continues to recall snatches of the two sentences during the rest of his day: once more in Telemachus, once in Aeolus, once in Circe, and once in Ithaca.

notes.title: Usurper.
notes.html_source:
From the Joyce Project:

Telemachus begins with “Stately, plump Buck Mulligan” seen through third-person narration that approaches his own subjective position, though the narrative voice is quickly pulled into the orbit of the lean and hungry Stephen. The episode ends with the same person seen entirely through Stephen’s eyes, as a “Usurper” similar to Claudius and Antinous.

Mulligan cooperates in this coercive casting by taking the key to the tower from Stephen, which Stephen regards as usurpation because he “paid the rent.“ In a less literal sense, Stephen may feel usurped because Mulligan would insinuate himself into a position of authority in his life—a life whose credo is evading subjection. In Circe, as Stephen approaches the climax of desperation signaled by his mother’s ghoulish appearance from the dead, he cries out against his "foes,” one in particular: “Break my spirit, will he?” The “he” remains unspecified, but no one is more likely than Buck.

notes.title: Fabled by the daughters of memory. And yet it was in some way if not as memory fabled it. A phrase, then, of impatience, thud of Blake’s wings of excess. I hear the ruin of all space, shattered glass and toppling masonry, and time one livid final flame. What’s left us then?
notes.html_source:
Discouraged by the story of Pyrrhus and by history in general, Stephen thinks of the apocalyptic alternatives to empirical knowledge proposed by the visionary English poet William Blake (1757-1827). The scholars Don Gifford and Robert Seidman trace “Fabled by the daughters of memory,” “Blake’s wings of excess,” and “the ruin of all space … and time one livid final flame” to particular passages in Blake’s writings.

The second plate of A Vision of the Last Judgment distinguishes “Fable or Allegory,” produced by the daughters of Memory (i.e. the nine Muses descended from Mnemosyne), from “Imagination,” produced by the daughters of Inspiration. Empirical understanding—knowledge based on memory—is a mere “Fable” in Blake’s estimation, while imagination yields what he calls “Vision.”

This anti-commonsense assertion appeals to Stephen because it would define all history as essentially false, but the Aristotelian empiricist in him quickly counters, “And yet it was in some way if not as memory fabled it.” The world is more than the mind’s conception of it; actual things happened to produce the reality that now enslaves us. As Stephen thinks a few paragraphs later, “They are not to be thought away. Time has branded them and fettered they are lodged in the room of the infinite possibilities they have ousted.”

“A phrase, then, of impatience,” Stephen thinks. One of the devils' Proverbs in The Marriage of Heaven and Hell holds that “The road of excess leads to the palace of wisdom,” and another one that “No bird soars too high, if he soars with his own wings.” Blake has characteristically overshot the mark, Stephen thinks, and his “wings of excess” strike the ear with (or fall to earth with?) a “Thud.”

But Stephen is enchanted by the language of apocalyptic transcendence, and will remain so throughout the novel. Blake also writes in The Marriage of Heaven and Hell that “The ancient tradition that the world will be consumed in fire at the end of six thousand years is true, as I have heard from Hell.” And when that fiery consummation occurs, “the whole creation will be consumed and appear infinite and holy, whereas it now appears finite & corrupt.” Stirred by this vision, Stephen thinks of “the ruin of all space” and the fiery annihilation of time.

Joyce Project

notes.title: The end of Pyrrhus?
notes.html_source:
After Asculum, Pyrrhus continued to barnstorm around the Mediterranean world, which was in a limbo of small-state anarchy with rivalries and lost causes enough for all the ambitious.

His “end” came in 272 BC: Pyrrhus had undertaken to assist one of the leading citizens of Argos in a town feud. His opponent was Antigonus II of Macedon. Pyrrhus was trapped inside the town; when he attempted to slip out, he was caught up in a street fight and was about to kill one of his assailants when the assailant’s mother threw a tile from a roof. Pyrrhus was stunned, thrown from his horse, and killed by one of Antigonus’s henchmen.

notes.title: Armstrong
notes.html_source:
The significance of this name is not known (Gifford & Seidman, p30). That readers and critics would delve so deep to ascertain its relevance illustrates the reader response to Ulysses.

Ulysses‘ Homeric parallels imply there are no actual Homeric figures and “although Ulysses contains a wealth of detail concerning Dublin and people’s lives there, the novel is hardly a realistic work of fiction; indeed, rather than creating "the illusion of reality,” these details become a sort of end in themselves, such as one finds in the art-form of the collage.“ (Ross C Murfin in A Companion to James Joyce’s Ulysses referring to the work of Wolfgang Iser).

Murfin adds how we look outward for Homeric parallels as well as inward to our own personal experiences. Merging the two is the task of the reader of Ulysses.

notes.title: Ghoststory
notes.html_source:
Stephen replies to the boys' clamoring for “a story, sir… . A ghoststory” by saying “After” (i.e., when the lesson is completed). He never gives them the story, but the riddle that he tells them instead does release a bit of the terrible emotional energy that he connects with ghosts.

In Telemachus Stephen recalls (twice) that he was visited “in a dream” by the ghost of his dead mother, and her specter will return to terrify him at a climactic moment in Circe. He gives the boys a miniscule window onto his terror by posing an unanswerable riddle and then, “his throat itching,” supplying the answer: “The fox burying his grandmother under a hollybush.” Gifford and Seidman note that the model for his riddle can be found in P. W. Joyce’s English as We Speak It in Ireland, where the answer to a very similar obscure riddle is “The fox burying his mother under a holly tree.” The riddle clearly functions as an expression of the guilt that Stephen feels about having “killed” his mother, though he masks it slightly by changing her into a grandmother. Later in Nestor he thinks guiltily of himself as a killer: “A poor soul gone to heaven: and on a heath beneath winking stars a fox, red reek of rapine in his fur, with merciless bright eyes scraped in the earth, listened, scraped up the earth, listened, scraped and scraped.”

Eventually, Stephen will tell “A ghoststory,” but not to the boys. In Scylla and Charybdis his talk on Shakespeare centers on the figure of Hamlet’s father’s ghost: “He will have it that Hamlet is a ghoststory … Like the fat boy in Pickwick he wants to make our flesh creep.

notes.title:
Weep no more, woful shepherds, weep no more
 For Lycidas, your sorrow, is not dead,
 Sunk though he be beneath the watery floor...
notes.html_source:
Negligently “opening another book,” Stephen moves on to whatever lesson may be next. It is the pastoral elegy Lycidas (1638), in which John Milton urges his Cambridge peers not to bemoan the drowning of their classmate Edward King: “Weep no more, woful shepherds, weep no more / For Lycidas, your sorrow, is not dead, / Sunk though he be beneath the watery floor.” King is not dead because he has been saved “Through the dear might of Him that walked the waves”: Jesus Christ, who walked on the waters in Matthew 14:29 to save his fisherman disciples.

As Talbot goes on reading Stephen veers into his own thoughts, just as he did while putting the boys through their Pyrrhus paces. The subject of his meditation now is Christ : “Here also over these craven hearts his shadow lies and on the scoffer’s heart and lips and on mine. It lies upon their eager faces who offered him a coin of the tribute… . A long look from dark eyes.” Christ’s dark eyes return a bit later in the persons of two non-Christian philosophers: “Averroes and Moses Maimonides, dark men in mien and movement, flashing in their mocking mirrors the obscure soul of the world, a darkness shining in brightness which brightness could not comprehend.” The three wise men occupy a metaphysical darkness, invisible within the bustling world of craven hearts and eager faces. As with Pyrrhus, then, Stephen continues to look for the Spirit within the seemingly mindless futility of everyday reality.

The passage from Lycidas also offers another drowning victim to complement the two mentioned in Telemachus: one who was saved by Mulligan, and a second who has been dead for nine days and is expected to surface soon.

Joyce Project

notes.title: It must be a movement then, an actuality of the possible as possible.
notes.html_source:
Moving on from Blake, Stephen thinks of a different model for relating tyrannically stubborn facts to intellectually liberating insights. Aristotle’s Metaphysics describes coming-into-being as passage from a state of potentiality (dynamis) to a state of actuality (energeia). Stephen rather loosely reads this argument as implying that, in any moment, there are “infinite possibilities” that might become actual. Only one possibility does become actual, so the others are “ousted.”

In the following two sentences, he checks himself. Perhaps other possibilities are not infinite; perhaps, in fact, “only” that which becomes actual ever was possible. This line of thought seems closer to what Aristotle says in the Metaphysics, but it is even more discouraging than thinking of unpleasant actualities “ousting” better ones. It would make history one long deterministic process of unrolling a script that has already been (all but) written.

After an unfortunate interruption caused by the need to speak with his pupils (Stephen is not much of a teacher), he returns to his silent Aristotelian interrogation of history: “It must be a movement, then, an actuality of the possible as possible.” The allusion here, Gifford and Seidman observe, is to Aristotle’s Physics: “The fulfillment [completion or actuality, entelecheia, a near-synonym of energeia] of what exists potentially [dynamis], in so far as it exists potentially, is motion [kinesis].”

Joyce Project

notes.title: Thought is the thought of thought. Tranquil brightness. The soul is in a manner all that is: the soul is the form of forms. Tranquility sudden, vast, candescent: form of forms.
notes.html_source:
Stephen has been thinking of “my mind’s darkness” as something hidden, “reluctant, shy of brightness.” Now, inspired perhaps by the “glowlamps” within the cavernous gloom of the St. Geneviève reading room, he thinks of the mind or soul instead as calm, capacious irradiation: “Tranquil brightness … Tranquility sudden, vast, candescent.” The abstract phrases that are woven through these vivid images of light—"Thought is the thought of thought… . The soul is in a manner all that is: the soul is the form of forms"—indicate that he is still thinking of Aristotle, but now turning his attention to what the philosopher has to say about the mind. In one important passage, Aristotle uses light as a metaphor for an aspect of Mind that is eternally active and perfectly capacious. In human beings, this active mindfulness is one part of the complex process of intellection. In God, it is the entirety of being.

notes.title: Riddling
notes.html_source:
The use of riddles here might be seen in the light of Aristotle’s appreciation of them. In Rhetoric, Book III, Chapter 2, he writes:

Good riddles do, in general, provide us with satisfactory metaphors: for metaphors imply riddles, and therefore a good riddle can furnish a good metaphor. Further, the materials of metaphors must be beautiful; and the beauty, like the ugliness, of all words may, as Licymnius says, lie in their sound or in their meaning. Further, there is a third consideration – one that upsets the fallacious argument of the sophist Bryson, that there is no such thing as foul language, because in whatever words you put a given thing your meaning is the same. This is untrue.

Deasy has a complete set of 12 apostle spoons:
An apostle spoon is a spoon (usually silver or silver-plated, but sometimes of other metals, such as pewter) with an image of an apostle or other saint as the termination of the handle, each bearing his distinctive emblem. Apostle spoons were particularly popular in Pre-Reformation times when belief in the services of a patron saint was still strong. notes.title: That’s not English. A French Celt said that.
notes.html_source:
From Wikipedia:

The phrase “the empire on which the sun never sets” has been used with variations to describe empires that were so extensive that there was always at least one part of their territory that was in daylight.

It was originally used for the Spanish Empire, mainly in the 16th and 17th centuries, and for the British Empire, mainly in the 19th and early 20th centuries.

Joyce scholars consider this one of Deasy’s mistakes; Hugh B. Staples tentatively proposed that Deasy meant Charles V as the “French Celt”, through either a simple blunder or an eccentric racial theory.

Staples, Hugh B. (Winter 1981). “Mr. Deasy and the "French Celt”“. James Joyce Quarterly (University of Tulsa) 18 (2): 199–201.

notes.title: Princely presence
notes.html_source:
Presumably referring to the portrait of Albert Edward, a horse fan. But further, the owners of the horses are princes of a sort, and there is Deasy meaning Nestor, who was a charioteer, so its highly appropriate that Deasy should have pictures of horses.

Take this section from the Iliad, showing Nestor’s involvement with horses:

“Nestor knight of Gerene hearkened to his words. Thereon the doughty squires, Sthenelus and kind-hearted Eurymedon, saw to Nestor’s horses, while the two both mounted Diomed’s chariot. Nestor took the reins in his hands and lashed the horses on; they were soon close up with Hector, and the son of Tydeus aimed a spear at him as he was charging full speed towards them. He missed him, but struck his charioteer and squire Eniopeus son of noble Thebaeus in the breast by the nipple while the reins were in his hands, so that he died there and then, and the horses swerved as he fell headlong from the chariot. Hector was greatly grieved at the loss of his charioteer, but let him lie for all his sorrow, while he went in quest of another driver; nor did his steeds have to go long without one, for he presently found brave Archeptolemus the son of Iphitus, and made him get up behind the horses, giving the reins into his hand.” From here

The Foot-and-mouth disease affected many animals involved in farming.

notes.title:
For Ulster will fight
 And Ulster will be right.
notes.html_source:
23 February 1886: Lord Randolph Churchill spoke at a meeting in Belfast in which he uttered the phrase ‘Ulster will fight and Ulster will be right.’

Lord Churchill was anxious to undermine the rapport that had developed between the Liberal Party under William Gladstone and the Irish Parliamentary Party under Charles Stewart Parnell. The Liberals had won the General Election the previous year but had not secured an overall majority. They then relied on Parnell to secure their hold on the House of Commons. The price for such support was Gladstone committing himself to bring forward a Bill for Home Rule for Ireland in the current session of Parliament.

Churchill was fundamentally opposed to Home Rule and planned to use his name in Ulster to give heart to those within the ranks of the Orange Order that were prepared to resist by any means the bringing in of such a measure. He had written to a friend some days previously what his plan was:

I decided some time ago that if the G.O.M.* went for Home Rule, the Orange card would be the one to play. Please God it may turn out to be the ace of trumps and not the two.

  • Grand Old Man – Mr Gladstone

The revitalised Orange Order had sponsored meetings for all who were against Home Rule. It arranged the meeting in the Ulster Hall at which the main speaker was to be Lord Randolph Churchill himself. He gave, to a wildly enthusiastic audience, a slogan that was to become their rallying cry in the years ahead:

Ulster will fight and Ulster will be right

Thus began the close association between the Conservative Party and the Unionists in Ireland that was to such a feature of Anglo-Irish relations for decades to come.
