notes.title: Because she never let them in
notes.html_source:
The history of the Jews in Ireland extends back nearly a thousand years. Although the Jewish community has always been small in numbers (not exceeding 5,500 by religion since at least 1891), it is well established and has generally been well-accepted into Irish life. Jews in Ireland have historically enjoyed a relative tolerance that was largely absent elsewhere in Europe.

There was an increase in Jewish immigration to Ireland during the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. In 1871, the Jewish population of Ireland was 258; by 1881, it had risen to 453. Most of the immigration up to this time had come from England or Germany. A group who settled in Waterford were Welsh, whose families originally came from Central Europe. In the wake of the Russian pogroms there was increased immigration, mostly from Eastern Europe (in particular Lithuania). By 1901, there were an estimated 3,771 Jews in Ireland, over half of them (2,200) residing in Dublin. By 1904, the total Jewish population had reached an estimated 4,800.

notes.title: Ineluctable modality of the visible:
notes.html_source:
The inescapable nature of what we can see.

The exact phrase has not been located, but it probably comes from Joyce’s translation of the French Aristotle. Each sense perceives particularly by means of the sensible qualities of the bodies perceived: hearing through sound, taste through savor, smell through odor, touch through weight, temperature, hardness/softness. Sight (in concert with the mind) perceives through color, which lies at the boundary of determined bodies. Stephen is contemplating (through Aristotle) the inescapability of the material world–in particular that aspect of it which is perceptible through the sense of sight.

notes.title: At least that
notes.html_source: At the beginning of Ulysses, Haines had suggested “Hamlet” was, by a theological reading, about the Son striving to be atoned with the Father (18). The suggestion has been applied to Ulysses (along with various others) in a more or less secular way, that the novel is about Stephen Dedalus meeting Leopold Bloom who is in need of a son in much the same way Stephen is in need of a father– and it is, it all very neatly corresponds to the Homeric frame. In Proteus, one can see a second thread which can be understood more broadly as a purpose of the novel, that the male consciousness is moving toward mother consciousness. Stephen’s desire for the mother is based in his need as a male, and especially as an artist, of anima or what has been called mother consciousness. A problem is that he continuously encounters the death-mother.

A neologism that echoes Stephen’s obsession with sex as he sees what the sea has washed up as its ‘spawn’.

Possibly a reference to Aphrodite. who was supposed to have been born from the ‘sea-foam’. The Bishop of Berkeley was an immaterialist/ subjective idealist. He believed material mass and objects only exist because of the minds which perceive them. An early theory on light expressed this philosophy.

I am reminded of the film ‘Being There’ with Peter Sellers where he becomes the attache of prominent men by adhering strictly to his limitations as they fawn on his oversimplified understanding of the natural world. notes.title: But he adds: in bodies. Then he was aware of them bodies before of them coloured
notes.html_source:
If Ulysses is about anything, it is the interaction of our thoughts with others to reveal the self. Stephen is a ‘very short space of time’ from the Tower where he was harangued by the gruff Mulligan. His friend Buck poked fun at him and using the sharpest sword in a bully’s armoury spread bizarre gossip about the most sensitive of topics – ‘the aunt thinks you killed your mother’.

It is no surprise that Stephen decides not to return to Buck Mulligan in the Tower after Buck assumes it’s ok to hold this mirror up to Stephen. You might think it’s ok to stick to your principles and not pray over your mother’s corpse but look at what the community thinks of you !

Why then is Stephen engaging in thought exercises on competing theories of light when he has nowhere to sleep that night ? The truth is we don’t know. The belligerent reader will know the ‘what’ of the introduction to Proteus (Aristotle/Locke/Berkeley) and also the ‘how’ (free association of thought via interior monologue) but no idea why!

PROPOSED SUGGESTION: errrrrrr what.

Sorry, I’ll put it in more direct terms, Ulysses is a series of happenings rather than a series of actions.

PROPOSED SUGGESTION: Sorry too, my suggestion wasn’t much of a suggestion, and pretty unhelpful. I was just a bit thrown off because this reads as a really interesting and ambitious annotation, but I found it quite difficult to unpack and to get at what its central point was. It seemed to kind of glaze over the actual bit of text under annotation; and the fairly arcane and obfuscated pondering of Aristotle’s and others' theories of light and colour, although you mention them in passing, could have done with a bit more of a direct explanation. And this also mainly discusses Stephen’s thoughts and dealings with Mulligan from the first two chapters, and I’m not sure how this is actually tied to ‘he was aware of them bodies before of them coloured’. There’s no problem with trying to make connections with different parts of the novel, but perhaps it would be a bit more digestible if you explained the ‘theories of light’ at the top, and then how this relates to what has happened between Stephen and Mulligan. For other readers not overly familiar with the novel, the fact that Stephen has decided, at the very end of ‘Telemachus’, not to return that night to the Martello Tower could be pinpointed more exactly, perhaps by an internal hyperlink to this moment (although I see now that nobody has yet annotated this moment).

I am very interested in your assertion that Ulysses is ‘a series of happenings rather than a series of actions’; I would be interested in having that idea mapped a bit more. Do you mean that Ulysses takes place mostly inside the characters' minds (where associations are free, and it’s difficult to pin down why one thought flows into the next), as opposed to orchestrated events that integrate together in an easily discernible plot? Similarly to your point at the top about ‘the interaction of thoughts with others’? (By the way, do you mean ‘with other thoughts’, or with ‘other people’?) Maybe it wouldn’t be a good idea to clog suggestions with fine points of discussion, but I’d like to encourage you to flesh out your observations.

notes.title: How? By knocking his
notes.html_source:
Compare the start of Proteus to a Passage from Pilgrimmage 1 by Dorothy Ricardson, a contemporary of Joyce –

It’s perfectly natural that they should all be excited about the holidays she told herself, stifling her thoughts. But it must not go too far. They wanted to be jolly …. If I could be jolly too they would like me. I must not be a wet blanket…. Mademoiselle’s voice was not heard.

Richardson flags up the interior monologue for us using the punctuation so we are aware of the transition. She has also highlighted where the interior monologue comes from and why she is thinking this using the preceding exterior narrative. Joyce doesn’t do this in Proteus. Whether readers are aware of it or not, they experience Stephen’s displacement using this technique.

notes.title: A very short space of time through very short times of space
notes.html_source:
Joyce isolates this abstract thought from action and the world, by omitting verbs and sandwiching it between both sides of the senses.

The simplicity of the words are transformed into a whole without apparent meaning . It hooks us into Stephen’s mind – we become Stephen as the intrigue stays with us moving onto the next lines.

Joyce has already established Stephen as a hero. (Note that the initial incarnation of Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man was called Stephen Hero – part of whose manuscript Nora Joyce rescued from a fire after James Joyce had thrown it in. This story is considered apocryphal, however.) He calmly dealt with Mulligan’s attempt to destabilise him in ‘Telemachus’. He stood up to Deasy’s anti-Semitic outburst in ‘Nestor’, and attempted to help a pupil who made an idiot of himself in the same chapter. This sentence, along with colloquialisms elsewhere (‘Open your eyes. No. Jesus!.’), endear Stephen to us. We need this attachment to him now, with there being some disquieting thoughts coming up – not to mention the challenge of negotiating Scylla and Charibdis.

notes.title: Audible
notes.html_source:
Stephen associates the audible with nacheinander (things happening in order, one after the other in time). Traditionally, what applies to the audible would apply to written works also. So, we understand a novel by what happens in time (nacheinander). But is that the only way to understand audible works?

Stephen immediately thinks of nebeneinader (things next to each other in space). This is how we understand pictures (paintings, drawings, maps). Can this be presented in a novel also?

notes.title: Beetles o’er his base
notes.html_source:
Quote from Hamlet, spoken by Horatio when warning Hamlet not to follow his father’s ghost in case it tricks him to falling to his doom. ‘Beetle’ is used in the uncommon sense of ‘to overhang’ (collinsdictionary.com)

Stephen has left Deasy in the school in Dalkey to deliver his letter to the editor of The homestead or to meet Mulligan in The Ship. A virgin reader won’t know which he chooses. The veteran reader (terminology coined by Margot Norris) knows there is a great stand off in the national library about Hamlet in a couple of hours. Joyce sets us a little hint as to what happens here. One reference to what Stephen intends to do amidst his wild philosophical musings on the strand indicates his displaced frame of mind that morning.

PROPOSED SUGGESTION: Missing that:
(1) Hamlet is used not merely as an external text which the characters are intrigued with and frequently reference but as a very metaphor for the action, the substance of the novel (You will find Haines himself draws a parallel between the Martello tower and the cliffs of Elsinore early on.)
(2) I agree with the last sentence; however, to continue the reading from this frame I have suggested, this should be considered as an explicit link between Hamlet and Stephen, the ghost of Hamlet’s father and Stephen’s dead mother who appears always smelling of rosewater and wetted ashes.
(3) This sentence and several that follow it, suggest the anxiety of walking blindly (I mean literally, since Stephen does shut his eyes). Readers may want to consider that Joyce was blind– therefore, the modality of sight would be a significant meditation.

PROPOSED SUGGESTION: Spanish translate: Si yo cayera sobre una escollera que se desborda sobre su base, ¡si me cayera a través del nebeneinander ineluctablemente! (Subirat)

But…
I read about this sentences and I don’t understand why to skip the ‘coleoptero’. Several species of dung beetle, especially the “sacred scarab” Scarabaeus sacer, were revered by the ancient Egyptians. The scarab was linked to Khepri, the god of the rising sun, from the supposed resemblance of the dung ball rolled by the beetle to the rolling of the sun by the god.[79] Plutarch wrote:
The race of beetles has no female, but all the males eject their sperm into a round pellet of material which they roll up by pushing it from the opposite side, just as the sun seems to turn the heavens in the direction opposite to its own course, which is from west to east.

(wikipedia)

notes.html_source:
Next to one another, adjacent. Gotthold Lessing observed in a book about the poetry and painting that art can be taken in bit after bit or all together. Poetry – the nacheinander consists of word sequences and painting are the artist’s comments beside each other.

Joyce uses it as another layer on top of Stephen’s observation ‘ thought through my eyes’ to form a metacommentary to the reader.

notes.title: Ineluctably
notes.html_source:
“This episode contains practically no action.Nothing happens, and yet in following the trail of Stephen’s thoughts, as he idles on the Dublin strand, we encounter a diversity of experience as exciting as any tale of adventure in ‘the land of Phenomenon’ (Gilbert, S. James Joyce Ulysses, p109).

Stephen is stuck between the abstract and the body, he can’t stop sensory perception – a conflict elucidated by Marxist critical theory:

“McGee uses the Marxist notion that art mediates between the material and social world on one hand and the realm of the ideal on the other to explain that Joyce’s Ulysses mediates "between bodily social existence and aesthetic form” by disclosing the reltionship between the two. The body is explored or even rediscovered through linguistic mediation; conversely, language is shown to be invested with the imaginary value of bodily sensation" (Murfin. A companion to James Joyce Ulysses, ed. M Norris, p215).

notes.title: Boots are at the ends of his legs, nebeneinander
notes.html_source: Mulligan and Stephen have conjoined as Blake and Milton did in Blake’s poem Milton. Joyce’s meaning lies not in Proteus but in Blake. Blake suggested he could transcend the ties which bind literature by extending the nacheinander form into his visionary creations, accessing the nebeneinander. Stephen’s feet, in borrowed tatty shoes joining with Mulligan’s legs as a launchpad to the eternal is pushing it a bit. Joyce mocks literature and reveals Stephen isn’t completely up himself to further our understanding of his plight.

It has been suggested that these lines reference Madeleine Lemaire, a French painter famous for portraits and flowers.

The sea also seams to represent a motherly figure. Further reinforcing the themes of the book. Mother Mary, the sea.

Also, mare might well be connected to nightmare. This builds on the dreams Daedalus has of his own deceased mother.

notes.title: Algy

Algernon Charles Swinburne (1837-1909) was an avant-garde poet and appears to be admired by Mulligan and maybe Stephen as well. In Chapter 1 – Telemachus, Mulligan quotes from two of Swinburne’s poems.

notes.title: Will you be as gods? Gaze in your omphalos. Hello! Kinch here. Put me on to Edenville.
notes.html_source:
This line shifts greatly in language, but has a consistent theme, that of Dedalus' navel, and its relation to his birth and his own psyche. Let’s take this piece by piece:

Will you be as gods?

is in reference to Genesis 3:5,

For God doth know that in the day ye eat thereof, then your eyes shall be opened, and ye shall be as gods, knowing good and evil.

relating to Adam and Eve. Then,

Gaze in your omphalos

Omphalos = navel, there was a major conflict in theology over the ages over Adam and Eve’s navels (also known as the Omphalos hypothesis), and whether they should be there or not, and this in turn connects with the sudden shift in tone, from Biblical high style, to that of a conversation between a telephone operator and a caller,

Hello! Kinch here. Put me on to Edenville.

which in turn connects with the Adam and Eve references in the previous sentences.

Whew!

notes.title: Adam Kadmon
notes.html_source:
Adam Kadmon is the Qabalistic name for Adam, the first man on earth, according the Christian theology, and is the sort of “primordial soup” of souls that are molded according to YHWH’s will. This finds its parallel within Ulysses, with all the talk of the transmigration of souls in the fourth chapter, (the “metempsychosis” conversation).

The concept of Adam Kadmon is used in another impenetrable work, the anime Neon Genesis Evangelion, and even though it is called “Human Instrumentality” in that show, it’s similarly a massive pool of souls waiting to be shaped.

This concept connects with the “Proteus” theme of the chapter: Proteus was a shapeshifting god with no real form.

notes.title: Contransmagnificandjewbangtantiality
notes.html_source:
http://www.jjon.org/joyce-s-words/c

PROPOSED SUGGESTION: The “-tantiality” is just a suffix for “con-” and “trans-”. The “con-” refers to consubstantiation, the belief in Catholic theology that the father, the son and the holy spirit are all of the same substance but each presents in a different form. The “-trans-” refers to transubstantiation, the belief in Catholic theology that during communion the bread and wine literally become the body and blood of christ; the mundane is transformed into the divine. These two first parts of the word indicate that the word has to do with the intersection between the divine (god) and the mundane (humanity), or christ. The “magnific” refers to the magnificent, the divine. The “-and-” simply refers to the word “and” and the “-jew-” refers to a Jew, specifically Mary. The “-bang-” is where things get tricky and we see a bit of Joyce’s (slightly blasphemous) humour: in one sense, “-bang-” refers to a collision between the divine and Mary (christ). It also refers to sex; Mary is impregnated by the divine and out of this tryst christ is born. Joyce intentionally juxtaposes sexuality and the virgin because he both believes that all human activities are beautiful and deserve to be represented in literature and because, in order for christ to have a human mother and a divine father, he must have blood from both.

notes.title: Omophorion
notes.html_source:
“Omophorion” is the Greek word for a cape-like garment worn by the bishop of the orthodox church on his shoulders (omos=shoulder, phero=bear, therefore omophorion=borne on the shoulders).

It is usually made of sheep’s wool in reference to the parable of the good shepherd that held the sheep on his shoulders to save it. It ties in with the “mitre” and “crozier” mentioned in the same sentence which are also parts of the bishop’s attire.

This refers to Oscar Wilde’s poem, Requiescat:

TREAD lightly, she is near
Under the snow,
Speak gently, she can hear
The daisies grow. //
All her bright golden hair
Tarnished with rust,
She that was young and fair
Fallen to dust. //
Lily-like, white as snow,
She hardly knew
She was a woman, so
Sweetly she grew. //
Coffin-board, heavy stone,
Lie on her breast,
I vex my heart alone,
She is at rest. //
Peace, peace, she cannot hear
Lyre or sonnet,
All my life’s buried here,
Heap earth upon it.

notes.title: Reading two pages apiece of seven books every night, eh?
notes.html_source:
Stephen steps into the universe of Sandymount Strand and bounds between different thought strands. As Ulysses can be seen as a series of happenings so can Stephen’s thoughts here however there is a pattern.

He tries an experiment (Joyce invents Experimental Philosophy).
He sees two women and explores birth, his birth, all births in the background of grieving for his mother.

He rebounds from this, with a memory of his family, not the close family link of his mother but extended family with quirky aunts and uncles.

Then explores himself, his wishes, ambitions, remembers the thoughts the family had about him.

He spirals into introverted questioning of his part in his world.

notes.title: I was young
notes.html_source:
Similar structure to the ‘Cousin Stephen, you will never….’ paragraph. There is a triangulation between the introductory negative thought phrase in both paragraphs, the pause (‘Isle of saints’ and ‘I was young’) and some lighter phrases later on (‘o si, cierto!’ and ‘Ay, very like a whale’).

The triangulation is an effective delivery mechanism to sustain Joyce’s challenge in the stream of consciousness : maintain the apparently random flow of thoughts, break-up the self criticism so Stephen doesn’t appear a maudlin git and develop enough interest in the reader whilst Joyce skims the surface of Stephen’s experiences.

The next sentence skims his narcissistic episode in front of a mirror in Portrait of the Artist.

notes.title: Epiphanies
notes.html_source:
Not religious. Joyce considered an epihany to be an awareness of the special in the mundane: an object, an instance, an interaction and that he had a duty to highlight the nature and types of epiphanies.

“Epiphanies” was also the proposed title for “Dubliners”.

notes.title: Mahamanvantara
notes.html_source: According to the Hindus, Mahamanvantara (Sanskrit) [from maha great + manvantara period of manifestation] is a great cycle of cosmic manifestation and activity, whether of a universe, solar system, or planet. Joyce frequently makes reference to Hindu esoteric words, texts and concepts. The mahamanvantara of a solar system also known as the Life of Brahma, is a period of 311,040,000,000,000 terrestrial years. A mahamanvantara of the earth-chain is a Day of Brahma or a period of seven rounds of the planetary chain. The day after the mahamanvantara is termed the Day-Be-With-Us a similar notion to the Christian Day of Judgment. At this point it is said all individualities are merged into one, each still possessing essential or intrinsic knowledge of itself. Hindus also state that at that time, what to us now is non-conscious or the unconscious, will be absolute consciousness.

notes.title: Pico della Mirandola
notes.html_source: Giovanni Pico della Mirandola (1463–94) is one the best known philosophers of the Renaissance era. Pico was known for his remarkably original, idiosyncratic thought. In fact so esoteric and abstruse were his ideas that they were little studied until many years after they were published. Perhaps Joyce is implying here that his own work, due to its cryptic character might remain somehow obscured until read many, many years later and perhaps like the works of Pico they would still be highly relevant due to dealing with fundamental questions about human existence, life and death. Like Joyce’s, Pico’s work was highly concerned with the spiritual, with the notion of man as a sentient being. Pico believed that men, unlike beasts could change themselves through exercise of free will. Pico believed that when man philosophizes, he ascends the chain of being towards the angels, and communion with God. When he fails to exercise his intellect, he vegetates.

notes.title: He halted. I have passed the way to aunt Sara’s. Am I not going there? Seems not. No-one about. He turned northeast and crossed the firmer sand towards the
notes.html_source:
In plot terms, Stephen is going to the National Library to deliver a letter for Deasy but mainly to deliver his theory on Hamlet to some literary figures. However Stephen doesn’t think about it at all in this chapter. Something else is going on. He has just left the Tower and said to himself that he won’t go back. He is at the time homeless. In this paragraph he indicates that he won’t go to his family (aunt Sara’s). The opportunity to go there leads to confused if not dark thoughts – maze of cunning nets, human shells, dreadful thirst, midden, man’s ashes.

In this paragraph he also shifts from this unsettling part of his life to ‘the firmer sand towards the Pigeon house’. This shift instigates thoughts/memories grounded in his experiences in Paris in which there are some home truths for Stephen but none of the dark words of the preceding paragraphs.

PROPOSED SUGGESTION: I would also add that the dissociation between Stephen’s mind and feet “Am I not going there? Seems not” mirrors the alienation he felt of his lower body described earlier in this chapter.

notes.title: Groatsworth
notes.html_source:
A groatsworth means not much. The groat was a (defunct by 1904) coin with a value of fourpence.

But the term is associated in Stephen’s mind with Shakespeare. He will use it again in his long discursus on Hamlet in the Scylla and Charybdis episode.

The reference is to Greene’s Groatsworth of Wit, a 1592 pamphlet famous for its early (and derogatory) mention of Shakespeare as an “upstart” young author.

This phrase is difficult to interpret.

Accompanied by the blue telegram ,distinctively French and bearing the news of Stephen’s dying mother, they are the travel mementos from Paris; suitably blue, white and red. notes.title: —Mother dying come home father.
notes.html_source: Stephen received this telegram while on an artistic missionary trip to Europe. The power of the death-mother to draw her son from Paris back to Ireland connects her power in depth and breadth to the sea as “our mighty mother.” Since this return trip disrupted Stephen’s budding life as an expat and contradicted his wish not to go back to Ireland, the telegram becomes a symbol of power and resentment. It is also a symbol of guilt for his absence in the wake of his mother’s condition and his denial to serve even at her dying request.

notes.title: Paris
notes.html_source:
Internal narrative again. Joyce echoes phrases from his poem: Giacomo Joyce which features the Italian city of Trieste. Joyce lectured (on Hamlet) there and tutored English lessons to the well todo of Trieste. Giacomo Joyce is overtly autobiographical and written as Portrait of the Artist was being finished (Ellmann, R. James Joyce: Poems and shorter writings, FF). Many, many phrases from Ulysses and Portrait are used, alluded to or morphed in Giacomo. The majority of notes (Ellmann, R. James Joyce: Poems and shorter writings, FF) refer to other works of Joyce – Exiles, Ulysses, Portrait.

It was in Trieste that Joyce changed to creating a subtle and imaginative art (Ellmann, James Joyce) :So he brought, in the person of Ulysses, the bright though unsentamentalized Mediterranean world to somber Dublin.

Joyce abandoned the poem and it only came to light through his brother Stanislaus. It is chronologically and artistically between finishing Portrait of the artist as a young man and Ulysses. (Ellmann, R & Whittier-Ferguson,J James Joyce Poems and Shorter Writings, ff).

notes.title: Colonel Richard Burke
notes.html_source:
Joseph Theobald Casey and colonel Richard Burke were involved with the IRB in England. In September 1867, a policeman was killed during the rescue of two Fenian leaders from a police van in Manchester. The following November, Joseph Casey and Colonel Richard Burke were arrested in London in connection with the Manchester rescue.

Casey and Burke were imprisoned in the high-security Clerkenwell prison, but that didn’t deter would-be rescuers. On 13 December 1867, a barrel of gunpowder was exploded outside the wall of Clerkenwell prison. The enormous explosion shattered the glass in the windows of the prison and destroyed not just the prison wall but also several nearby tenement houses, resulting in the deaths of twelve people and the injury of many more. The prisoners, who had been moved to another part of the prison, didn’t escape and would certainly have been killed had they been near the site of the explosion.

Casey was acquitted at a subsequent trial and moved to Paris where he worked as a typesetter at the New York Herald of Paris, founded by James Gordon Bennett jr in 1877. Casey and Joyce sometimes lunched together at the Restaurant des Deux-Écus, near the Herald’s offices on rue du Louvre. Casey’s wife, from whom he was separated, also lived in Paris as did their son, Patrice, a soldier in the French army. Both Joseph and Patrice Casey often lent Joyce small sums of money during his time in Paris in 1902-03. Joseph Casey died in Paris in 1907.

Casey was the model for the character Kevin Egan with whom Stephen Dedalus associates in Paris in Ulysses. The one-time rebel lives a life of quiet obscurity in Paris, disconnected from his rebel friends and his rebel past, and from his wife and son. Stephen recalls recalls Kevin Egan drinking absinthe and reminiscing about Kilkenny and his rebel exploits

notes.title: Damascened with flyblown faces of the gone
notes.html_source:
From the works of Emile Zola. Described by Don Gifford in ‘Ulysses Annotated: Notes for James Joyce’s Ulysses’:

“Gervaise Macquart, the protagonist of L'assommoir (The Grog Shop or Gin Mill) (1877), lives in what Zola calls the quartier de la Goutte d'Or and, with her husband, declines into derelection, filth, inanition, and finally death as a result of alcoholism. Her daughter Nana (From Nana, 1880) is born and comes of age in the quartier; she is en route to supreme success as a grand cocotte (prostitute) when she meets a premature, and symbolic, death from small pox. The second to the last paragraph of Nana is a particularly vigorous description of the face of Nana’s corpse, devastated by smallpox as though the ‘virus’ with which she had ‘poisoned a people had mounted into her face and rotted it’ (my translation).”

notes.title: Form of forms
notes.html_source:
Aristotle suggested that the Prime Mover, which is the divine or godlike force called the active intellect, acts upon human brains to produce thought in them, and therefore is thought thinking itself.

The soul, which is the form of the body, can take on the form of sensation by processing the sensible forms of external objects. Because objects also have forms, the rational soul can assimilate these forms as well, so that the soul can become all things.

notes.title: Oomb,
notes.html_source:
As Stephen kisses the ghost, the death-mother pulls him back through her womb, through the Earth, and to the darkness of the evening sky. The intensity of the pull back to the mother causes Stephen to lose control to speak rationally and what issues from his mouth is a primal yell that is the “roar of cataractic planets, globed, blazing, roaring wayawayawayawayawayaway.” He has gone so far in to the darkness of the universe that he has felt blinded. When he regains thought, he turns his back to the sun and begins scribbling words, which are likely related to the experience he has just had of the death-mother. Stephen’s controlled experience of blindness at the chapter’s beginning culminates in this experience of mother consciousness which ends in cosmic darkness. Where before he thought of the limits of the diaphane and adiaphane, he has now perceived them through direct perception.
Feeling constrained by limits, he wonders why he may not transcend them. He has found, through the lens of Aristotle, less translucence in his body than he has found darkness. The experience of the death-mother leads Stephen to suggest that darkness is in the soul, which holds all of one’s psychic events, but is most damaged by one’s “sins.” The experience can be read also as Stephen’s union with the mem-aleph which constitutes the primary mother syllable, MA, and has acted as the force of feminine wisdom behind his desire to write the alphabet books.

PROPOSED SUGGESTION: Any further reading on this analysis? I’m interested.

notes.title: Wilde’s love that dare not speak its name.
notes.html_source:
‘Two Loves’ by Lord Alfred Douglas

I fell a-weeping, and I cried, ‘Sweet youth,
Tell me why, sad and sighing, thou dost rove
These pleasent realms? I pray thee speak me sooth
What is thy name?‘ He said, ‘My name is Love.’
Then straight the first did turn himself to me
And cried, ‘He lieth, for his name is Shame,
But I am Love, and I was wont to be
Alone in this fair garden, till he came
Unasked by night; I am true Love, I fill
The hearts of boy and girl with mutual flame.‘
Then sighing, said the other, ‘Have thy will,
I am the love that dare not speak its name.’

Oscar Wilde quoted “The ‘Love that dare not speak its name’ in this century is such a great affection of an elder for a younger man as there was between David and Jonathan… . It is that deep, spiritual affection that is as pure as it is perfect… . There is nothing unnatural about it. It is intellectual, and it repeatedly exists between an elder and a younger man, when the elder man has intellect, and the younger man has all the joy, hope, and glamour of life before him.”

notes.html_source:
In some typical Joyceian free association, Stephen connects the sight of a drowned body being pulled from the sea with Ariel’s song from The Tempest act 1, scene 2:

Full fathom five thy father lies;
Of his bones are coral made;
Those are pearls that were his eyes:
Nothing of him that doth fade
But doth suffer a sea-change
Into something rich and strange.
Sea-nymphs hourly ring his knell

which also describes a death at sea. These same lines were also referenced in the poetic counterpart to this novel, T.S. Eliot’s The Waste-Land,

Here, said she,
Is your card, the drowned Phoenician Sailor.
(Those are pearls that were his eyes. Look!)

as part of a section entitled “Death By Water”

notes.title: God becomes man becomes fish becomes barnacle goose becomes featherbed mountain.
notes.html_source:
Debated; transformations of spirituality.

God becomes man = Jesus

Man becomes fish = Symbol for Christianity

Fish becomes barnacle goose = Taken from the medieval belief that Geese were born from barnacles. Being feathered they eventually take free flight (from Christianity).

Barnacle Goose becomes featherbed mountain = Death, given the rejection of Christianity and hence “eternal” life.

This dark analysis is given a more positive light in the previous annotation, whereby Ariel sings not of God saving Alonso’s soul but of the sea making something beautiful of his drowned body.

notes.title: Be a warm day I fancy. Specially in these black clothes feel it more. Black conducts, reflects, (refracts is it?), the heat.
notes.html_source:
Is this true? Let’s let The Straight Dope take this one away. First of all, it’s white clothing that reflects sunlight–but there’s a catch:

White clothing reflects sunlight, but also reflects internal heat back towards your body, so the net effect under identical conditions is less cooling than if you wore black.

Black clothing actually keeps you cooler, for reasons related to wind speed:

…black clothing absorbs sunlight and the heat radiating from your body, but if it is loose-fitting, and there is wind, the wind convects the heat away faster than it is absorbed.

The full breakdown is here. By the way, refraction of light is something totally different–that’s when light waves change direction due to a change in transmission medium, as from air to water. It’s what causes objects half-in, half-out of water to appear broken or distorted:

Bottom line: Bloom’s a smart guy, but he’s a little off base on this one.

notes.title: Somewhere in the east: early morning: set off at dawn. Travel round in front of the sun, steal a day’s march on him. Keep it up for ever never grow a day older technically.
notes.html_source:
If one sets off from Troy, and attempts to outpace the sun, one must be travelling west, as Ulysses would have initially been on his journey home to Ithaca. We know, of course, that after the big storm that pushed them well off course to the Land of the Lotus Eaters, Ulysses and his men were well to the west of Ithaca. Events then pushed them farther northwest until they arrived at the Land of the Dead (quite possibly Monaco), some 1,100 miles west of home: a great distance even by today’s car and ferry.

Monaco

From there, staying ahead of the sun on his way home wouldn’t make sense – unless the appearance on its headpiece of the sun rising from the northwest behind the Bank of Ireland in the risible attempt at nationalism by the newspaper for which Bloom sold advertising, the Freeman Leader, weren’t astronomically absurd.

In that case, if one were passing, say Thrinacia, home of sun god/cattleman Helios, and had been warned by goddess of magic, Circe, as well as the spirit of blind prophet, Tiresius, to avoid the place, one’s judgment and strength of character might be called into question if he were persuaded to stop there by the nagging of his subordinates, as long as they promised not to bother the cattle. If he hadn’t stopped, and had stayed ahead of the sun, not only would Ulysses have gained a day on the sun, and “never [have grown] a day older technically,” he presumably would have returned to Ithaca seven years younger than he was when he eventually did arrive.

notes.title: Sodachapped hands
notes.html_source:
In Calypso it is clear what Leopold is thinking though not why as opposed to Stephen’s disjointed thoughts in Proteus. Having been privvy to Leopold’s enjoyment of seeing the woman, we now hear his negative thoughts about the reality of his brief fantasy.

Chapped hands and crusted toenails introduce the reader to Bloom’s tendency to weigh things up but don’t go near prepping us for the horrific chain of thoughts which culminate in the shocking regard he has for the female state in four paragraphs time:
‘Dead: an old woman’s: the grey sunken cunt of the
world.’
The contrast between the ordinary, the clear thoughts about Jewish settlements and the negative internal monologue sequence adds to the suspense of the chapter. The reader knows nothing yet of Bloom’s knowledge of Molly’s affair with Boylan, very possibly what has lead to the internal negative narrative.

notes.title:
A cloud began to cover the sun slowly, wholly. Grey. Far.
 
 No, not like that. A barren land, bare waste. Vulcanic lake, the dead sea: no fish, weedless, sunk deep in the earth. No wind could lift those waves, grey metal, poisonous foggy waters. Brimstone they called it raining down: the cities of the plain: Sodom, Gomorrah, Edom. All dead names. A dead sea in a dead land, grey and old. Old now. It bore the oldest, the first race. A bent hag crossed from Cassidy’s, clutching a naggin bottle by the neck. The oldest people. Wandered far away over all the earth, captivity to captivity, multiplying, dying, being born everywhere. It lay there now. Now it could bear no more. Dead: an old woman’s: the grey sunken cunt of the world.
 
 Desolation.
notes.html_source:
Joyce here makes no illusions about Bloom’s religion and about his awareness of the horrors of World War I, and the horrors previously visited upon Jewish people, evoking Sodom and Gomorrah, both consumed by Yahweh’s fire and brimstone, on the edge of the dead sea, and now dead names, uncertain even to have ever existed.

Bloom is reminded of the ancient Jewish people by an elderly woman bent double, clutching a naggin of some spirits, and thinks on the traumas visited upon Jewish people, their births and deaths in captivity, musing on the dual meaning of ‘bear’, that they can suffer no more these traumas, that the elderly, broken woman can bear no more children.

PROPOSED SUGGESTION: I would also mention that this may be a similar time to when Stephen witnesses the same event in Telemachus:

“A cloud began to cover the sun slowly, shadowing the bay behind him in deeper green.”

The event appears to produce a similar effect in the minds of both men, which is then followed by an uplifting feel when the sunlight returns.

notes.title: A strip of torn envelope peeped from under the dimpled pillow. In the act of going he stayed to straighten the bedspread.
notes.html_source: The dialogue here is a kind of pantomime between husband and wife. Bloom knows of Molly’s affair with Boylan. Molly took the letter from Bloom and hid it under her pillow. Bloom sees the letter is open now and asks who it is from, knowing full well it was from Boylan. But before she can say Bloom thinks, “Bold hand. Marion.” “Bold hand” is how Bloom knows the letter is from Boylan. Joyce lets us into Bloom’s thoughts. On the surface Bloom and Molly have a simple conversation but it takes on epic proportions given the rest of the novel. Molly will give her soliloquy at the end of the novel from the bed she’s in here and will think of Bloom at the end as she falls to sleep making him the comic hero after all.

notes.title: Yes, she said. There’s nothing smutty in it. Is she in love with the first fellow all the time?
notes.html_source:
The use of conversational implicature in “Calypso” builds suspense between Poldy and Molly. The incongruous ‘There’s nothing smutty in it’ implies they’ve had a previous conversation or there’s a tension between them about smut! We don’t know what it refers to but know it refers to something, one of many hiatuses in “Calypso”.

PROPOSED SUGGESTION: Isn’t the question of smuttiness just part of Poldy and Molly’s relationship as sexually open and comfortable with each other (to some degree; infidelity is no huge secret between them both, and Poldy is pretty chilled and accepting about Molly’s sexual transgressions, esp. in “Ithaca”)? I don’t think Poldy cares at all whether his wife reads “smut”; I always thought that the reason she tells him there’s no smut is to warn him against wasting his own time reading it. We know that Poldy likes smut, and it seems Molly does too. So when she says, ‘There’s nothing smutty in it’, she’s actually expressing her frank disappointment. At a time when smut was relatively difficult to come by, people would direct people to the good stuff and warn them away from the bad stuff. It’s also possibly a comment on the charges of obscenity levelled against Ulysses, and its being the eventual focus of an obscenity trial: the hypocrisy of readers seeking smut out and then being “shocked” when they find it.

I think you make a good point about them having had a conversation about the same book before, presumably at another period in her reading it, and about all the unseen implied exchanges that exist between these characters. I’m not convinced that this specific exchange is a very good example of conversational implicature—if at all, strictly speaking. There’s something different, I feel, between the linguistic elements and functions of implicature (processing bits of language in practical ways that don’t necessarily follow logically from their grammatical construction) on the one hand, and on the other the fact that people will refer implicitly to past conversations and habits. Still, it is useful to illuminate the ways that Ulysses manages to mimic realistic interactions, where people don’t deal in exposition about why they are saying what they are; and conversational implicature is indeed one of those things we use effortlessly all the time without realising it.

Anyway. There is a nice awareness here of how dialogue and characterisation works in Ulysses, and this chapter in particular.

PROPOSED SUGGESTION: Why church bells sound somber: The classic church bell possesses highly non-harmonic overtones. These are typically tuned by thinning the walls of the bell along the circumference at certain heights. A distinctive feature in the sound comes from the fact that apart from the fundamental pitch, the predominant overtone of the church bell sounds as the minor third above the prevailing tone. This accounts for the somber nature of the sound.

notes.title: Could have given that address too
notes.html_source:
More implicature in the internal narrative continuing the single phrase enigmatic suspense of “Calypso”.

‘Bloom reflects that he could have used this post office as a blind in addition to the one in Westland Row towards which he is circling’ (Gifford, Ulysses Annotated: Notes for James Joyce’s Ulysses, p. 85).

PROPOSED SUGGESTION: I love this observation, which is to do with one of the most challenging and yet rewarding things about reading Ulysses …

But perhaps there are some clearer ways of putting it. “Implicature” is actually quite a specific term in the study of linguistics (esp. what you might call “pragmatic” linguistics) and while I understand the point, I think, I’m not sure it’s the most illuminating way to frame it.

Please disagree with me; I am very wiling to have my understanding of linguistic terms argued over. I have no real idea, for instance, whether other Joyce commentators have specifically discussed “implicature” w/r/t Ulysses.

notes.title: Bethel. El, yes: house of: Aleph, Beth
notes.html_source:
Bethel is a stand-in for House of God where the ark of the covenant was kept (Gifford,p85). Bloom makes the connection and then rattles off the first two letters of the Hebrew alphabet, Aleph, Beth. This is another allusion to his Jewish ethnicity, which is part of his marginal identity, a persistent theme throughout the novel.

This also parallels a moment in Stephen’s monologue in “Proteus”, when he imagines making a phone call to the Garden of Eden. These occasional mental connections between both minds serve to highlight their affinities, what they have to learn from each other, while at the same time indicating certain fundamental differences—in this instance, Bloom’s Jewish and Hungarian background is set against Stephen’s own in Irish Catholicism; but the two are also linked in this, being both essentially secular people.

notes.html_source: Archimedes Principle, physical law of buoyancy, stating that any body completely or partially submerged in a fluid (gas or liquid) at rest is acted upon by an upward, or buoyant, force the magnitude of which is equal to the weight of the fluid displaced by the body. notes.title: Mrs Marion Bloom. Not up yet. Queen was in her bedroom eating bread and. No book. Blackened court cards laid along her thigh by sevens. Dark lady and fair man. Letter. Cat furry black ball. Torn strip of envelope.
notes.html_source:
This is emblematic of Joyce technique of inner monologue. Often referred to as Stream of Consciousness. But the term limits Joyce’s brilliance.

Bored with M'Coy’s rambling, Bloom’s thoughts return to the narration. He thinks, “Mrs. Marion Bloom,” which was the way the letter from Boylan was addressed to her rather than Mrs. Leopold Bloom as was the custom. This is a slight by Boylan to Bloom and becomes a symbol of Bloom’s cuckoldness. His mind slips to Molly. “Not yet up” is a neutral tone but then comes a harsher sarcasm, “Queen was in her bedroom eating bread and.” The sentence stops on a conjunction mimicking the rhythm of the mind. Next is is a sweeter thought, “No book” being in reference to the erotic book Molly asks Bloom to buy her. His mind still on the sexual, he wanders to the tarot cards Molly has laid out on her thigh. Later in the novel she will foresee Stephen in them. “Dark lady and fair man” could be the Dark Lady of Shakespeare’s sonnets and a nod toward the coming of Fair Stephen and the mysteries of Dark Molly. Again Bloom thinks of the letter, the symbol of his wife’s infidelity. Then the cat. Then the fact that she’s already open the letter and read Boylan. Much like Molly’s complex relationship with Bloom is reveled in the Penelope section so to does Bloom struggle with loving her as his thoughts go back and forth. This is Joyce’s honest inspection of human emotion and thought.

All this of course is packed in to nine lines. One of them only half a sentence. This is a great example of Joyce’s micro to macro-ism. Ulysses is the epic story of two nations, Israel and Ireland, and a little story of the day. So then the seemingly random thoughts of a Jewish-Irishman ad salesman walking through Dublin hold the weight of the epic struggles of all mankind with womankind.

notes.title: Leah tonight. Mrs Bandmann Palmer.
notes.html_source:
Millicent Palmer (1865-1905), an American actress who made her first tour of the British Isles in 1883. Her performance in ‘Leah’ at the Gaiety Theatre in Dublin was advertised in the ‘Freeman’s journal’, 16 June 1904.

‘Leah the Forsaken’ (1862) was a translation and adaption by the American playwright John Augustin Daly (1838-99) of the German ‘Deborah’ (1850) by Salomon Hermann Mosenthal (1821-77), a German-Austrian playwright and activist. The play is set in an Austrian village in the early eighteenth century; its central theme involves an attack on anti-Semitism. The villain, Nathan, is an apostate Jew who masquerades as a pharisaical (marked by hypocritical censorious self-righteousness) and anti-Semitic Christian to protect his place in the village. Leah, the Jew, is hounded by Nathan and “forsaken” by her Christian lover, achieving peace only by self-immolation (killing oneself as a religious sacrifice) at the play’s end. The part of Leah lent itself to flamboyant performance; hence the list of important actresses in this paragraph.

notes.html_source: The origins of El Dorado lie deep in South America. And like all enduring legends, the tale of El Dorado contains some scraps of truth. The Spaniards started calling this golden chief El Dorado, “the gilded one.”

notes.title:
La ci darem la mano
 La la lala la la.
notes.html_source:
From Don Giovanni (opera) by Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart

“There we will be hand in hand”

This is the first line of Don Giovanni’s attempt to seduce Zerlina, who is betrothed to Masetto. It is an especially poignant feature of Bloom’s mental wandering as it layers distinct memories and infidelities.

Firstly, it refers back to the conversation that Bloom and Molly have in the morning, after she has received a letter from her lover/manager, Blazes Boylan.

– Who was the letter from? he asked.
Bold hand. Marion.
– O, Boylan, she said. He’s bringing the programme.
– What are you singing?
– La ci darem with J. C. Doyle, she said, and Love’s Old Sweet Song.

Moreover, this bit of song stuck in Bloom’s head precedes his reading of the letter from Martha, his lover-by-correspondence.

The biggest irony, however, is that the context for why the song is stuck in his head in the first place has to do with the connection that Bloom has to his wife and his longing to be restored fully as her principal love and partner. As cheeky as it is to think of Bloom as the Don Giovanni to his numerous half-mistresses, the request for union, of being “hand in hand” with his wife again provides the ironic pathos of this unconsciousness.

notes.title: Martha, Mary
notes.html_source:
Mary and Martha are sisters portrayed in the Gospels of Luke and John. In one story, Martha is practical, preparing Jesus’s dinner, but Mary sits at Jesus' feet listening to him. When Martha complains that Mary should help with the work, Jesus tells her to stop worrying, that Mary has made the better choice. Luke 10. This scene is depicted in the picture Bloom remembers in the next paragraph.

He refers to the Martha in the painting as “the other one,” despite mentioning her first, and observes she “was getting the supper.” Whereas he fantasizes about the dark eyed Mary in the painting listening to him rapturously.

There is something to the comparison of the biblical characters of Martha and Mary, and the Martha and Molly (Marion, a variation on Mary) in Bloom’s life.

Is it that Molly is languorous and Martha industrious? (“I do wish I could do something for you.”)

Is it irony that he has neither a Mary nor a Martha? That Bloom feels Molly is not enthralled by him, and that the grammatically challenged Martha could not be the typist he has advertised for?

notes.title: Saint Peter Claver
notes.html_source:
St. Peter Claver was born at Verdu, Catalonia, Spain, in 1580, of impoverished parents descended from ancient and distinguished families. He studied at the Jesuit college of Barcelona, entered the Jesuit novitiate at Tarragona in 1602 and took his final vows on August 8th, 1604. While studying philosophy at Majorca, the young religious was influenced by St. Alphonsus Rodriguez to go to the Indies and save “millions of perishing souls.”

In 1610, he landed at Cartagena (modern Colombia), the principle slave market of the New World, where a thousand slaves were landed every month. After his ordination in 1616, he dedicated himself by special vow to the service of the Negro slaves-a work that was to last for thirty-three years. He labored unceasingly for the salvation of the African slaves and the abolition of the Negro slave trade.

notes.title: Lourdes
notes.html_source: In 1858 in the grotto of Massabielle, near Lourdes, France, the Blessed Virgin Mary appeared 18 times to Bernadette Soubirous, a 14 year old peasant girl. notes.html_source: From a story in James Ridley’s Tales of the Genii (two volumes, 1764); it is a faux-Oriental tale allegedly from a Persian manuscript, but actually the work of Ridley himself. notes.title: Knock apparition
notes.html_source:
On the evening of Thursday, 21 August 1879, two women from the small village of Knock, County Mayo, Ireland, Mary McLoughlin and Mary Beirne, were walking near the local church when they noticed luminous figures at the gable end. As they got closer they realised there were three moving figures and that one of them looked like the Blessed Virgin.

They surmised that the others were St. Joseph and St. John the Evangelist, and as it got darker Mary Beirne went off to alert her family, and so soon other neighbours joined them in the pouring rain. As the crowd gathered they could also see an altar, with a young lamb on it, in front of a cross, while one boy saw angels over the altar, but they heard no sounds and no verbal message was given. The apparition lasted for several hours, and was witnessed independently, as a globe of light, by a farmer who lived about a half mile away.

notes.title: Statues bleeding
notes.html_source: A weeping statue is a statue which has been claimed to be shedding tears or weeping by supernatural means. Statues weeping tears of a substance which appears to be blood, oil, and scented liquids have all been reported. Other claimed phenomena are sometimes associated with weeping statues such as miraculous healing, the formation of figures in the tear lines, and the scent of roses. notes.title: The invincibles
notes.html_source:
The Irish National Invincibles, usually known as the Invincibles, were a radical splinter group of the Irish Republican Brotherhood. This group of assassins were active in Dublin between late 1881 and 1883, with an intent to kill then Chief Secretary “Buckshot” Forster, jurists, informers, and the like.

A large number of suspects were arrested. By playing off one suspect against another, the Dublin Metropolitan Police got several of them to reveal what they knew. The Invincibles' leader, James Carey, and Michael Kavanagh agreed to testify against the others. Joe Brady, Michael Fagan, Thomas Caffrey, Dan Curley and Tim Kelly were hanged in Kilmainham Gaol in Dublin between 14 May and 4 June 1883. Others were sentenced to serve long prison terms.

notes.title: Crawthumpers

Noun
crawthumper ‎(plural crawthumpers)
(Ireland) ostentatiously pious person
The term suggests that the person is always beating (thumping) their chest (craw) a gesture of piety and submission. It also implies an extreme obsequiousness towards the Catholic Church, priests, monseignours, and especially junior bishops. A crawthumper will know every gradation of the clergy, from curate to pope, supplicant to reverend mother and the correct form of address in canon law. notes.title: Philosopher’s stone
notes.html_source: The philosopher’s stone is a legendary substance, allegedly capable of turning inexpensive metals into gold. It was sometimes believed to be an elixir of life, useful for rejuvenation and possibly for achieving immortality. For a long time, it was the most sought-after goal in Western alchemy. The concept of the philosopher’s stone may have been inspired by the knowledge that metals like gold and silver could be hidden in alloys and ores, from which they could be recovered by the appropriate chemical treatment. Though the notion of a simple philosopher’s stone of the alchemic sense fell out of scientific conception by at least the 19th century, its metaphors and imagery persisted: man’s attempt to discover the essential secret of the universe, redemptively transforming not just lead into gold, but death into life.

notes.title: Never know who will touch you dead. Wash and shampoo. I believe they clip the nails and the hair. Keep a bit in an envelope. Grows all the same after. Unclean job.
notes.html_source:
I think Bloom is musing about Catholicism and Judaism. In Judaism, a deceased body is always guarded, never left alone. Washing the body is a ritual, considered a mitzvah, and done in conjunction with prayers and blessings. To just leave this job to the women of the town or family, to leave the corpse unattended, and to not follow the rituals would be considered “unclean”, or not in accordance with Kosher laws in their broader application. A devout Jew may not know specifically who might touch him dead, but is assured that he will be treated with respect and reverence.

Cutting and disposing of fingernails is also ritualistic in Judaism, though I don’t know what is to be done with the nail and hair clippings of the deceased. I don’t imagine keeping them in an envelope is approved.

Interesting that his musings are about shampoo, washing, and cleanliness – and he is transported from being “in his head” back to the physical world by the reality of the soap in his pocket.

notes.title: Pills. All breadcrumbs they are
notes.html_source:
Bloom nods to the common use of sugar pills—for treating illnesses for which there are no effective treatments. These pills, although they should have no medical effect, can often engender what is known as the placebo effect.

From medicine.net:

A remarkable phenomenon in which a placebo – a fake treatment, an inactive substance like sugar, distilled water, or saline solution – can sometimes improve a patient’s condition simply because the person has the expectation that it will be helpful.

The placebo effect, although widely documented, is poorly understood and remains something of a mystery. Research has also shown that the effect can still be observed even when the patient is told that what they are receving is a placebo; and that a “placebo injection” is often more effective than a placeb pill.

notes.title: Whooping cough they say it cures
notes.html_source:
Oddly, people thought the smelly air around gasworks could cure whooping cough.

From The Gippsland Times, Australia, Thursday 7 January 1926:

[T]here are certain properties in the smells emitted by a gasworks which might be of value in getting rid of this tiresome whoop. Just lately the South Suburban Gas Co. Ltd. at their works in Lower Sydenham, on the south-eastern boundary of the London area, have taken up the idea of gas being good for the affected child. They have turned their pump room into a clinic where children who are suffering can go and ‘take the smells’. In this case one cannot say ‘take the waters’….It is more or less a case of killing to cure, for in most instances the fumes from the gas liquor bring on violent fits of coughing. But the trouble in the throat, which causes the whoop, is often removed in this manner.

notes.title: Thanks to the Little Flower. Sadly missed. To the inexpressible grief of his. Aged 88 after a long and tedious illness. Month’s mind: Quinlan. On whose soul Sweet Jesus have mercy.
notes.html_source:
Typical snippets of obituary-column prose, “The Little Flower” is a popular name for St. Teresa of Lisieux (St. Teresa-of-the-Child-Jesus, 1873-97), whose cultus grew with such rapidity and intensity after her death that ‘Butler’s’ “Lives of the Saints” calls it “the most impressive and significant religious phenomenon of contemporary times”. St Teresa (beatified in 1923, canonized in 1925) promised: “After my death I will let fall a shower of roses”; hence her nickname, “The Little Flower.”

Another “little flower,” a poem by Tennyson titled “Flower in the Crannied Wall” (1869), appears at the top of the right-hand column of the ‘Evening Telegraph’ of 16 June 1904 under the heading “Gleaned from All Sources”: “Flower in the crannied wall, / I pluck you out of the crannies, / I hold you here, root and all, in my hand, / Little Flower-but if I could understand / What you are, root and all, and all in all, / I should know what God and man is.”

Month’s mind: a commemorative requiem mass said on the thirteenth day after death.

The Queen’s Royal Theatre advertised the Elster-Grimes Grand Opera Company in that “Irish” opera (1862) – a melodramatic, musical version of ‘The Colleen Bawn’, libretto [A libretto is the text used in, or intended for, an extended musical work such as an opera, operetta, masque, oratorio, cantata or musical.] by Dion Boucicault (1822-90) and John Oxenford (1812-77), music by the German-English composer Sir Julius Benedict (1804-85).

Plot summary: Eily, the Colleen Bawn (Irish: “the blond”), is a peasant girl secretly married to a gentleman, Hardress Creegan. Creegan and his mother are in financial straits, but these are apparently to be resolved because Creegan is apparently betrothed to a rich gentlewoman, Anne, the Colleen Ruaidh (“the redhead”). Then Creegan’s best friend, Kyrle, falls in love with Anne and she with him, but she mistakenly thinks that he, not Creegan, is Eily’s husband. The melodramatic tangle is compounded by Creegan’s pride; by a pettifogging [placing undue emphasis on petty details; petty or trivial] lawyer with a mortgage to foreclose unless Mrs. Creegan marries him; by Creegan’s faithful servant, whose mistaken zeal leads him to attempt to murder Eily; by the lawyer, who has Creegan arrested for the murder that has not been committed; etc. All is resolved by relevation and confession: Creegan is reunited with Eily, Anne marries Kyrle, the mortgage blows away, and the lawyer is ducked in the horsepond.

notes.title: Snuff at a wake
notes.html_source:
According to the website irishidentity.com, this idiom has an intriguing origin: at a wake,

It was […] customary for a bowl of snuff to be placed on the chest of the dead person. This had a dual function in the snuff being a desirable commodity, brought the mourners close to the coffin to say a prayer for the deceased [sic]. Should the person in the coffin not be dead, the bowl on his or her chest would be seen to rise and fall, though no record exists of anyone being rescued by snuff. So many came forward that the bowl had to be replenished regularly, giving rise to the saying “disappeared like snuff at a wake”.

They are referring to Reuben J. Dodd, an actual citizen of Dublin who, inter alia, was a money lender. There are further references to him throughout Ulysses. All the characters in the book, including Bloom, appear to assume Dodd is Jewish, although in life he was not. notes.title: One and eightpence too much, Mr Dedalus said drily
notes.html_source:
Perhaps this is just Mr Dedalus' generalized, cranky humor, but it is probably antisemitic. The men have taken pains to point out that Reuben J Dodd is Jewish (“of the tribe of Reuben”) and ridiculed him for paying his son’s rescuer so little (“like a hero” probably an expression of the prejudicial view that Dodd is a penny pincher).

If so, Mr Dedalus takes this further, observing that the child wasn’t even worth that little. Again, if so, the comfort with which the men in the carriage make these “jokes” in front of Bloom demonstrates the pervasiveness of this prejudice.

There may also be buried in this joke a hint at how little Mr Dedalus values his own son Stephen.

notes.title: John Barleycorn
notes.html_source:
noun
a personification of barley, or of malt liquor.

John Barleycorn is an old English folksong that originated in the 16th century. It was a popular tale, though remains somewhat disturbing, even today. Primarily an allegorical story of death, resurrection and drinking, the main character—the eponymous John Barleycorn—is the personification of barley who is attacked and made to suffer indignities and eventually death. These correspond roughly to the stages of barley growing and cultivation, like reaping and malting.

notes.title: Found in the riverbed clutching rushes
notes.html_source:
Perhaps a reference to Ophelia in Hamlet, who drowned herself. Queen Gertrude describes the place of Ophelia’s drowning as:

There with fantastic garlands did she come
Of crow-flowers, nettles, daisies, and long purples
That liberal shepherds give a grosser name
But our cold maids do dead men’s fingers call them:
There, on the pendent boughs her coronet weeds
Clambering to hang, an envious sliver broke;
When down her weedy trophies and herself
Fell in the weeping brook.
Hamlet Act IV, Scene VII

This thought leads Bloom to think about Mr Cunningham’s troubled wife.

Both of these thoughts are probably Bloom’s attempts to crowd out memories of his father’s suicide.

notes.title: Rattle his bones
notes.html_source:
An allusion to the poem A Pauper’s Drive by Thomas Noel, about a dead pauper being roughly conveyed to the cemetery in a cheap hearse. The driver shouts: “Rattle his bones, over the stones, he’s only a pauper, whom nobody owns.”
https://www.bartleby.com/71/1414.html

The “nobody owns” phrase comes a few lines later.

Much earlier in the chapter, the men complain about the shoddy carriage (not a “commodious yoke”) in which they are riding.

Just before this, Bloom thinks both lines of this poem. The first time, they seem to be a reference to Paddy Dignam, the dead man in whose cortege Bloom is rolling “over the stones.” The repetition here seems to be more referential to Bloom’s father – his next thoughts explicitly about his father’s suicide. There is also the intervening thought about the death of Bloom’s son Rudy after seeing a child’s casket hurrying on its way to the funeral.

As often happens with Joyce, these thoughts can coexist, informing each other.

Throughout this chapter, Joyce evokes Odysseus' time in Hades by having Bloom encounter many of the dead.

notes.title: A poor lookout for Corny
notes.html_source:
A second instance in this chapter where Bloom favors modernization.

Bloom first wondered why someone couldn’t invent an automatic railway switch. It might put pointsmen out of work but “another fellow would get a job making the new invention.”

Now, Bloom envisions a livestock train and a funeral tram, rather than cattle droving and horse-drawn funeral carriages.

When Mr Power observes that a funeral tram would cut into Corny Kelleher’s undertaking business, Bloom thinks modernization is the better course. He seems to convince the other men in the carriage.

Beyond the characterization of Bloom as a forward-thinking person, there might be a slight hint here of old things passing away in this chapter that so often addresses death.

notes.title: More women than men in the world
notes.html_source: The number of men and women in the world is roughly equal, though men hold a slight lead with 102 men for 100 women (in 2010). More precisely, out of 1,000 people, 504 are men (50.4%) and 496 are women (49.6%). For every 100 girls, 107 boys are born, but males have a higher risk of dying than females, both in childhood and at adult ages. So at a certain age, the numbers of men and women even out. In France this occurs at age 25 (in 2010). Beyond this age, women outnumber men and the numerical difference between the two sexes increases with age. In France, eight centenarians in ten are women (in 2010).

notes.title: Muscular christian
notes.html_source:
Muscular Christianity can be defined as a Christian commitment to health and manliness. Its origins can be traced to the New Testament, which sanctions manly exertion (Mark 11:15) and physical health (1 Cor. 6:19-20).

The phrase “muscular Christianity” probably first appeared in an 1857 English review of Charles Kingsley’s novel Two Years Ago (1857). One year later, the same phrase was used to describe Tom Brown’s School Days, an 1856 novel about life at Rugby by Kingsley’s friend, fellow Englishman Thomas Hughes. Soon the press in general was calling both writers muscular Christians and also applying that label to the genre they inspired: adventure novels replete with high principles and manly Christian heroes.

notes.title: Tantalising for the poor dead.
notes.html_source:
This is a complex allusion: in terms of the passage, Bloom is simply saying that having sex in a graveyard would make the dead jealous. However, Joyce is also alluding to the story of Tantalus, who cooked his son up as a meal for the gods. Nice.

His punishment was to eternally reach for apples – hence the word ‘tantalising’ for something we want but which is just out of reach.

In another reference to the Underworld, Joyce is hinting at this chapter’s correspondent passage in the Odyssey. When Odysseus visits Hades, he must sacrifice a ram in order to speak with the dead prophet Tiresias. When he does this, the dead spirits are drawn to the blood and crowd in upon him.

A seventh gravedigger came beside Mr Bloom to take up an idle spade.

notes.html_source:
For Bloom to be standing next to an idle spade is significant. In Judaism, it is customary for the community to bury the dead – to take up shovels themselves and cover the coffin. It is the very definition of a “Mitzvah” – a final act of kindness that can never be returned. At a Jewish funeral, this custom is ritualized; it’s highly unlikely that Bloom would not be aware of it.

“He stepped aside nimbly”. Stepping away from the shovel in this context is symbolic.

notes.html_source: Grave robbing might seem like the stuff of horror films, but back in the 18th century it was a remarkably common activity, and in one way actually contributed towards the evolution of medicine and surgery. It was only legal for surgeons to carry out anatomies on the bodies of convicted murderers who were hung for their crimes – but as these usually numbered only around 20 or 30 a year, this wasn’t enough to satisfy the need of the medical experts (who would perform autopsies to educate their students as well as learn more about the human body). Grave robbing brought body snatchers money, while surgeons could charge money to people who wanted to watch a dissection.

notes.title: How grand we are this morning!
notes.html_source:
Bloom goes from being hurt by John Henry Menton, to hoping that Mr Cunningham will put Menton in his place, to suggesting that Menton might regret his treatment of Bloom on further reflection, to closing with this thought.

At one layer, this is Bloom sarcastically mocking Menton’s overinflated sense of his own importance, or at least Menton’s sense that he is superior to Bloom.

At another layer, it is Joyce’s poetic exclamation about the entirety of these characters and this work.

notes.title: IN THE HEART OF THE HIBERNIAN METROPOLIS
notes.html_source:
Joyce delighted in an array of styles across Ulysses, and for Aeolus employed a style befitting the newspapers of the time, complete with section headings a la the Freeman’s Journal and National Post.

The style continues throughout, with the rhetorical style of a newspaper sometimes comically contrasted with the witty dialogue.

PROPOSED SUGGESTION: The ‘Aeolus’ episode is set in the offices of the Freeman’s Journal, located on Prince street, just behind the Hotel Metropole on Sackville street.

notes.title: Nelson’s pillar trams
notes.html_source:
The Nelson Pillar was a large granite pillar topped by a statue of Horatio Nelson in the middle of O'Connell Street in Dublin. It was built in 1808–1809, and was among the first and grandest monuments erected in memory of Nelson in the then United Kingdom. It survived until March 1966, when it was destroyed by a bomb planted by Irish republicans.

Of course, with this book being published in 1922, the monument was still erect.

Nelson’s pillar trams are what they call the area’s trams, named after the historical location the trams are near.

notes.title: E. R.,
notes.html_source:
King Edward, a.k.a Edward Rex. Not Emergency Room.

As king, Edward played a role in the modernization of the British Home Fleet and the reorganization of the British Army after the Second Boer War.

He re-instituted traditional ceremonies as public displays and broadened the range of people with whom royalty socialized.

He fostered good relations between Britain and other European countries, especially France.

The Edwardian era, which covered Edward’s reign and was named after him, coincided with the start of a new century and heralded significant changes in technology and society, including steam turbine propulsion and the rise of socialism. He died in 1910 in the midst of a constitutional crisis that was resolved the following year by the Parliament Act 1911, which restricted the power of the unelected House of Lords.

notes.title: Barrels rolled by grossbooted draymen out of Prince’s stores.
notes.html_source:
Note the alternation from the men making the barrels thud to the passive structure of the barrels being rolled by the draymen. The parrallel structure of these three lines suggests a possible reference to Aeolus.

The Aeolian harp
is an instrument that is played by the wind. Hence the active force making the music is absolutely ignorant of its own creation and the instrument is the real artist.

In this sequence it is suggested that the same holds for men, as they ‘make the barrels thud’ while in fact the barrels do the thudding themselves, and the draymen are merely the ignorant ‘force’ behind their music.

notes.title: Davy Stephens
notes.html_source:
Davy Stephens was a ‘newsagent’ in Kingstown, a busy location because of the mailboats and railway station; he left only to attend the Epsom Derby every year.

Davy wrote an autobiography titled ‘The Life and Times of Davy Stephens: the renowned Kingstown Newsman’ where he describes himself thus: “His exterior is peculiar but prepossessing. Standing a little below the usual height for the proverbial Irishman, this point is quickly lost sight of in a deep well of wit, not yet completely sounded, beaming forth in his eyes. No one can say whether it is in the merry glance of his eye or in the quick repartee that issues from his lips, never for a moment sealed, that Davy’s fortune lies. The corners of his mouth are turned up in a perpetual smile which his clean shaven chin tends to emphasise[emphasize?]. […] His hair hangs down over his shoulders in long strings, reminding one of that of Ulysses when tossed by the sea at the feet of the charming Nausicaa, and the fresh breezes of the Channel has reduced his complexion to a compromise between red and brown. In a black frieze overcoat and a soft Trilby hat he braves the cross-Channel gales in winter as readily as be broils beneath the portico of the railway station when the temperature is only 88 degrees in the shade. Atmospheric variations seemingly exert no influence on the perfect constitution of Davy. The scent of the briny and the glint of the sunshine are alike to him. Add to these particulars a fine rich brogue and the man is complete.”

notes.title: Galleypage
notes.html_source:
In printing and publishing, proofs are the preliminary versions of publications meant for review by authors, editors, and proofreaders, often with extra-wide margins. Galley proofs may be uncut and unbound. They are created for proofreading and copyediting purposes, but may be used for promotional and review purposes also.

Galley proofs are so named because in the days of hand-set letterpress printing, the printer would set the page into galleys—the metal trays into which type was laid and tightened into place—which would then be used to print limited copies for proofreading.

mangiD kcirtaP = Patrick Dignam

The Linotype typesetting machine, designed by the German inventor Ottmar Mergenthaler in 1884, is a “‘one casting’ machine used in printing. The name of the machine comes from the fact that it produces an entire line of metal type at once, hence a ‘line-o’-type', a huge improvement over manual typesetting.
The Linotype machine operator enters text on a 90-character keyboard. The machine assembles matrices, which are molds for the letter forms, in a line. The assembled line is then cast as a single piece, called a slug, of type metal in a process known as ‘hot metal’ typesetting. The matrices are then returned to the type magazine from which they came, to be reused later. This allows much faster typesetting and composition than original hand composition in which operators place down one pre-cast metal letter, punctuation mark or space at a time.
The linotype revolutionized typesetting especially newspaper publishing, making it possible for a relatively small number of operators to set type for many pages on a daily basis. Before Mergenthaler’s invention of the Linotype, no newspaper in the world had more than eight pages.

PROPOSED SUGGESTION: Distributing type means hand setting type in a composing stick. It is done backward because the type is a mirror image of the printed page. Type setters using a Linotype use a keyboard, so they enter the characters in the normal order.

notes.title: Ned Lambert said
notes.html_source:
Joyce uses overlapping dialogue in this section. Film director Robert Altman used the same technique in his films for the same reason.

“Robert Altman’s films may be most easily recognized through the director’s unique approach to dialogue. Rather than utilizing the more traditional give-and-take approach to a conversation, Altman would have two, three, or even entire rooms full of people delivering their lines at the same time. This overlapping dialogue, while unconventional and often difficult to comprehend, created a sense of realism that became a staple of Altman’s films. Altman never seemed to be overly concerned with creating a digestible piece of cinema–he recreated life and dropped us right in the middle of it. We do not simply view a Robert Altman picture, we experience it in full immersion.”
By Jacob T. Swinney | Press Play
June 22, 2015

notes.title: Gumley
notes.html_source:
We learn that a night watchman named Gumley was a member of the Invincibles Gang that murdered the Chief Secretary and Under-Secretary on May 6, 1882 (22 years prior to Bloomsday) in Phoenix Park.

In Chapter 12 “Cylops” we learn that Gumley was sued by Reuben J. Dodd for not paying a debt but the Recorder hears his hard luck story and dismisses the case.

Shortly after 1:00 A.M. Stephen spots Gumley in a watchman’s sentry-box in Chapter 16 Eumaeus. He knows that he is a friend of his fathers but avoids his detection.

There was no chance that Stephen would be detected because Bloom sees that Gumley is asleep on the job.

A little later, a street noise wakes the dozing night watchman and we learn that in spite of once having a decent income, he is a “broken down” alcoholic and nearly broke. It appears that he has been given the watchman’s job out of charity.

Gumley is still asleep When Bloom and Stephen emerge from the cabman’s shelter and head for Bloom’s house. Bloom thinks that it is appropriate that the ex-revolutionary is asleep on the job and “guarding” stones.

This, being Stephen’s stream of consciouness that springs everynow and then in this chapter intercalated with Bloom’s own thoughts, is a direct reference to a line, spoken by the own Dedalus, in chapter 2, http://genius.com/James-joyce-ulysses-chap-2-nestor-annotated.

The line is: History is a nightmare from which I am trying to awake.

History is a recurring motif in that chapter, since Stephen is giving a class about Pyrrhus, a Greek general and statesman. Also, it alludes a conversation he and Haines had on the preciding chapter, where the englishman says that he feels that England has “treated you rather unfairly”, talking about the colonization of the irish people by the english.

So, this thought of Stephen not only shows his pessimistic view from the current state of Ireland as it also is an insight of his own life: the improductive time he spent on Paris and his mother’s death.

History (of Ireland) is not the unique nightmare, but also his own life, which he can’t awake from.

Stephen goes deeper on his feelings about the death of his mother, Paris and his own solitude on the chapter Proteus.
