He escaped the revenge of the Versailles government, and crossed the frontier in safety. He was condemned to death in absentia in 1873, but came back to Paris after the general amnesty of July 1880. notes.title: Per l’aer perso
notes.html_source: “Lost through the air.” Again, a reference to wind. M.J.C. Hodgart points out in “James Joyce’s Ulysses: Critical Essays” that The nature of the “wind” in this case, consistent with Joyce’s frequent reference to the Hebrews and the Greeks, is elucidated by the Hebrew “ruach”, meaning, not only wind, but spirit, soul, mind, intellect, passion, as well as by the Greek “anemos” which likewise means wind and breath, the spiritual principle of human life, rational soul, disposition. Latinized for us English speakers, “The etymology of the verb “inspirare”, then, leads us to “to breathe into”, “to blow upon”, “to excite”, “to inflame”, “to arouse by divine influence.” The noun “spiritus” points us to “breath of life”, “spirit”, “soul”, “mind”. This all has to do with artistic inspiration. “Lost through the air” may refer to the fleeting nature of such inspiration brought on, perhaps, by the sight of three girls, the way they are dressed, and by the way they hang on to each other. How to capture that image while out for a walk?

notes.title: Saint Augustine
notes.html_source: Saint Augustine, b. Nov. 13, 354, d. Aug. 28, 430, was one of the foremost philosopher-theologians of early Christianity. He saw the human being as a perfect unity of two substances: soul and body. In his late treatise On Care to Be Had for the Dead, section 5 (420 AD) he exhorted to respect the body on the grounds that it belonged to the very nature of the human person. Augustine’s favourite figure to describe body-soul unity is marriage: caro tua, coniunx tua — your body is your wife. Initially, the two elements were in perfect harmony. After the fall of humanity they are now experiencing dramatic combat between one another. They are two categorically different things. The body is a three-dimensional object composed of the four elements, whereas the soul has no spatial dimensions. Soul is a kind of substance, participating in reason, fit for ruling the body.

notes.title: Isis and Osiris, of Horus
notes.html_source:
The Story of Osiris, Isis and Horus: The Egyptian Myth of Creation
From Geb, the sky god, and Nut, the earth goddess came four children: Osiris, Isis, Set and Nepthys. Osiris was the oldest and so became king of Egypt, and he married his sister Isis. Osiris was a good king and commanded the respect of all who lived on the earth and the gods who dwelled in the netherworld.
However, Set was always jealous of Osiris, because he did not command the respect of those on earth or those in the netherworld. One day, Set transformed himself into a vicious monster and attacked Osiris, killing him. Set then cut Osiris into pieces and distributed them throughout the length and breadth of Egypt.
With Osiris dead, Set became king of Egypt, with his sister Nepthys as his wife. Nepthys, however,
felt sorry for her sister Isis, who wept endlessly over her lost husband. Isis, who had great magical powers, decided to find her husband and bring him back to life long enough so that they could have a child. Together with Nepthys, Isis roamed the country, collecting the pieces of her husband’s body and reassembling them. Once she completed this task, she breathed the breath of life into his body and resurrected him. They were together again, and Isis became pregnant soon after. Osiris was able to descend into the underworld, where he became the lord of that domain. The child born to Isis was named Horus, the hawk-god.

notes.title: Hosts at Mullaghmast
notes.html_source:
Massacre of Mullaghmast.
In 1577, Sir Francis Cosby, commanding the queen’s troops in Leix and Offaly, formed a diabolical plot for the permanent conquest of that district…he invited to a grand feast all the chief families of the territory; attendance thereat being a sort of test of amity. To this summons responded the flower of the Irish nobility in Leix and Offaly, with their kinsmen and friends—the O'Mores, O'Kellys, Lalors, O'Nolans, etc. The “banquet"—alas!—was prepared by Cosby in the great Rath or Fort of Mullach-Maisten, or Mullaghmast, in Kildare county. Into the great rath rode many a pleasant cavalcade that day; but none ever came forth that entered in. A gentleman named Lalor who had halted a little way off, had his suspicions in some way aroused. He noticed, it is said, that while many went into the rath, none were seen to reappear outside. Accordingly he desired his friends to remain behind while he advanced and reconnoitered. He entered cautiously. Inside, what a horrid spectacle met his sight! At the very entrance the dead bodies of some of his slaughtered kinsmen! In an instant he himself was set upon; but drawing his sword, he hewed his way out of the fort and back to his friends, and they barely escaped with their lives to Dysart! He was the only Irishman out of more than four hundred who entered the fort that day that escaped with life! The invited guests were butchered to a man..
From Stroy of Ireland By A. M. Sullivan

notes.title: Antisthenes
notes.html_source:
Antisthenes (c. 446—366 B.C.E.)
Known in antiquity as an accomplished orator, a companion of Socrates, and a philosopher, Antisthenes presently gains renown from his status as either a founder or a forerunner of Cynicism. Initially he was a pupil of Gorgias the rhetorician. He chose to live in poverty, and more than one of the surviving anecdotes surrounds the ragged state of his cloak, usually involving those areas where the cloak is torn. In addition to eschewing luxuries so many of his fellow Athenians sought, he demonstrated an ad hoc and improvisational sense of humor which allowed him to ridicule commonly held beliefs and the mores of Athenian culture.
Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy

notes.title: Fifteen children he had. Birth every year almost. That’s in their theology or the priest won’t give the poor woman the confession, the absolution. Increase and multiply
notes.html_source:
Bloom is referring here to how the Catholic faith denies its adherents the use of birth control, to use preventative measures would be a mortal sin.
For the Vatican, the primary purpose of intercourse was for the sacred act of procreation. If couples were interested in having intercourse, then they had to be willing to accept the potential for the creation of another life. For devout Catholics, that left only abstinence or the church-approved rhythm method (the practice of abstaining from sex during the woman’s period of ovulation).In fact the Roman Catholic Church officially banned any “artificial” means of birth control in 1930. Condoms, diaphragms and cervical caps were defined as artificial, since they blocked the natural journey of sperm during intercourse. Douches, suppositories and spermicides all killed or impeded sperm, and were banned as well. According to Church doctrine, tampering with the “male seed” was tantamount to murder. A common admonition on the subject at the time was “so many conceptions prevented, so many homicides.” To interfere with God’s will was a mortal sin and grounds for excommunication.

notes.title: Crossbuns. One meal
notes.html_source: A crossbun is a pastry usually eaten hot, containing spices and raisins with a cross on the top to signify the crucifixion of Jesus. Typically eaten on Good Friday by Christians. Here Joyce contrasts two religious holidays, Yom Kippur, a day of fasting, prayer and atonement, and Good Friday. Although the Catholic Church treats Good Friday as a fast day, this is understood as having only one full meal and two collations (a smaller repast) and on which the faithful abstain from eating meat. This is why many places have the typical ‘Fish Friday’. Here again Bloom, when he says `for fear he’d collapse..‘ is implying that Catholics are unable, possibly too weak, to fast as Jews do.

notes.title: Rats get in too
notes.html_source:
Apparently there have been urban myths about rats in Guinness vats since before the internet.

The more outrageous stories about Guinness include the ones about how dead rats were found at the bottom of the vats in the St James’s Gate brewery in Ireland, thus explaining the unique taste of stout. This one is classic barroom BS at its finest. The basics of Guinness are barley, hops, yeast and water. Guinness derives its toasted flavor, which tastes anywhere from coffee to chocolate, and bitter hint from the manner in which its malted barley is roasted and the amount of hops used. The creamy taste of the head is a result of nitrogen bubbles released during the pouring process.

notes.html_source:
Looking down into the river Liffey reminds Bloom of the story in Chapter 6 Hades about Reuben J’s son and Simon Dedalus' humorous response:

That’s an awfully good one that’s going the rounds about Reuben J and the son…There was a girl in the case, Mr Bloom began, and he determined to send him to the Isle of Man out of harm’s way but when they were both … on the way to the boat and he tried to drown … the son himself …

–Reuben and the son were piking it down the quay next the river on their way to the Isle of Man boat and the young chiseller suddenly got loose and over the wall with him into the Liffey.

–For God’s sake! Mr Dedalus exclaimed in fright. Is he dead? … Not he! A boatman got a pole and fished him out by the slack of the breeches and he was landed up to the father on the quay more dead than alive. Half the town was there… And Reuben J… gave the boatman a florin for saving his son’s life.

–One and eightpence too much, Mr (Simon) Dedalus said drily.

notes.title: Y lagging behind drew a chunk of bread from under his foreboard, crammed it into his mouth and munched as he walked.
notes.html_source: This is a classic example of James Joyce’s predilection for punning and literary ‘easter eggs.’ While on the surface this line is merely a comical, if quotidian, image, it is particularly notable for the crossing over of the “Y” and the “S” in “H.E.L.Y.S.” The first word of Ulysses is “stately” and the last Molly Bloom’s emphatic, feminine “Yes”, one starting with “s” and one “y.” Therefore, the “s” and the “y” must at some point cross over and here, the middle of the book, 12:00 noon, is where this happens. While this is likely meant as a simple structural nuance, perhaps not conveying any great meaning, it is nonetheless interesting to see how Joyce’s overarching scheme for the novel fits together.

notes.title: Cherchez la femme
notes.html_source:
‘Cherchez la femme’ is sometimes mistakenly thought to refer to men’s attempts to pursue romantic liaisons with women. In fact, the phrase, which is occasionally used in its loose English translation ‘look for the woman’, expresses the idea that the source of any given problem involving a man is liable to be a woman.

The expression was coined by Alexandre Dumas (père) in the novel The Mohicans of Paris, 1864, in the form of ‘cherchons la femme’. In John Latey’s 1878 English translation, Dumas' detective, Monsieur Jackal, concludes that a woman must have been involved in the crime being investigated:
“Where’s the woman? Seek her.”
His opinion was later confirmed by a colleague:
“Ah! Monsieur Jackal, you were right when you said, ‘Seek the woman.’”

notes.title: King of Ireland Cormac

Cormac Mac Art (son of Art), also known as Cormac ua Cuinn (grandson of Conn) and Cormac Ulfada (Long Beard), King of Ireland. Cormac became king of Ireland in 218 and reigned until 254, when he handed the throne to his son.
Cormac is said to have turned to Christianity some years before his death. One account of his death says he choked on a fish bone, but according to Lebar na h-Uidhre, he was killed by the siabhra, or fairy beings, for abandoning the old religion. Cormac died at Cleaiteach in 260. His sons tried to bury him at Brugh na Boinne, but the River Boyne rose three times to oppose them because of Cormac’s Christianity. Cormac was buried at Ros na righ.

notes.title: Fizz and Red bank oysters. Effect on the sexual. Aphrodis. He was in the Red Bank this morning.
notes.html_source:
This is another great example for Joyces technique of visualizing his characters chains of thought. Though it is just four short lines, the allusions are rather complex and challenge the readers attention and background knowledge.

(1) A region famous for its oysters are the red-bank beds in County Clare, situated on the west coast of Ireland (see: Gifford: Ulysses Annotated, 8.865-66). Hence, Bloom is referencing fizz (champagne) and red-bank oysters as a delicacy, contrasting it with the “garbage, sewage they [oysters] feed on”.

(2) Oysters are rumored to be aphrodisiacs (“Aphrodis”). Bloom is consequently lead into thinking about their “effect on the sexual”.

(3) The Red Bank Restaurant (“the Red Bank”) is a restaurant in Dublin, named after the famous oysters being served there. It was first referenced in Chapter 6 when Bloom and his companions saw Blazen Boylan, the man Molly is having an affair with, standing in front of its entrance.

This allows us to fully understand Blooms train of thought. His meditations on food lead him to thinking about oysters, particularily about red-bank oysters and their rumored “effect on the sexual”. “Red-bank”, in turn, reminds him of the restaurant, which brings up seeing Boylan there earlier in the day. The thought of him eating oysters with all its sexual connotations, especially in light of the scheduled meeting of Boylan and Molly later that day (compare Chapter 4), serves as a painful reminder of the adultery and further intensifies the worries that haunt Bloom all day long.

notes.title: No June has no ar no oysters. But there are people like things high. Tainted game.
notes.html_source:
Since the 18th century, oysterfishing was prohibited in France, the United Kingdom and the United States during the months without the letter “r” in their names (i.e. May, June, July and August). These close seasons were instituted to combat the decline in oyster populations due to constant overfishing.

As Ulysses is set in June and “June has no ar”, Bloom concludes that there are currently no oysters being served.

The next two sentences (starting with “But there are…”), however, show Bloom sharing the widely held belief that the “r-rule” was originally implemented because of a lack of reliable refrigeration. After noting “no ar no oysters”, he is thus led into thinking about spoiled goods (“things high”, “tainted game”), continuing his train of thought.

It is worth noting that connoisseurs are adhering to the “r-rule” up until today, even though both the refigerating and breeding problems have been solved for a long time.

For further information about the “r-rule”, click here (in German).

We’ve had Stephen on the strand , on his own, not wanting to return to the Martello. Leopold’s had the close exclusion of the funeral, the physical buffeting in the press works and the conversation in Davy Byrne’s. Now Stephen is about to further the ‘outsider’ theme with a debate on art with AE and John Eglington, poet and critic respectively. It’s not since the last lines of Portrait of the artist as a young man that we’ve heard significantly from Stephen.

Using the simple mechanics of the time of day and two characters, this theme is extended in the National Library. The armchair nationalists have been explored at the press works and now Stephen will forge in the smithy of my soul the uncreated conscience of my race by having a crack at the literati.

notes.title: —Monsieur de la Palice, Stephen sneered, was alive fifteen minutes before his death.
notes.html_source:
Jacques de la Palice was a famous French Marshal who had an epitaph that was often misread for humorous effect. The epitaph read:

Ci gît Monsieur de La Palice: Si il' n'était pas mort, il ferait encore envie.

i.e. “Here lies Monsieur de la Palice: were he not dead, he would still be admired.”

A humorous misreading of this has the last word as “en vie” instead of “envie”, which makes it read idiotically as “were he not dead, he would still be alive.”

notes.title: Gaptoothed
notes.html_source:
The eponymous title character of Yeats' play Cathleen ni Houlihan, which Joyce is referencing here, is a poor old woman. Thus, the adjective is, first of all, used disparagingly. With Kathleen symbolising Ireland as a whole, the allusion gains more poignancy.

Beyond that, the county town Wicklow, that was mentioned in the preceding sentence, is called Cill Mhantáin in Irish, meaning “church of the toothless one”. The origin of the name is rich in folklore:

“Saint Patrick and some followers are said to have tried to land on Travailahawk beach, to the south of the harbour. Hostile locals attacked them, causing one of Patrick’s party to lose his front teeth. Manntach (toothless one), as he became known, was undeterred and returned to the town, eventually founding a church.” (See: Wikipedia)

The name could, however, also be a toponym and refer to the St. Patrick’s Church in Wicklow, which is said to resemble a gappy set of teeth.

Nevertheless, Wicklow and Ireland are superimposed upon each other via the corresponding adjective “gaptoothed”.

notes.title: Gustave Moreau
notes.html_source:
Gustave Moreau (1826-1898)
An early exponent of Symbolism, and an influential figure in French painting of the 19th century, the artist Gustave Moreau was known for his visionary style of mythological painting and imaginative history painting. More than any other artist, he had a natural flair for introducing “magic” into painting, and for incorporating the incomprehensible and unconscious into his compositions. This made him one of the leading Symbolist artists, but it also makes him an important source for 20th century Surrealism.

notes.title: Finest flower of corruption in Mallarme
notes.html_source:
Stéphane Mallarmé, (born March 18, 1842, Paris—died Sept. 9, 1898, Valvins, Fr.), French poet, an originator (with Paul Verlaine) and a leader of the Symbolist movement in poetry.
By 1868 Mallarmé had come to the conclusion that, although nothing lies beyond reality, within this nothingness lie the essences of perfect forms. The poet’s task is to perceive and crystallize these essences. In so doing, the poet becomes more than a mere descriptive versifier, transposing into poetic form an already existent reality; he becomes a veritable God, creating something from nothing, conjuring up for the reader, as Mallarmé himself put it, “l’absente de tous bouquets”—the ideal flower that is absent from all real bouquets.
Encyclopedia Britannica

notes.title: Limbo patrum
notes.html_source:
Place in hell for the righteous souls that died before the birth of Christ and, thus, have to dwell there through no fault of their own. It is no official doctrine of the Catholic Church but rather theological speculation.

It appears, for example, as the first circle of hell in Dante’s Divine Comedy and is described by Virgil, the guide of the poetic persona, as follows:

“Inquirest thou not what spirits
Are these which thou beholdest? Ere thou pass
Farther, I would thou know, that these of sin
Were blameless; and if aught they merited,
If profits not, since baptism was not heirs,
The portal to thy faith. If they before
The Gospel lived, they served not God aright;
And among such am I. For these defects,
And for no other evil, we are lost;
Only so far afflicted, that we live
Desiring without hope.”

Canto IV, Lines 29-39

notes.title: Playhouse by the bankside
notes.html_source:
The History of The Rose Theatre
By David Nash Ford
London is well known today for its theatrical attractions. Before the first of these were built in Shoreditch in the 1570s, plays were mostly performed in tavern yards, sometimes in the streets or on temporary stages or carts. Bankside in Southwark, outside the jurisdiction of the City fathers, quickly became the home of Elizabethan theatre, and it all started with the playhouse called ‘The Rose’.

notes.title: Composition of place. Ignatius Loyola, make haste to help me!
notes.html_source:
Advice from St Iggy on contemplation and spiritual betterment is firstly to find composition of place.(The line Appeared in Giacomo Joyce as Ignatius Loyola, make haste to help me).
From the man himself:

*It should be noted here that for contemplation or meditation about visible things, for example a contemplation on Christ our Lord (who is visible), the ‘composition’ will consist in seeing through the gaze of the imagination the material place where the object I want to contemplate is situated. By ‘material place’ I mean for example a temple or a mountain where Jesus Christ or our Lady is to be found—according to what I want to contemplate. Where the object is an invisible one, as is the case in the present meditation on sins, the composition will be to see with the gaze of the imagination, and to consider, that my soul is imprisoned in this……‘.

Note the reference to the visible : see Proteus line 1 : ‘'The ineluctable modality of the visible: at least that if no more, thought through my eyes’.

notes.title: Villiers de l’Isle has said
notes.html_source:
Auguste comte de Villiers de l'Isle-Adam,
a Breton who moved to Paris, met Mallarmé and Baudelaire and pursued his own writing career.

Baudelaire translated Poe for him and inspired him to write short story collections.

Villiers is seen as a link between the curiosity which attracted Baudelaire towards the occult and the sudden enthusiasm which enflamed the Symbolists, together with a general exasperation at the rise of materialism in society, again part of Baudelaire’s polemic. Villiers was admired by the Symbolists and in particular by Verlaine who added an essay on him to his book the Poètes maudits of 1888, thus emphasising the role of prose writers in a movement broadly considered to be poetic. (Kimber, G. Reading University)

notes.title: Flow over them with your waves and with your waters
notes.html_source:
From Deirdre a play by AE.

The Deirdre legend was popular at the time with AE and Synge writing a Deirdre play.

Synge’s was finished by his girlfriend, Molly Algood and Yeats after dying at 37 years of age from cancer.

Deirdre was the subject of a prophecy by the druid, Cathbad, that she would kill the king, Conchubar. She was secreted away and was beautiful when grown up. She fell in love with a warrior Naoise (neesha) and eloped with him.

The legend tells the story of Conchubar tracking these two down and the bloody consequences.
The allusion is to a line in Deirdre , AE Let thy waves flow over them spoken by Cathbad in a curse against the heroes chasing Deirdre. AE/George Russell played this part when the play was first produced (Gifford).

notes.title: Absit nomen!
notes.html_source:
Another example of a harmless expression that contains rather complex wordplay. First of all, absit nomen! (literally “let the name be absent”) is a play on absit omen, which is is the Latin equivalent of “Knock on wood!”. Stephen is obviously referring to some ominous meaning of the name “Myrto”. What could it be?

“Myrto” is derived from the Greek Μυρτε, which translates to “myrtle”. It is the name of a plant used to adorn brides in wedding ceremonies. Thus, “myrtle” has become associated with virginity.

In other words, when Stephen is saying “Myrto (absit nomen!)” he is actually making a dirty joke.

notes.title: If the earthquake did not time it we should know where to place poor Wat, sitting in his form, the cry of hounds, the studded bridle and her blue windows. That memory, Venus and Adonis, lay in the bedchamber of every light-of-love in London.
notes.html_source:
These sentences contain five references to Venus and Adonis, Shakespeare.

It is a narrative poem written in approximately 1593 (Wikipedia). It borrows from Ovid’s Metamorphoses Book 10 and significantly for Stephen’s oration has considerable characteristics of Aristotle’s -theory of tragedy.

That theory is firmly rooted in us – people. It is showing not telling. An unnarrated series of incidents the audience experiences. It is far from AE’s views of universal truths (a philosophy of Plato) which can only be accessed by humans through art and the artist.

It’s also a comment on Shakespeare by Joyce. Shakespeare wrote Venus and Adonis deliberately for the court market and he was rewarded with a fifteen edition run up to the 1640’s.

Internal narrative, a cascade of references to theosophy and George Russell.

Pali book – Pali was a form of Sanskrit refereed to in Isis Unveiled.

We – Joyce and Gogarty got up to some shenanigans in Dawson chambers where the Hermetic society met.

umbrel undershoot – umbrella

Aztec logos – Helena Petrovna Blavatsky argues ancient religions have the awareness of universal truths

Astral levels – a level of awareness above the material

Oversoul – a linkage between all souls on a higher consciousness than the norm

Mahamahatma – wise one, reached nirvana.

Chelaship – chela is a Buddhist novice

Louis H Victory and T. Caulfield – Irish essayists/poets

Lotus ladies – Hindu nymphs

tended them ‘I the eyes – Allusion to Antony and Cleopatra 2,2.

pineal gland – a theosophical third eye enabling visions

Gulfer of souls, engulf – theosophical concept of souls deriving from and returning to God.
Hesouls…….. – fusion of he sells seashells on the seashore and canto 5 of Inferno.

notes.title: The quaker librarian came from the leavetakers. Blushing, his mask said
notes.html_source:
Quaker librarian is mentioned twelve times in this episode. Lyster (his name) is only written twice. it is not surprising that he should have a mask, that is he is a nameless part of the chorus to the protaganists AE and Eglinton.

Joyce believed drama to be ‘literature in dialog form’ and ‘the interplay of passions to portray truth, drama is strife, evolution, movement in whatever way unfolded; it exists, before it takes form, independently; it is conditioned but not controlled by its scene’(Drama and Life. Occasional, Critical and Political Writings, Joyce).

This episode has many theatrical parallels and Joyce seems to paint Lyster as a minor character in the Irish literary pantomime.

The mention of “mask” is particularly telling: it probably alludes to Attic Tragedy where all members of the play wore masks that reflected the plays themes – sad and grand for tragedy, silly and buffoonish for comedy and satyr plays.

(Ancient Greek red figure painting of a tragic actor with a mask)

As the quaker librarian is a minor character, he would probably either be a messenger, slave, nurse or even chorus member. According to Aristotle (Poetics), Greek tragedy originally consisted solely of a chorus – a group of men who sung and danced religious themed songs – and a single actor who interacted with them. Supposedly, Aeschylus added a second actor, and Sophocles later added a third third (which Aeschylus used thereafter). Chorus literally means “dancing group”, signaling one of the original purposes of this theatrical branch.

notes.title: Christfox
notes.html_source:
Lyster gets similar treatment to AE in Stephen’s internal narrative although there is a stronger structuralist element to this inner string of Stephen’s. Strucutralism is the placing of a story in the foundations of another, in this case what T.S. Elliott, impressed at Ulysses, called the Mythic Method (in so doing Joyce rescued art for the 20th century).

Nominally , Joyce placed Bloom’s day in the foundations of The Odyssey wishing to render it sub specie temporis nosrti (of our own time). There are other structuralist parallels (Garber.M, Shakespeare and Modern culture, p212):

man, son, wife are reproduced numerous times:

Ulysses, Telemachus, Penelope
Bloom, Stephen, Molly
Shakespeare, Hamnet Shakespeare, Ann Hathaway
Ghost, Hamlet, Gertrude
God, Christ, Mary.

Stephen looks at Lyster and thinks of the origin of the Quakers, George Fox,but for seven lines, his thoughts are a slurry of Fox, Christ and Shakespeare with strings of their relationships (above) attached.

This is the nub of modernism. The plot is dead, once aware of the meaning of the allusions in his thoughts, you experience the ache of his lost yearn for a father which of course is that of jj.

notes.title: And I heard the voice of that Egyptian highpriest
notes.html_source:
From John F Taylor’s speech at the Law Student Debating Society, 24th October 1901. Taylor was a King’s Counsel and spoke in defence of the Irish language. This was part of the general movement against the Anglicisation of Ireland. The speech was part of the nationalist hubbub in Chapter 7 of Ulysses (Aeolus episode).

The speech concludes with Taylor telling how an Egyptian high priest compared their mighty achievements to the lowly language and culture of Jews. Taylor finishes with ‘ ‘If Moses had listened to the counsels of that learned Professor he would never have come down from the mountain, his face glowing as a star, and bearing the Tables of the Law…’
(James Joyce Centre).

Joyce, with the help of his ally, Sylvia Beach made a recording of a version of the speech published by the nationalist Roger Casement in 1924.

notes.title: L’art d’être grand...
notes.html_source:
L'Art d'être grand-père (“The Art of Being a Grandfather”) is a substantial book of poems by Victor Hugo, published in 1877. They were among the last he wrote.

On 13 March 1871, Hugo’s 44-year-old son Charles died of a stroke while riding in a carriage to a farewell dinner for some of Victor’s friends at a restaurant in Bordeaux. Charles’s wife died shortly afterwards, and Victor Hugo became the guardian of their children, Georges and Jeanne Hugo. The poems describe the feelings of a grandfather entrusted with innocent young children. Love and tenderness are celebrated, discipline is discounted; the freshness and laughter of the young soften the potential bleakness of old age. A trip to the zoo sets the poet musing. Many charming scenes are depicted. He keeps up his attack on tyranny and bigotry, and his search for truth.

The English version by Timothy Adès is How to be a Grandfather, Hearing Eye, London 2002. (wikipedia)

notes.title: The dark lady of the sonnets
notes.html_source:
The Dark Lady of the Sonnets is a 1910 short comedy by George Bernard Shaw in which William Shakespeare, intending to meet the “Dark Lady”, accidentally encounters Queen Elizabeth I and attempts to persuade her to create a national theatre. The play was written as part of a campaign to create a “Shakespeare National Theatre” by 1916.

The Dark Lady is a woman described in Shakespeare’s sonnets (127–152), and so called because the poems make it clear that she has black wiry hair, and dark, “dun”-coloured skin. The description of the Dark Lady distinguishes itself from the Fair Youth sequence by being overtly sexual. Among these, Sonnet 151 has been characterized as “bawdy” and is used to illustrate the difference between the spiritual love for the Fair Youth and the sexual love for the Dark Lady. The distinction is commonly made in the introduction to modern editions of the sonnets. As with the Fair Youth sequence, there have been many attempts to identify her with a real historical individual. A widely held scholarly opinion, however, is that the “dark lady” is nothing more than a construct of Shakespeare’s imagination and art, and any attempt to identify her with a real person is “pointless”.

notes.title: Auk’s egg, prize of their fray
notes.html_source:
The great auk was a flightless bird of the alcid family that became extinct in the mid-19th century. It was the only modern species in the genus Pinguinus. The eggs, unusual looking, white, mottled with black marmoreal markings featured a rather unique pointed oval shape. They became an expensive and prized acquisition for ornithologists and other collectors, which prior to the bird’s extinction, contributed to the population’s demise. The bird was flightless and awkward which compounded its vulnerability. Joyce frequently references birds throughout this book, in particular in reference to Stephen. Towards the end of the chapter, Stephen refers to himself as a hawklike man and speaks of his lapwing.

The reference to the auk’s egg here might have a double signification. Firstly this could refer on a visual level to the shape of Stephen’s head. However more importantly, like the auk, Stephen is a rare creature. The sentence, the use of the word ‘meek’ suggests he may, like the bird, be somewhat ungainly, sensitive and susceptible to the other’s who surround him. For example, we get the feeling Buck Mulligan bullies him around somewhat. Yet his intellectual brilliance is unusual and makes him a rare oddity, like the auk, his thoughts, like the eggs of the auk, are prized. His genius is coveted by the others who in their verbal disputes seek to win him over or sway him to their arguments. I cannot help feeling that Stephen represents a young Joyce, an unusually erudite and intelligent young man whose rare brilliance makes him at once overly sensitive yet also makes others crave his company or approval.

notes.title: Lucrece
notes.html_source:
Lucrece, a legendary Roman housewife whose fate played a vital role in the transition from a Roman Kingdom into a Roman Republic. According to accounts from the Roman historian Livius and the Greek-Roman historian Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Lucretia’s suicide after her rape by an Etruscan king’s son was the immediate cause of the anti-monarchist rebellion that overthrew the monarchy.
The incident kindled the flames of dissatisfaction over the tyrannical methods of the last king of Rome, Lucius Tarquinius Superbus. As a result, the prominent families instituted a republic, drove the Royal Familyfrom Rome. Due to its sheer impact the rape itself became a major theme in European art and literature. Shakespeare penned a narrative poem entitled ‘The Rape of Lucrece’. He made allusion to this poem in some of his other work. He used this idea in Cymbeline (circa 1609–1610). In this play, Iachimo bets Posthumus (Imogen’s husband) that he can make Imogen commit adultery with him. He does not succeed. However, Iachimo convinces Posthumus otherwise using information about Imogen’s bedchamber and body. Iachimo hid in a trunk which was delivered to Imogen’s chamber under the pretence of safekeeping some jewels, a gift for her father, King Cymbeline. The scene in which he emerges from the trunk mimics the scene in The Rape of Lucrece. Indeed, Iachimo compares himself to Tarquin in the scene: “Our Tarquin thus, / Did softly press the rushes ere he waken’d / The chastity he wounded” (2.2.12–14).

notes.title: Sir Walter Raleigh
notes.html_source: Sir Walter Raleigh’s aggressive actions toward the Spanish did not sit well with the pacifist King James I, Elizabeth’s successor. Raleigh’s enemies worked to taint his reputation with the new king and he was soon charged with treason and condemned to death. However, the sentence was commuted to imprisonment in the Tower in 1603. He was released in 1616 to search for gold in South America. Against the king’s approval, he invaded and pillaged Spanish territory, was forced to return to England without booty, and was arrested on the orders of the king. His original death sentence for treason was invoked, and he was executed at Westminster.

Refers to Aristotle’s will, which mentions his mistress Herpyllis:

And until Nicanor marries my daughter, I appoint Aristomedes, Timarchus, Hipparchus, Dioteles, and Theophrastus, if he will consent and accept the charge, to be the guardians of my children and of Herpyllis, and the trustees of all the property I leave behind me; and I desire them, when my daughter is old enough, to give her in marriage to Nicanor; but if any thing should happen to the girl which may God forbid, either before or after she is married, but before she has any children, then I will that Nicanor shall have the absolute disposal of my son, and of all other things, in the full confidence that he will arrange them in a manner worthy of me and of himself. notes.title: Legal fiction
notes.html_source:
Legal fiction is an assumption that something is true even though it may be untrue. In order to do justice, the law will permit or create a legal fiction. It is the presumption of facts arrived based on the circumstantial evidence or situation prevailing in that case, with an objective to achieve justice. Legal fiction is the assumption that a certain thing is true, and which gives to a person or thing a quality which is not natural to it, and consequently establishes, a certain disposition, which, without the fiction, would be repugnant to reason and to truth.
USLegal.com

notes.title: Bulldog of Aquin
notes.html_source:
Saint Thomas Aquinas (1225—1274)
Aquinas rejects the notions from Arianism and Sabellianism, and proposes that there are three persons in God, with distinctive roles but of the same divine substance. Aquinas is very cautious here in his selection of his words, as he states that to avoid the error of Arius and Sabellius, “we must shun the use of terms diversity and difference in God” and that “we must shun the term “singularity.” Thus, the core idea of Aquinas regarding Trinity is the “unity of essence” and “communicability of the divine essence.”
Paul Kang, The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity

notes.title: Delta in Cassiopeia
notes.html_source:
This phrase is recurs at several points in the novel. It is first seen back in Proteus (“Darkly they are there behind this light, darkness shining in the brightness, delta of Cassiopeia”).

When Shakespeare was 8 years old, a bright light appeared in the sky in the constellation Cassiopeia. It was a supernova explosion, but most people (including Tycho Brahe) took it to be a new star forming. (Indeed, Brahe published a tract called “Concerning the Star, new and never before seen in the life or memory of anyone.”) It is one of only 8 supernovae witnessed in recorded history and caused much ado in Elizabethan England. Many took it to be a sign of the second coming of Christ. The brightness grew and grew relative to other objects in the night sky, only to disappear altogether after 16 months (when Shakespeare would have been 9).

For more on Cassiopeia in Ulysses (including later mentions and thus spoilers), see this blog post.

notes.title: I am tired of my voice, the voice of Esau. My kingdom for a drink.
notes.html_source:
An allusion to Richard III’s cry “A horse! A horse! My kingdom for a horse!” in Richard III, Act V.

Also an allusion to Genesis 25-27, the rivalry between Issac’s elder son Esau and his younger son, Jacob, who cheats Esau.

Once, when Esau is exhausted from a hunting trip, he sells his birthright to Jacob for a bowl of stew.

Later, when Issac is blind and on his deathbed, Jacob disguises himself as Esau and tricks Issac into giving Jacob a blessing meant for Esau. Jacob’s voice is his only tell. Gen 27:22 reads:

“Jacob went close to his father Isaac, who touched him and said, ‘The voice is the voice of Jacob, but the hands are the hands of Esau.’ ”

Esau arrives too late and is distraught. Verse 34: “When Esau heard his father’s words, he burst out with a loud and bitter cry and said to his father, ‘Bless me—me too, my father!’ ”

Stephen’s comparison of his voice with Esau’s voice in the context of brothers and fathers in conflict is complex. Does he feel wronged by his younger brother as Esau was by Jacob, as he argues Shakespeare was by his younger brothers?

notes.title: Age has not withered it. Beauty and peace have not done it away. It is in infinite variety everywhere
notes.html_source:
In Antony and Cleopatra, Act II, Scene 2, Domitus Enobarbus praises Cleopatra, observing that Antony will never leave her because:

“Age cannot wither her, nor custom stale
Her infinite variety”

Stephen is arguing that Shakespeare’s evergreen theme is Anne Hathaway’s infidelity, which he categorizes as “banishment.” Stephen cites literal banishment and includes betrayal or infidelity or unrequited love as varieties of banishment. These things are found throughout Shakespeare, although Stephen throws a pretty broad net.

notes.title: Gravediggers bury
notes.html_source:
Hamlet Act V, Scene 1 begins with two “clowns” digging a grave for Ophelia. Horatio and Hamlet (the prince/pere) arrive. One clown debates with Hamlet about whose grave it is, as follows:

HAMLET: Who is to be buried in’t?
First Clown: One that was a woman, sir; but, rest her soul, she’s dead.

The scene, like this section of Stephen’s discourse, examines the nature of being, and the nature of the personhood of the deceased.

notes.title: Hamlet (père?) and Hamlet fils
notes.html_source:
Stephen is echoing (mocking?) Eglinton’s confusion about which Dumas he is quoting, by noting that both the king and prince are named Hamlet, both are dead by end of the play, but that both are products of Shakespeare’s imagination and thus, projections of his self, and so both, in some sense, die with Shakespeare because the complexity of Shakespeare’s conflicting aspects of self die with Shakespeare.

Of course, this is also presented by Joyce as irony because these characters are intimately and passionately engaged in attempts to understand Shakespeare through his work, which implies a belief that, though dead, Shakespeare is capable of being, at least somewhat, understood.

notes.title: A king and a prince
notes.html_source:
Throughout this chapter, Stephen’s theory that Shakespeare acted the part of Hamlet the father, not Hamlet the son, though agreeing with Eglinton that Shakespeare was, in a sense, both Hamlets, expresses a similar conundrum of how or how much Joyce “is” Stephen or Bloom (or both) in Ulysses.

It would be difficult to observe all the ways Joyce’s schema title of Scylla and Charybdis, i.e., trying to find a passage between two dangers, finds expression in the chapter, but this is as good a place as any to note one such expression. Hamlet the king or Hamlet the prince? Shakespeare the human being or Shakespeare’s work? Bloom or Stephen? On and on.

notes.title: The Lord has spoken to Malachi
notes.html_source:
A little blasphemy from Malachi “Buck” Mulligan.

The biblical Book of Malachi is constructed as God’s message to the people of Israel through the prophet. The book opens thusly (Mal 1:1-3):

The burden of the word of the Lord to Israel by Malachi.
“I have loved you,” saith the Lord.
Yet ye say, “Wherein hast thou loved us?”
“Was not Esau Jacob’s brother?” saith the Lord, “yet I loved Jacob. And I hated Esau, and laid his mountains and his heritage waste for the dragons of the wilderness.”

Not only is this bit of scripture structured as a dialogue, as is much of this chapter of Ulysses, it observes the Esau/Jacob conflict to which Stephen has recently alluded.

notes.title: Help me to believe or help me to unbelieve?
notes.html_source:
Stephen twists the language of Mark 9:24, which, in context is pretty hard to read any way other than an anguished father begging Jesus for help in believing more deeply so that his son will be healed.

But in a vacuum, the phrase could be read the other way: Please help strengthen my unbelief.

If the unbelief is unbelief in God, then it would be odd to ask God to help you form a stronger unbelief, so Stephen carries that question into the next few sentences.

notes.title: Egomen
notes.html_source:
Greek. As a rhetorical term means roughly “on the other hand” but could be literally translated “I, certainly.”

So, Stephen ruminates philosophically: Who helps to believe or, on the other hand, to unbelieve?

Also, Stephen assures himself: Who is an effective persuader? Me. Who is ineffective? The other guy.

Or perhaps: Who helps to believe? I Am. (YHWH) Who (helps) to unbelieve? The other chap (the devil.)

notes.title: You are the only contributor to Dana who asks for pieces of silver. Then I don’t know about the next number. Fred Ryan wants space for an article on economics.
notes.html_source:
Eglinton’s assertion that no other contributors want to be paid for their contributions is a little dubious. Coupling that to the observation that Fred Ryan, the other editor of the Dana, wants to write about economics underscores that point.

Stephen will contemplate this in the next passage.

The “pieces of silver” idiom probably evokes the price paid to Judas by the Sanhedrin in order to buy his betrayal of Jesus (see Matthew 27). Stephen has recently mentioned Judas in his quotation of Maeterlinck.

Is Eglinton hinting that a writer seeking payment for his work from a publication is akin to Judas seeking payment to betray Jesus? If so, this is employed, comfortable Eglinton expressing his disdain for poor, struggling Stephen.

notes.title: The whipping lousy Lucy gave him
notes.html_source:
Sir Thomas Lucy (1532-1600), a gentleman and owner of lands in Warwickshire. Some sources report that Shakespeare was whipped or imprisoned by Lucy for poaching on Lucy’s land, which was one cause of Shakespeare’s move to London.

There is a ballad attributed to Shakespeare which lampoons Lucy, punning his name with “lousy”:

A parliament member, a justice of peace,
At home a poor scarecrow, at London an ass,
If lousy is Lucy as some folks miscall it
Then Lucy is lousy whatever befall it.

This ballad suggests that Lucy’s wife was unfaithful to him, keeping with Stephen’s theme about Shakespeare.

notes.title: O, Kinch, thou art in peril. Get thee a breechpad.
notes.html_source:
We can identify that Buck is talking about Bloom as he dubs him “the wandering jew.” He then jokingly—but also maliciously— tells Stephen (Kinch) that he’s in trouble because Bloom looked at him in a manner that Buck perceives as lustful (he had previously suggested Bloom is gay). The word “breechpad” used in this context gives the reader the idea that he is telling Stephen to protect his body from Bloom’s homosexual desires: the word “breech” can be used to refer to a person’s buttocks. This ridiculous idea builds on the character of Buck, demonstrating his flippant personality and willingness to say anything.

Because this entire chapter is devoted to Stephen and his Shakespeare/Hamlet theory, it is also worth noting that the way Buck says “Get thee a breechpad,” is reminiscent of Hamlet saying to Ophelia “Get thee to a nunnery” (3.1.138-139), thus implying that Ophelia is sexually promiscuous. The two lines not only sound and read similar to one another but both also have sexual connotations.

notes.title: Onelegged sailor
notes.html_source: The onelegged sailor roams around Dublin singing “The Death of Nelson”, a patriotic song which portrays sacrifice; and he is significant through out the episode. For instance, the sailor seems to relate to Nelson, since both men have given their all for their nation: his loss of limb is a symbol of sacrifice. He wanders around Dublin Begging for charity, and the song seems to construct the notion of continuity throughout the episode as it appears multiple times. Joyce uses the motif of music introduced in the beginning of the episode to form a pattern throughout that connects events in the episode to an instant whole.

notes.title: Cardinal Wolsey
notes.html_source:
Cardinal Thomas Wolsey, (born c. 1475, died Nov. 29, 1530), cardinal and statesman who dominated the government of England’s King Henry VIII from 1515 to 1529. His unpopularity contributed, upon his downfall, to the anticlerical reaction that was a factor in the English Reformation.
The immediate cause of Wolsey’s fall from power was his failure to persuade Pope Clement VII to grant Henry an annulment of his marriage to Catherine of Aragon. There had long been a party of nobles who hated the lowborn, overbearing cardinal. When his final attempt to obtain the annulment collapsed in July 1529, these enemies easily turned the king against him. Wolsey was arrested on Nov 4, 1530 in York on charges of treason (for corresponding with the French court), but he died at the end of the month while on his way south to face the king.
Just before his death he reputedly spoke these words, “I see the matter against me how it is framed. But if I had served God as diligently as I have done the King, he would not have given me over in my grey hairs.”

notes.title: The corner of Dignam’s court
notes.html_source: This is an interpolation, the first indisputable one in the chapter, in which lines that appear in the text of one episode are not directly related to that episode. These interpolations interfere, at least momentarily, with the reader’s ability to follow and comprehend the narrative. The next line, “Was that not Mrs M'Guinness?” is a trap, leading the reader to think this is Denis Maginni asking Father Conmee, and putting them in the same scene. The question of “where the corner of Dignam’s court is” is distinct and difficult to answer on its own. It likely is the “Four Courts” building on the banks of the Liffey, some 1.3 miles southwest of where Father Conmee is at the time, about a 25-minute walk from the court building. The reference to “Dignam” here is likely to allude to the reality that the priest is on his way to take care of a matter for a family, whose name he can hardly recall.

notes.title: Bad cess
notes.html_source:
To say bad cess to you to somebody is to wish them bad luck, so it’s not pleasant, though as curses go there are worse.

The first cess was an obligation put on the Irish people to supply the Lord Deputy’s household and garrison with provisions at prices “assessed” by the government. The word has been since become widely known throughout the English-speaking world and is still used for a tax in Ireland, Scotland and India.

notes.title: He gazed over Stephen’s shoulder at Goldsmith’s knobby poll.
notes.html_source:
The bronze statue of the poet Oliver Goldsmith (1728-1774), outside Trinity College where he graduated. “poll” refers firstly to his head, “knobby” because of his baldness. But it also refers to the famous couplet, penned by David Garrick, based on Goldsmith’s poor speaking manner:

Here lies Nolly Goldsmith, for shortness called Noll,
Who wrote like an angel, but talked like poor Poll. [Poll here meaning a parrot.]

notes.title: Gunpowder plot
notes.html_source: The Gunpowder Plot of 1605 was a failed assassination attempt against King James I of England by a group of provincial English Catholics led by Robert Catesby. Catesby may have embarked on the scheme after hopes of securing greater religious tolerance under King James had faded, leaving many English Catholics disappointed.

notes.title: Cashel cathedral
notes.html_source: In 1649 Oliver Cromwell was named Lord Protector of England after defeating the forces of the Catholic King Charles I, whom he had beheaded. Having secured England for the Parliamentarians (the Roundheads and Puritans), Cromwell turned his attention to the subjugation of Ireland, which was largely Catholic. In September his forces conquered Drogheda and had its 3500 defenders as well as women and children slaughtered. Cashel, too, was sacked by Cromwell’s troops under the leadership of one Murrough O’Brien. Fearing a similar slaughter, the Catholic soldiers and town’s people of Cashel took refuge in the cathedral thinking they would be safe under the medieval rule of “sanctuary,” which allowed felons and others to seek refuge in a church or monastery where they could not be harmed or forced to leave. Notwithstanding this centuries old custom, Cromwell’s troops piled turf around the cathedral, lit it and roasted the refugees to death.

notes.title: Banana peel
notes.html_source:
In the mid-19th century, a man named Carl B. Frank began importing Panamanian bananas to New York City. The fruit quickly became a popular street food throughout America, but the surge in urban migration and lack of sanitation regulation posed a major problem in cities. People often tossed their garbage into the streets, leading to a general foul stench and public waste buildup. A fresh banana peel might seem non-threatening, but a rotting banana peel was a slime-covered booby trap. Around 1880, Harper’s Weekly admonished anyone who tossed their banana peels on a public walkway, as this would likely result in broken limbs.

notes.title: The Awful Disclosures of Maria Monk
notes.html_source:
Maria Monk’s Awful Disclosures was first published in January, 1836. In it, Monk exposed various scandalous events that, according to her, had occurred at the Hotel Dieu convent in Montreal. She claimed convent nuns were having sexual relations with priests from the neighboring seminary who supposedly entered the convent through a secret tunnel. All babies born of these illicit encounters, Monk claimed, were baptized before being strangled and dumped in a lime pit in the basement of the convent. Maria Monk said she had lived in the convent for a total of seven years before becoming pregnant by a priest. Unable to bear the thought of having her child killed and dumped in the basement, she finally fled.

The publication of Maria Monk’s Awful Disclosures caused an enormous public outcry that fed on the widespread anti-Catholic sentiment of the era. Leading protestants in New York and Montreal demanded an investigation of the convent, to which demand the Bishop of Montreal eventually acquiesced. It turned up no evidence to support Maria Monk’s claims. With her claims discredited, Maria Monk fell from public view. A rumor emerged that she had actually been a prostitute in Montreal.

notes.title: General Slocum
notes.html_source:
The General Slocum Disaster
The PS Slocum, built in 1891, was a paddle boat or sidewheel passenger ship. On June 15, 1904, the ship carried 1,358 passengers, plus crew from New York. Most of the passengers were women and children. As the ship made its way up the East River, good times turned bad very quickly. There have been varying accounts of how the fire started, but it spread rapidly within a half hour of leaving dock around 9 a.m. The panic was horrific among the passengers as they faced death by drowning or being burned alive on the ship. For days afterward, bodies would wash ashore. Only 321 passengers survived from a total of 1,358 passengers.

notes.title: Drawn and quartered
notes.html_source: To be hanged, drawn and quartered was from 1351 a statutory penalty in England for men convicted of high treason, although the ritual was first recorded during the reign of King Henry III (1216–1272). Convicts were fastened to a hurdle, or wooden panel, and drawn by horse to the place of execution, where they were hanged (almost to the point of death), emasculated, disembowelled, beheaded and quartered (chopped into four pieces). Their remains were often displayed in prominent places across the country, such as London Bridge.

notes.title: Beingless beings. Stop!
notes.html_source: It may be Stephen is thinking of the literati in the library, it may be of those he encounters everywhere in his journeying, but he hurls the word, “Stop” at beingless beings, soulless shells of humanity. “You sing of your heart, well let me tell you about my heart,” he seems to say. There are a number of dichotomies over which Stephen agonizes. There are enduring heart throbbings from without and those from within. the heart being the repository of the most intense, stirring personal longings and emotions perhaps those from without for Stephen are for artistic and professional success as a writer/poet, acceptance by those who had just dismissed him earlier that day, and those yearnings from within, those involving the most enduring longings, those for unity with the three entities from which he had emotionally exiled himself, viz. God, family, and country, a return to unity with which was his private, probably subconscious odyssey. Immanuel Kant taught that there are two ways of seeing the world; we can see it either as a world as it appears, or as a world as it is in itself, but which we cannot see due to our human limitations. Martin Buber saw that, implicit in Kant’s views, there were two ways of being in the world. The first way is choose life in its fullness here and now, to encounter it in its wholeness. The other is to live in the world of things including the persons one experience as mere things.

notes.title: Between two roaring worlds
notes.html_source:
The two roaring worlds that swirl on either side are of the church in Rome, and of the government in England symbolized respectively by Father Conmee at the beginning of the chapter, and the Viceroy at its end. There are also the worlds of the East and the West, and of the Hebrews and the Greeks, all of which are roundly discussed in Ulysses. Blake T. Ostler in For on the Horizons, writes,

There is a vast difference in the way the Hebrews felt we come to knowledge and the way the Greeks thought of it. Whereas the Hebrews… constantly refer to the heart as an instrument of knowledge and choice, the [Greeks] hardly ever do. The [Hebrews] regard the heart as the source of knowledge and authentic being. For the Greeks, the head is the place of knowing everything we can know.

notes.html_source:
There are parallel meanings for Stephen.

The term was later used in psychology to refer to an irrational obsession that so dominates an individual’s thoughts as to determine his or her actions. An outgrowth of Romanticism, the concept enjoyed its widest circulation during the 19th and the early 20th century.

notes.title: Pokorny of Vienna

Julius Pokorny (1887-1970) was a German Celtic scholar who supported Irish nationalism and the Gaelic League. And he was a German nationalist who lost his chair in Berlin because of Jewish ancestry, after which an Irish visa saved his life…
In 1922 his name cropped up in no less a place than James Joyce’s new novel, Ulysses, where the idea that the ancient Celts had no concept of hell is attributed to him. The scene is curiously anachronistic, because on 16 June 1904, the day on which Ulysses is set, Pokorny was a seventeen-year-old schoolboy in Austria whose name was unknown in Dublin.

notes.title: Purgatory
notes.html_source:
Master Dignam hopes his father is not somewhere worse than purgatory.

The Catechism of the Catholic Church defines purgatory as a “purification, so as to achieve the holiness necessary to enter the joy of heaven,” which is experienced by those “who die in God’s grace and friendship, but still imperfectly purified” (CCC 1030). It notes that “this final purification of the elect … is entirely different from the punishment of the damned” (CCC 1031).

notes.title: Heard the hoofirons, steelyringing
notes.html_source:
Hoofirons are Joyce’s way of saying horseshoes. The odd re-wording was used to keep our attention on the thumping sound of metallic hooves on the ground, rather than on the image of a horse.

The introduction of this episode is interpreted as a musical overture thus the sound the horseshoes make can be thought of as that of cymbals crashing, that’s the “steelyringing”.

This and some of what follows is a recreation of a band playing music. All the motifs for the rest of the episode are to be found in this introduction. Think of it as a sort of strange musical summary of the chapter to follow.

notes.title: Trilling, trilling: Idolores.
notes.html_source:
This initial disjointed section of Sirens has numerous sounds, musicality and musical allusions.

The short phrases, compound words and sounds introduce the ‘Fuga per Canonem’ technique Joyce employs, although the reader may not be fully aware of it before completing the episode. Joyce stated ‘It is a fugue with all musical notations: piano, forte, rallentando, and so on’, (Ellmann p459).
The fugal elements are :
Subject : the Siren’s song
Answer : Mr. Bloom’s entry and monologue
Counter-subject : Boylan
Divertimenti : Songs of Ben Dollard and Mr Bloom
(Gilbert, S. James Joyce’s Ulysses).
Idolores refers to a character in an 1899 opera: Florodora (spelt Floradora in Gifford p291).

notes.title: Full tup. Full throb.
notes.html_source:
This chapter is highly sexual throughout, animal and sensual imagery spices this section of the book. The barmaids, Martha, Molly etc. seem to be sirens luring the men and seducing them with their feminine wiles. The men, Bloom, Lenehan etc. seem almost drunken and out of control with animalistic lust and desire.
‘Full tup. Full throb.’
Tup in British English refers to a male sheep; ram also it refers to the head of a falling hammerlike mechanism, as of a steam hammer or pile driver. Finally as a verb it is used in reference to a ram copulating with a ewe. Full throb obviously is a way of writing about the engorged male member. This whole section and many that follow are about desire for sex, wanton lust.

notes.title:
Pwee! Little wind piped wee.
 
 True men. Lid Ker Cow De and Doll. Ay, ay. Like you men. Will lift your tschink with tschunk
notes.html_source:
Bloom is being truly emasculated in this section. ‘Pwee! Little wind piped wee.’ Wee in Scottish dialect which has influenced Northern Ireland, means small. Here the little wind piped wee, alludes to a wind instrument, following on from the musical theme, Joyce refers frequently to wind instruments throughout the chapter, like the fife. Pwee is the noise the wind pipe makes. But as usual Joyce is employing ‘double entendre’ and here the little wind pipe also alludes to BLoom’s small phallus. The idea is further reinforced in the next section when Joyce speaks of ‘True men…Like you men. Will lift your tschink with tschunk.’ i.e. they are real men, men that women like Molly desire and would in Bloom’s mind be potential suitors for his unfaithful wife, because they are able to perform the deed with gusto and possess virile attributes that Leopold does not have, like chunky sized phalluses. Joyce alludes to this when he says ‘they can lift women up with their 'tschunk.’
Joyce deliberately chooses to emasculate Bloom the main character of this book in contrast to Ulysses in the Odyssey, Bloom is not depicted as strong, manly and vigorous but instead meek, cuckolded and not well endowed. Joyce is creating a true anti-hero in every sense of the word. From the description of Bloom’s small penis to his toilet habits and the derisory comments of others, we are constantly invited to scrutinize Bloom.

waiting for their teas to draw is not immaterial but in the context of the already established ‘tea’ event, acts as a refrain. Its purpose is to produce the sound ’T' rather than prosaic. The meaning of reef is lost in the sound.

notes.title: Solfa fable
notes.html_source: A music score featuring Aesop’s fable ‘The fox and the stork’. The Sol-fa system is a sight-singing and notation schema first mooted by D. Sower in 1832, developed by Sarah Ann Glover (1785–1867) as Norwich Sol-fa, and pioneered by John Curwen (1816–80) in the 1840s. Based on movable-doh system of solmization. Notes of major scale are named (in ascending order) doh, ray, me, fah, soh, lah, te, where doh is the tonic, other notes being thus related to tonic of the moment, not fixed in pitch.

notes.title: Ah fox met ah stork. Said thee fox too thee stork
notes.html_source:
Two of Aesop’s fables conflated here:
ONE:
Wolf and Crane (sometimes Wolf and Stork)
A Wolf had been gorging on an animal he had killed, when suddenly a small bone in the meat stuck in his throat and he could not swallow it. He soon felt terrible pain in his throat, and ran up and down groaning and groaning and seeking for something to
relieve the pain. He tried to induce every one he met to remove the bone. “I would give anything,” said he, “if you would take it out.” At last the Crane agreed to try, and told the Wolf to lie on his side and open his jaws as wide as he could. Then the Crane put its long neck down the Wolf’s throat, and with its beak loosened the bone, till at last it got it out.

“Will you kindly give me the reward you promised?” said the Crane.

The Wolf grinned and showed his teeth and said: “Be content. You have put your head inside a Wolf’s mouth and taken it out again in safety; that ought to be reward enough for you.”

TWO:
The Fox one day thought of a plan to amuse himself at the expense of the Stork, at whose odd appearance he was always laughing.

“You must come and dine with me today,” he said to the Stork, smiling to himself at the trick he was going to play. The Stork gladly accepted the invitation and arrived in good time and with a very good appetite.

For dinner the Fox served soup. But it was set out in a very shallow dish, and all the Stork could do was to wet the very tip of his bill. Not a drop of soup could he get. But the Fox lapped it up easily, and, to increase the disappointment of the Stork, made a great show of enjoyment.

The hungry Stork was much displeased at the trick, but he was a calm, even-tempered fellow and saw no good in flying into a rage. Instead, not long afterward, he invited the Fox to dine with him in turn. The Fox arrived promptly at the time that had been set, and the Stork served a fish dinner that had a very appetizing smell. But it was served in a tall jar with a very narrow neck. The Stork could easily get at the food with his long bill, but all the Fox could do was to lick the outside of the jar, and sniff at the delicious odor. And when the Fox lost his temper, the Stork said calmly:

Do not play tricks on your neighbors unless you can stand the same treatment yourself.

notes.title:
Hugh
 
 MacHugh
notes.html_source:
MacHugh appears briefly in the Aeolus episode. His biggest moment is re-enacting a speech by John F. Taylor on the revival of the Irish tongue. Later, Stephen tells him “Parable of the Plums,” which he very much enjoys.

In his discourse with Stephen, we see that MacHugh is actually something of an intellectual and one of the first men that Stephen openly respects. The two of them are able to banter back and forth in highly erudite language that goes over the head of other people present (like Myles Crawford). Beyond this, we don’t get too much of a sense for MacHugh. Like Stephen, he is taken with historical antecedents for the contemporary Irish condition. He compares them to the Greeks and then to the Jews. But MacHugh is not an artist. He is an intellectual and while he enjoys discussing such ideas, it is clear that he does not struggle with them to the degree that Stephen does.

notes.title: Trained by owner
notes.html_source:
This may be a reference to Pavlov’s bell used to train dogs. It suggests that Lenehan and Boylan are responding like dogs to the barmaid’s flirtation.

During the 1890s Russian physiologist Ivan Pavlov was looking at salivation in dogs in response to being fed. In his experiment, Pavlov used a bell as his neutral stimulus. Whenever he gave food to his dogs, he also rang a bell. After a number of repeats of this procedure, he tried the bell on its own. As you might expect, the bell on its own now caused an increase in salivation. So the dog had learned an association between the bell and the food and a new behavior had been learned. Because this response was learned (or conditioned), it is called a conditioned response.

notes.title: Vamping
notes.html_source:
A vamp is a passage of instrumental music of fixed length – usually pretty short – which can be played as many times as needed to create time for some purpose. In musical theatre or cabaret, vamps are often used to allow singers to deliver dialog or carry out stage directions within a song; since the time this takes can vary, it’s useful to have a short snippet of music that can be repeated as needed to allow for the time.

When a theatre orchestra is “in a vamp,” they are repeating such a passage in a loop. The conductor will use a hand signal of some kind to indicate “this is the last time,” after which the ensemble will continue forward in the music.

notes.title: Emptying spittle
notes.html_source:
When you play a brass instrument, your warm, moist breath will condense inside the instrument as it travels through the cooler metal tubes of the instrument. When this happens, it turns from a gas to a liquid and sits in the metal tubes of the instrument. As this water vapor (some of it will consist of saliva or “spit") collects in the instrument, it can affect its sound.

To remove the accumulated water (or what players call “spit"), players open the spit valve — also called the “water key.” The water key or spit valve is a small hole that’s usually closed.

notes.title: Fetter lane

In chapter 9, Stephen’s thoughts go as follows:

Do and do. Thing done. In a rosery of Fetter Lane of Gerard, herbalist, he walks, greyedauburn. […] One life is all. One body. Do. But do.

The astute reader and Joyce are aware of the coming together of Stephen’s and Leopold’s minds. The astute reader is very aware of the writer at this point – a technique which occurs in other chapters (Paul Franssen, A. J. Hoenselaars. notes.title: I was just passing the time of day with old Troy of the D. M. P. at the corner of Arbour hill there and be damned but a bloody sweep came along and he near drove his gear into my eye.
notes.html_source:
Joyce opens the chapter, and continues throughout, with puns on ‘I’/‘Eye’ – playing on the Cyclops' single eye, and his eventual unfortunate encounter with a giant, sharpened piece of olive wood, hidden under some dung in Homer’s Odyssey.

Arbour Hill, incidentally, is a street in Stoneybatter, Dublin, that was renowned for its colourful characters and sharp wit, to say nothing of its famous jail and prostitutes.

PROPOSED SUGGESTION: Old Troy had been an official with the Dublin Metropolitan Police (D.M.P.). “Old Troy” is also a reference to the site of the Trojan War where Odysseus plays a prominent role, especially with respect to the huge, hollow horse, whereby he and his men gain access within the walls of the city. Could it be that Odysseus/Bloom, as the sweep, is trying, at this point, to enter “Troy” with only traditional tools and strategies, as with brooms and ladders, as the narrator complains of when the sweep and his equipment are “obstructing the thoroughfare" shortly below?

notes.title: In Inisfail the fair there lies a land, the land of holy Michan. There rises a watchtower beheld of men afar. There sleep the mighty dead as in life they slept, warriors and princes of high renown. A pleasant land it is in sooth of murmuring waters, fishful streams where sport the gurnard, the plaice, the roach, the halibut, the gibbed haddock, the grilse, the dab, the brill, the flounder, the pollock, the mixed coarse fish generally and other denizens of the aqueous kingdom too numerous to be enumerated. In the mild breezes of the west and of the east the lofty trees wave in different directions their firstclass foliage, the wafty sycamore, the Lebanonian cedar, the exalted planetree, the eugenic eucalyptus and other ornaments of the arboreal world with which that region is thoroughly well supplied. Lovely maidens sit in close proximity to the roots of the lovely trees singing the most lovely songs while they play with all kinds of lovely objects as for example golden ingots, silvery fishes, crans of herrings, drafts of eels, codlings, creels of fingerlings, purple seagems and playful insects. And heroes voyage from afar to woo them, from Eblana to Slievemargy, the peerless princes of unfettered Munster and of Connacht the just and of smooth sleek Leinster and of Cruahan’s land and of Armagh the splendid and of the noble district of Boyle, princes, the sons of kings.
notes.html_source: Joyce again dips into another style, this time epic Irish mythic poetry, which again serves as a contrast between the demotic language of the characters in the story, and the high falutin language of these sections. In keeping with the interrogation of the idea of nationality, this begins with a reasonable approximation of mythic language before becoming increasingly ridiculous, comically showing that the myths and ideas of a nation become absurd when brought into the context of the modern age.

notes.title: Rory of the hill
notes.html_source:
The last lines of the ballad, Rory of the Hill

The poet, and the orator,
The heart of man can sway,
And would to the kind heavens
That Wolfe Tone were here to-day!
Yet trust me friends, dear Ireland’s strength,
Her truest strength is still
The rough-and-ready roving boys,
Like Rory of the Hill.

This may be a central theme of the Cyclops chapter, as it was of Sirens; while the flamboyant, garish language of poets, and the empty rhetoric of oratory can sway, Ireland’s genius and future lie with the best of Irish everyman, at least with those who rise above the type of fecklessness and dissolution exhibited throughout much of Ulysses, and especially in these two chapters, a challenge perhaps as daunting as Odysseus and a few of his faithful Greek “Rapparees” penetrating the walls of Troy.

notes.title: Irish heroes and heroines
notes.html_source:
Joyce dismisses traditional heroes and idols-made-demigods, as he denigrates the myths and folklore that inevitably exaggerate their virtues and deny their vices. Again, the true heroes are like the one he presents to us in his great novel. It is Bloom with all his faults, fears, and eccentricities, whom he prototypes as the true Irish hero.

Joyce intended to have novel, style, myth and symbolism work together organically (Morris, N. A companion to James Joyce Ulysses, p22).

This seems to be a jab at Irish nationalism.

Whether Bloom is/was actually a freemason is a question Joyce leaves open to debate.

notes.title: The brothers Sheares

From D. S. Sullivan’s Speeches from the Dock, 1886. It displays the kind of florid speech being parodied here.

“Among the many distinguished Irishmen who acted prominent parts in the stormy events of 1798, and whose names come down to us hallowed by the sufferings and sacrifices inseparable in those dark days from the lot of an Irish patriot, there are few whose fate excited more sympathy, more loved in life, more Honored in death, than the brothers John and Henry Sheares. Even in the days of Emmet and Wolfe Tone, of Russell and Fitzgerald, when men of education, talent, and social standing were not few in the national ranks, the Sheareses were hailed as valuable accessions to the cause, and were recognized by the United Irishmen as heaven-destined leaders for the people. notes.title: Speranza’s plaintive muse
notes.html_source: This refers to the pen name of Lady Jane Wilde, who not only gave birth to her famous literary son Oscar, but was a poet of some fame herself. Her activism for Irish independence led to her being considered “Speranza of the Nation.” Her poem To Ireland, contained the kind of extreme passionate nationalism that Joyce seems to be lampooning in this parody. Robert Emmet, whose public funeral the parody supposedly describes, was executed in 1803, eighteen years prior to Lady Jane’s birth. There was, in fact, no public funeral for Emmet. Joyce was wary of such excessive emotionalism would devolve into kitsch.

James Stephens was the head of the organization that would eventually become the Irish Republican Brotherhood, and he was arrested in 1865. In just the matter of a fortnight he escaped prison, supposedly with assistance, and fled to France.

In Calypso, Bloom mentions the same aphorism about “the boxpay man at the bathhouse”.

notes.title: The adulteress and her paramour brought the Saxon robbers here
notes.html_source: The adulteress in question is “MacMurrough’s wife” Devorgilla (Derbforgaill or Derval), wife of Tiernan O'Rourke (Ua Ruaric), Prince of Breffni. Her fabled paramour was Dermot MacMurrough (Mac Murchada), King of Leinster. The story goes that while Prince O'Rourke was away, Devorgilla was “captured” (willingly, as is told) by King MacMurrough and taken back to his capital. Prince O'Rourke sought aid from Rory O'Connor, High King of Ireland, who had MacMurrough deposed. He sought refuge in Bristol and when denied help from Henry II of England, Henry’s enemy Richard de Clare (2nd Earl of Pembroke) was more receptive and with his forces regained his kingdom (in exchange for his daughter Aiofe MacMurrough’s hand in marriage). This opened the door for further conquest and subjugation of Ireland, which occurred later at the hands of Henry II in 1171, resulting in total Norman control of the island.

notes.title: We fought for the royal Stuarts that reneged us against the Williamites and they betrayed us.
notes.html_source:
The Williamite War in Ireland (in Irish, Cogadh an Dá Rí, meaning “War of the Two Kings”) took place from 1688–1691. In 1688, during the Glorious Revolution, Stuart King James II was deposed by Dutch Protestant Prince William of Orange, James' own nephew and son-in-law, amid growing fears about James' Catholicism, his ties to France, and the birth of a son who would interrupted the expected succession of his Protestant daughter Mary (wife of William and later Queen, co-regnant with William) to the throne.

James was supported by the mostly Catholic Ireland (supporters of the Stuart dynasty were known as “Jacobites”, cf. “James”) and tried to use the country as a base to regain his kingship. However, Protestants in the north of the country (“Williamites”) supported an invasion by William and forces from several other nations (including Dutch and Danish troops). In the ensuing wars in Ireland, James was outmanned; the turning point was at the Battle of the Boyne (1690) which saw many Jacobite losses, after which James fled the Island. The war had a lasting impact on Ireland, confirming British (and Protestant) rule over the island that would last for more than 200 years.

notes.title: Limerick and the broken treatystone
notes.html_source:
The Treaty of Limerick (in Irish, Conradh Luimnigh) ended the Williamite War in Ireland (1688-1691) and was reputedly signed on a large block of limestone called the Treaty Stone. To this day, the stone is displayed on a large pedestal in Limerick. It remains intact, so references to breaking it here must be figurative: several articles in the treaty protecting the rights of Jacobites and Catholic gentry were ultimately not honored.

After the Jacobites (supporters of the deposed King James II) lost the Battle of the Boyne (1690), William issued the Declaration of Finglas which pardoned Jacobite soldiers but not senior officers. The officers kept fighting and saw a major victory in the Siege of Limerick (1691). However, in the next year they suffered decisive losses at the hands of the Williamites at the Battle of Aughrim and the Second Siege of Limerick.

notes.title: Each of the four masters
notes.html_source:
In the 1630s, four individuals working at a Franciscan friary compiled a chronicle of Irish history from the deluge up to 1616 in what came to be known as the Annals of the Four Masters. Joyce gave each of the masters a symbol akin to that of each of the Four Evangelists. These symbols feature more prominently in Finnegan’s Wake.

From the Wikipedia article:
The chief compiler of the annals was (1) Brother Mícheál Ó Cléirigh from Ballyshannon, who was assisted by, among others, (2) Cú Choigcríche Ó Cléirigh, (3) Fearfeasa Ó Maol Chonaire and
(4) Peregrine Ó Duibhgeannain. Although only one of the authors, Mícheál Ó Cléirigh, was a Franciscan friar, they became known as ‘The Four Friars’ or in the original Irish, Na Ceithre Máistrí.

*The note on page 1077 (431.1) in the Penguin Classics Annotated Students Edition is completely incorrect.
