notes.title: Love loves to love love.
notes.html_source:
As pointed out in Ulysses Annotated, Joyce is winking at St. Augustine’s discussion of the state of loving in Confessions:

I loved not yet, yet I loved to love, and out of a deep-seated want, I hated myself for wanting not. I sought what I might love, in love with loving, and safety I hated, and a way without snares.

Here, though, Joyce treats Augustine with a kind of loving pastiche, as the transcendent qualities of Confessions are projected onto the local sphere: this paragraph essentially amounts to a “love is in the air” kind of celebration, but the Augustinian underpinning hints that all love is, or can be, rarified love.

Don Gifford and Robert J. Seidman, Ulysses Annotated (Oakland, CA: University of California Press, 1989).

notes.title: The apple of discord
notes.html_source:
Refers to a famous episode from Greek myth. As the Vermont Apples website for some reason explains:

Minerva (Athena) was the goddess of wisdom, but on one occasion she did a very foolish thing; she entered into competition with Juno (Hera) and Venus (Aphrodite) for the prize of beauty. It happened thus: At the marriage of Peleus and Thetis all the gods were invited with the exception of Eris (Discord). Enraged at her exclusion, the goddess threw a golden apple among the guests, with the inscription, “For the Fairest.” Thereupon Juno, Venus, and Minerva each claimed the apple. Jupiter (Zeus), not willing to decide in so delicate a matter, sent the goddesses to Mount Ida, where the beautiful shepherd Paris was tending his flocks, and to him was committed the decision.

The goddesses accordingly appeared before him. Juno promised him power and riches, Minerva glory and renown in war, and Venus the fairest of women for his wife, each attempting to bias his decision in her own favor. Paris decided in favor of Venus and gave her the golden apple, thus making the two other goddesses his enemies. Under the protection of Venus, Paris sailed to Greece, and was hospitably received by Menelaus, king of Sparta. notes.title: Wigs on the green
notes.html_source:
Humorous old phrase meaning a fracas or violent confrontation, chiefly Irish. It originated in the 1700s when wigs were part of the typical male costume. Back then, if a fight were to break out, the combatants' wigs would often be dislodged in the proceedings and could then be observed rolling around on the lawn, an odd and comic sight.

It’s most common usage is “there’ll be wigs on the green [if XYZ]…” as a warning or a prediction that an altercation will occur if condition XYZ is satisfied.

“Green” is a byword for park in Ireland (see, e.g., St. Stephen’s Green)

notes.title: About the halcyon days what they meant
notes.html_source:
A (past) period of idyllic calm, peace, and happiness; often nostalgic.

The phrase derives from the mythological Alcyone, daughter of wind god Aeolus. When her husband died in a shipwreck, Alcyone threw herself into the sea and the pitying gods transformed both her and her husband Ceyx into halcyon birds (kingfishers). When she made her nest on the beach, waves threatened to destroy it. Aeolus restrained the winds, providing seven days of calm each year so she could lay her eggs. These became known as the “halcyon days,” when storms do not occur.

notes.title: The memory of the past
notes.html_source:
The phrase “the memory of the past” alludes to a line in the song There Is a Flower That Bloometh in Wallace’s opera Maritana. The significance of references to “flowers”, and, of course, especially to “Bloometh” in the novel suggests a special significance to Joyce here. Perhaps it is to his lingering regrets for the turn his life took early on as he recreates it for Stephen in Portrait of the Artist. There on Sandymount Strand, the same setting as in Nausicaa, (“[Young Stephen] looked northward toward Howth,” the promontory the narrator mentions six times in Nausicaa), Stephen wonders, “Where is my boyhood now? Where was the soul that had hung back from her destiny, to brood alone upon the shame of her wounds and in her house of squalor and subterfuge… Or where was he?”

When Stephen is described in Portrait as “alone amidst… the veiled grey sunlight and gayclad figures of children and girls and voices and girlish in the air,” the similarities to Nausicaa could not be starker. The girl he is captivated by is described thusly: “Her long slender bare legs were delicate… Her thighs, fuller and soft-hued as ivory, were bared almost to the hips… Her slate-blue skirts were kilted boldly about her waist… But her long fair hair … touched, with wonder of mortal beauty, her face.” The narrator continues, “ She was… gazing out to sea; and when she felt his presence and the worship of his eyes, her eyes turned to him in quiet sufferance of his gaze…”

This moment radically transformed Stephen’s outlook, and led to a life of indulgence it is possible he came to deeply regret, and which may have contributed greatly to the sadness Gerty saw in Bloom’s face. That period of Stephen’s life, “[he] bore cynically with the shameful details of his secret riots in which he exulted to defile with patience whatever image had attracted his eyes.” Now, mature Bloom, despite whatever remorse he may feel, was about to defile the image that had attracted his eyes, the image he had nearly deified,with a secret, conscience-betraying act Stephen had habituated during, and despite, his virtue-seeking youth.

notes.title: Forty hours’ adoration
notes.html_source:
Forty Hours Devotion
This is a special period of continuous prayer during which the Eucharist is exposed in a monstrance for adoration. The devotion begins with a Mass followed by continuous adoration over a 40-hour period, and it ends with a Mass and Benediction. In the Bible the number 40 is associated with a sacred period of time: the rain at the time of the flood of Noah lasted 40 days and nights, and the Hebrews wandered in the desert for 40 years on the way to the Promised Land. Jesus fasted for 40 days before beginning his public ministry.

notes.title: Those evening bells
notes.html_source: “Those Evening Bells” is the title of another Thomas Moore song. The lyrics add to the melancholy of this part of the chapter, and of a sense of nostalgia and lost youthful innocence that seem to affect Bloom. “Those evening bells! those evening bells! / How many a tale their music tells, / Of youth and home, and that sweet time, / When I last heard their soothing chime…. / And so ‘twill be when I am gone, / That tuneful peal will still ring on, / While other bards shall walk these dells, / And sing your praise, sweet evening bells.” Since Joyce seems to have also obsessed over competition from “other bards” than himself who then, and would later, walk the dells of Ireland.

notes.title: The new I want
notes.html_source:
In Proteus, Stephen contemplates various characters as models.The narrator says of them, “Houses of decay, mine, his and all. You told the Clongowes gentry you had an uncle a judge and an uncle a general in the army. Come out of them, Stephen. Beauty is not there.”

Phillip M. Weinstein says of these figures, “Each of these identities is a pose, all too common… in an Ireland that is a ‘Paradise of pretenders then and now.” In Nausicaa, Bloom’s thought on this is “The new I want. Nothing new under the sun… Think you’re escaping and run into yourself. Longest way round is the shortest way home.“ In all these examples of escapism, what is realized is that, rebellious as they may be, each carries himself away in the exile, indelibly marked by the very influences he seeks to reject. Weinstein points out: “Nothing new under the sun: sons are born into families, churches, countries… Stephen’s true enemy is sonship itself. He desires to create the world out of himself… Not for nothing does he muse throughout Ulysses over [heresy].” What mature Bloom discovers is that escape is impossible, leaving only acceptance as an option, but an acceptance that leaves him as a “keyless citizen,” which image Joyce imposes on both Bloom and Stephen not just figuratively. What Bloom, partly in his Jewishness, is able to achieve is exile while yet a citizen of Dublin. This has Weinstein, therefore, asserting that, “Ulysses is the greatest celebration of presence in modern fiction. Joyce has created an image of experience in which Yes accommodates No without ceasing to be Yes.

notes.title: Send us bright one, light one, Horhorn, quickening and wombfruit.
notes.html_source:
A sentence that begins like an ancient invocation or prayer ends with two references to childbirth. Throughout this chapter, the language Joyce uses evolves, from Anglo-Saxon and its Greco-Latin influences to Modern English. This parallels the theme of development and birth that is seen in the birth of the Purefoy child. Joyce manages to allude to both of these developmental elements in the chapter in one of his opening statements.

PROPOSED SUGGESTION: an invocation to the sungod Helios (“bright one, light one”)

Horhorn refers to Sir Andrew Horne, who in 1904 was administrator of the Holles Street hospital. Joyce plays a joke here at the expense of Horne, making his already phalic name a symbol of fertility.

notes.title: Thole
notes.html_source:
Verb meaning to suffer, endure, tolerate, bear.

Full etymology from wiktionary reproduced below:

From Middle English thōle, from tholen, tholien (“to be made to undergo a penalty; to suffer; to experience (something unpleasant); to bear, endure, put up with; to allow, permit”), from Old English þolian (“to endure, suffer, undergo; to thole”), from Proto-Germanic þuljaną (“to suffer”), from Proto-Indo-European telh₂- (“to bear, suffer; to support”). The word is cognate with Danish tåle (“to tolerate”), Middle Low German dōlen (“to endure”), Middle High German doln (“to allow, bear, suffer”), Latin tollō (“to cancel, lift off, remove”), tolerō (“to bear, endure”), Norwegian Bokmål tåle (“to tolerate”), Norwegian Nynorsk tola (“to tolerate”), Swedish tåla (“to tolerate”). It is also related to English thild.

notes.title: That last end that is thy death
notes.html_source: Joyce chooses well for imitating Middle English prose. The simplicity and didactic nature of the work is sufficiently distinct to make of it a good model. Yet, Everyman may present another message for the earnest reader. Consistent with a life-quest for returning from exile from God, which the reader must determine for himself as to whether Joyce derides or advocates it (there is ample evidence to support either view), the play suggests that “everyman” will, in fact, experience that reunion at death, but warns that the quality of the experience will vary greatly based on one’s choices in life. E.A. Gamini Fonseka writes of the play, “While noted for its simplicity, Everyman remains a piece of morality theatre teaching every man and woman on how to face death bravely and wisely on the strength of leading his/her life in accordance with the norms of Christian morals and principles of charity. Nevertheless, the style does not overdo to the theme in making it too complex for the spectator to understand the plain truth of life… The play dramatizes God’s expectation of everyman and his frustration over his degeneration.” Does Joyce also actually lament the dissolute behavior he seems to relish so in portraying it all in Ulysses?

To swink is a term meaning to work or labor at (can be used as a noun to mean toil, work, drudgery, etc.). Here it seems to be used to mean something like “forge” which is a bit of a stretch.

It also has interesting etymology (wiktionary):
From Middle English swinken, from Old English swincan (“to labour, work at, strive, struggle; be in trouble; languish”), from Proto-Germanic swinkaną (“to swing, bend”), from Proto-Indo-European sweng-, *swenk- (“to bend, swing, swivel”). Cognate with Old Norse svinka (“to work”). Related to swing.

notes.title: Wight
notes.html_source:
A wight is a living creature, usually a human being.

You may have learned the term from Tolkien’s LOTR (cf. barrow-wights)

Etymology:
From Middle English wight, wiȝt, from Old English wiht (“wight, person, creature, being, whit, thing, something, anything”), from Proto-Germanic wihtiz (“essence, object”), from Proto-Indo-European wekti- (“cause, sake, thing”), from Proto-Indo-European *wekʷ- (“to say, tell”). Cognate with Scots wicht (“creature, being, human”), Dutch wicht (“child, baby”), German Low German Wicht (“girl; wight”), German Wicht (“wretch, wight, little creature, scoundrel”), Norwegian Bokmål vette (“underground creature, gnome”), Swedish vätte (“underground creature, gnome”), Icelandic vættur (“imp, elf”). See also whit.

What follows is a parody of Sir Ector’s eulogy for sir Lancelot.

Malory’s version:

Ah Launcelot, he said, thou were head of all Christian knights, and now I dare say, said Sir Ector, thou Sir Launcelot, there thou liest, that thou were never matched of earthly knight’s hand. And thou were the courteoust knight that ever bare shield. And thou were the truest friend to thy lover that ever bestrad horse. And thou were the truest lover of a sinful man that ever loved woman. And thou were the kindest man that ever struck with sword. And thou were the goodliest person that ever came among press of knights. And thou was the meekest man and the gentlest that ever ate in hall among ladies. And thou were the sternest knight to thy mortal foe that ever put spear in the rest. Then there was weeping and dolour out of measure.

notes.title: Saint Ultan of Arbraccan
notes.html_source:
St Ultan was abbot-bishop at Ardbraccan in Co Meath, an important ecclesiastical centre in the middle ages.

Ultan is thought to have been a holy and learned man, possibly a pupil of St Declan, who founded a monastery and school at Ardbraccan, near Navan, Co Meath. Here he educated and fed poor students. He may also have illuminated manuscripts and written a life of St Brigid. He may also have been a bishop of the Desi of Meath.

During the yellow plague (Buidhe Ghonaill) which broke out not alone in Ireland, but also in England, Scotland, and many European countries at that time, St Ultan made a shelter for children who suffered from the plague and at one time had up to 150 children near his monastery.

He was original and inventive. The annals tell us he designed a feeding bottle using cows’ teats, which he filled with milk and put into the babies’ mouths with his own hands, probably the first mentioned baby’s feeding bottle on record.
CatholicIreland.net

“The Song of the Cheerful (but slightly Sarcastic) Jesus” is a poem by Oliver St. John Gogarty. notes.title: Entweder_ transubstantiality ODER consubstantiality but in no case subsubstantiality
notes.html_source:
(German) Either … or.

In Catholic theology, transsubstantiation is the technical term to describe the principle underlying the doctrine of the Real Presence, according to which the consecrated bread and wine in the Eucharist take on the actual substance of the body and blood of Jesus Christ, while retaining the outward appearance or accidence of bread and wine.

Consubstanstiation is the term used to describe an alternative interpretation of the mystery of the Eucharist, according to which the consecrated bread and wine comprise the substance of Christ alongside that of the original unconsecrated bread and wine. The doctrine of consubstantiation is usually associated with Lutheranism, though Martin Luther himself held a slightly different position. This, presumably, explains Stephen’s use of German terms.

Needless to remark, subsubstantiality is Stephen’s drunken contribution to the theology of the Real Presence. In his intoxicated state, he is confusing two different theologial controversies: (1) the relationship between the consecrated Host in theEucharist and Jesus Christ, and (2)the relationship between the Virgin Mary and Jesus Christ. According to Catholic doctrine, Mary was the mother of Jesus Christ the man and of Jesus Christ the God. this is also held by Lutherans.

notes.html_source:
To Mistress Margery Wentworth
- John Skelton. 1460?–1529

WITH margerain gentle,
The flower of goodlihead,
Embroidered the mantle
Is of your maidenhead.
Plainly I cannot glose;
Ye be, as I divine,
The pretty primrose,
The goodly columbine.

Benign, courteous, and meek,
With wordes well devised;
In you, who list to seek,
Be virtues well comprised.
With margerain gentle,
The flower of goodlihead,
Embroidered the mantle
Is of your maidenhead.

In Elizabethan herbals, margerain (marjoram) was the herb of calm and gentleness, a remedy for diseases of the brain. - Gifford

notes.title: An exquisite dulcet epithalame of most mollificative suadency for juveniles amatory whom the odoriferous flambeaus of the paranymphs have escorted to the quadrupedal proscenium of connubial communion.
notes.html_source:
Wow – what a line, has taken me a day of research to even hypothesize what it might mean.

Dulcet – (Especially of sound) sweet and soothing (often used ironically)
Epithalame – from Epithalamium – a song in praise of bride and bridegroom, sung by a number of boys and girls at the door of the nuptial chamber
Mollificative – that makes soft or supple
Suadency – to persuade
Paranymphs – From Middle French, French paranymphe and its etymons post-classical Latin paranymphus male wedding attendant, best man and paranympha bridesmaid from ancient Greek παράνυμϕος (masculine noun) friend of the bridegroom, best man, in Byzantine Greek also (feminine noun) bridesmaid from παρα- + νύμϕη bride

So, it might mean (with Joyce you never know what all it could mean) — A most beautiful sweet & soothing song of soft persuasion sung by boys & girls outside the nuptial chamber as the Best man & Bridesmaids escort the young bride & bridegroom under the light of flaming torch (might symbolize Hymen – the Greek god of marriage) to the four footed theatrical stage (curtained bed in Nupital chamber) for them to consummate their marital union.

notes.title: Hamlet his father showeth the prince no blister of combustion
notes.html_source:
The ghost of Hamlet’s father says to Hamlet,

But that I am forbid
To tell the secrets of my prison house,
I could a tale unfold whose lightest word
Would harrow up thy soul […]
But this blazon must not be
To ears of flesh and blood.

The inference is not about Hamlet Sr.’s murder; he is telling his son that he is imprisoned in an environment that would act as if to explode in blistering flames, were he allowed to describe it. This description of the reward for decadence, combined with that referred to in the succeeding sentence, referring to Dante’s Inferno, appears to be a warning of dark and dismal Hell. Again, the reader must determine for himself whether this is Joyce’s satire or seriousness.

notes.title: As the ends and ultimates of all things accord in some mean and measure with their inceptions and originals, that same multiplicit concordance which leads forth growth from birth accomplishing by a retrogressive metamorphosis that minishing and ablation towards the final which is agreeable unto nature so is it with our subsolar being.
notes.html_source:
This difficult, but not insignificant, passage paraphrases Aristotle quoting Empedocles, who argues a cyclical theory of creation, in whose first stages love adjoins things in such an indiscriminate manner as to produce monstrous beasts such as the ox-man. These creatures, unable to reproduce, gradually disappear from the population, a manifestation of nature’s self-correcting tendencies.

Aristotle: “Thus in the original combinations the ‘ox-progeny’ if they failed to reach a determinate end must have arisen through the corruption of some principle corresponding to what is now the seed.” The corrupted principle stressed in the Oxen of the Sun chapter is that of man’s duty to “multiply and replenish the earth,” avoided by young Irishmen of the time.

notes.title: _Talis ac tanta depravatio hujus seculi, O quirites, ut matresfamiliarum nostrae lascivas cujuslibet semiviri libici titillationes testibus ponderosis atque excelsis erectionibus centurionum Romanorum magnopere anteponunt_
notes.html_source:
(Latin) Such and so great is the depravity of our generation, O Citizens, that our materfamiliases greatly prefer the lascivious titillations of any barbaric half-man whomsoever to the ponderous testicles and extraordinary erections of Roman centurions.[1] Needless to say, this is not a quotation from the Classics, though the style is deliberately Ciceronian.

Mulligan’s libici is problematic. Thornton translates it as lustful, which would actually be libidinosi. Gifford translates it as Gallic, an allusion to the Libici, a Gallic people;[2] but Libicorum would be the correct form. In the first draft Joyce wrote Libycci (or Libyeci), so his original intention seems clear: Libyci (Libyan, African).[3]

The point of the passage is that Roman matrons prefer sexual satisfaction to conception: copulation without population, another form of contraception, which is the interpretation Joyce puts on the slaughter of the Oxen of the Sun in this episode.

Source:https://en.wikibooks.org/wiki/Annotations_to_James_Joyce%27s_Ulysses/Oxen_of_the_Sun/384

notes.title: But the word of Mr Costello was an unwelcome language for him for he nauseated the wretch that seemed to him a cropeared creature of a misshapen gibbosity, born out of wedlock and thrust like a crookback toothed and feet first into the world, which the dint of the surgeon’s pliers in his skull lent indeed a colour to, so as to put him in thought of that missing link of creation’s chain desiderated by the late ingenious Mr Darwin.
notes.html_source:
While impersonating Burke, Joyce can’t resist an allusion to Shakespeare here. In Act V, Scene VI of Henry VI, Gloucester, who would soon become Richard III, stabs the protagonist, who has just compared himself to Daedalus, and his son to Icarus, and exclaims:

“I, that have neither pity, love, nor fear.
Indeed, ‘tis true that Henry told me of;
For I have often heard my mother say
I came into the world with my legs forward.”

Gloucester/Richard, we know, was born with a “crookback” deformity, and Joyce’s addition of “gibbosity,” which also means “hunchbacked”, further establishes the mention, whose purpose here is not only to echo “Burke’s” denouncing Irish youth as having “neither pity, love, nor fear,” but is also to point us to the Ulysses-specific reference to Daedalus and Icarus. The key to this reference occurs in the “"Scylla and Charybdis” episode as Stephen is expounding his Shakespeare/Hamlet theory. Stephen is brought to remember the final entry in his diary in A Portrait*:

“Fabulous artificer. The hawklike man. You flew. Whereto? Newhaven-Dieppe,steerage passenger. Paris and back. Lapwing. Icarus. Pater, ait. Seabedabbled, fallen, weltering.Lapwing you are. Lapwing be.”

What is the significance of “lapwing”? George L. Geckle, in his Winter 1969 article in the James Joyce Quarterly, takes us to an unsurprising third level of depth in answering it; William M. Schutte, quoting from Blake’s Gnomic Verses, describes a lapwing and then observes, “Blake’s lapwing, flying around on the barren heath instead of where the corn grows, ignorant both of where the soil is fruitful… , is a good symbol for the ambitious but often misdirected young man to whom Stephen refers… , a young man that could fly by all the nets that sought to restrain him.” Geckle argues that, while some critics may argue that Joyce would have been aware of the implications of these references, Stephen would not. He writes, “The Stephen in Ulysses, I would argue, becomes well aware of the implications of his references, especially when such references show the irony of his past aspirations and present failures. The ‘lapwing’ passage is proof that such is the case.”

The residents rushed to meet the gurney and immediately recognized the unconscious shooting victim: he was the teenage delivery boy from their favorite all-night restaurant, and he’d been mugged bringing their dinner. What is Twin Reversed Arterial Perfusion (TRAP) Sequence?
TRAP sequence is a very rare condition that only occurs in twin pregnancies that share a common placenta (monochorionic twins). notes.title: Sepsis
notes.html_source:
Sepsis is a serious illness. It happens when your body has an overwhelming immune response to a bacterial infection. The chemicals released into the blood to fight the infection trigger widespread inflammation. This leads to blood clots and leaky blood vessels. They cause poor blood flow, which deprives your body’s organs of nutrients and oxygen. In severe cases, one or more organs fail. In the worst cases, blood pressure drops and the heart weakens, leading to septic shock.

notes.title: Grissel Steevens
notes.html_source:
Griselda Steevens (1653 – 18 March 1746) was left an large income by her twin brother. A clause in Dr Steevens' will stipulated that on Griselda’s death, the income was to be used to provide a hospital for the poor of Dublin. Although the terms of Dr Steevens' will were that work on the hospital would not begin until after Griselda Steevens' death, she decided to begin work on the hospital in 1720. As a youth Griselda had suffered a disorder of the eyes, and since then had worn a veil while in sunlight. Shy and reclusive, while conducting her charitable works in the Dublin slums she would remain in her carriage while servants gave out alms to the poor. By 1723 a sufficient portion of the new Dr Steevens' Hospital was completed to accommodate 40 patients, in addition to Griselda’s apartments. Griselda lived in the hospital from 1723 until her death.
At some point, it became a common belief in Dublin that Griselda Steevens had a pig’s face. It is unclear when the rumour arose. Robert Chambers and Irish Georgian Society founder Desmond Guinness claim that the rumour was current in her lifetime, but Thomas Kirkpatrick, author of History of Dr Steevens' Hospital Dublin, says that “There is absolutely no evidence of this story in contemporary records, nor indeed does it appear to have been connected with the good lady until the nineteenth century”
Wikipedia

notes.title: He conjured up the scene before them.
notes.html_source:
In Oxen of the Sun, Joyce has another objective in addition to just parodying Horace Walpole; he also adds commentary on the state of affairs in Ireland. He appoints Buck Mulligan spokesman, and has him relate, in his typically caustic and flippant manner, a tale that “began to freeze them with horror.” As R. M. Adams reminds us, “Ireland is a land of walking ghosts and barely vitalized corpses,” and Mulligan presents his listeners, in an ante room in the National Maternity Hospital, a highly unique staging for a mostly rowdy conversation among mostly young men, only some of whom, as medical students and residents, have a clear reason for being there. “The secret panel beside the chimney slid back and in the recess appeared… Haines!”

This highly symbolic character, and roommate to Mulligan and Stephen, is used at times in Ulysses to caricaturize the upper-crust, superior, dominating English who have “usurped” Ireland for their own exploitation. That, of the three roommates in the Martello tower, he, the Englishman, was the only one to have studied the “Erse” (Gaelic) language indicts the Irish as having abandoned its culture, and Haines is all too willing to laud it over the others for his eminence. Haines claims responsibility for the Childs murder case, in which the victim and his family, despite the victim’s brother being accused of the crime, were respectable, upper-middle class, the father a former service provider to the Viceroy, the victim a literary and highly respected Church of Ireland clergyman, whose open book on the history of the Bible was splattered with blood at the scene, the accused a successful accountant.

Could Joyce be inferring that Haines, as surrogate for the English, had destroyed this respectable, genteel part of Ireland, and left it with the crudeness and boorishness such as was displayed by this band of young men that evening at the hospital, educated, and seemingly accomplished as they were? The guilt-ridden ghost Haines exclaims, “My hell, and Ireland’s, is in this life. It is what I tried to obliterate my crime. Distractions, rookshooting…, laudanum…, In vain! His [Ireland’s?] spectre stalks me. Dope is my only hope… Ah! Destruction! The black panther!”

notes.title: The black panther
notes.html_source:
Haines had experienced a nightmare in which appeared a black panther, whose terror he tried to end by shooting [destroying] it. Samuel Chenevix Trench, on whom Haines’s character is modeled, actually shot off a round from a revolver in experiencing the dream. The black panther, or leopard, is used several times in Biblical imagery. Jeremiah 5:6, for instance: “…a leopard shall watch over their cities: every one that goeth out thence shall be torn in pieces: because their transgressions are many, and their backslidings are increased.“ The “leopard” doing the watching is a Christ figure, the choice of “cities,” here Dublin, whose “transgressions are many, and their backslidings are increased.” The black panther is also, in Slovenian folklore a symbol for Deep understanding and spirituality.

In Gracious Wild: A Shamanic Journey with Hawks, Stacey L. L. Couch tells us the black panther is a symbol of darkness, not just because of the color, but also because, “Jungles are wet, messy, jumbled places and they mirror the unkept [sic] and unknown part of our unconscious. Black panther spirit animal is adept at navigating the unconscious, hidden parts of ourselves. She ventures into the unknown, comfortable with the darkness. Black panther spirit animal understands that the jungle is fraught with danger and rich with resources. The shadow is both good and bad.” She also delves into many themes from Ulysses as she asserts that, “Black panther symbolism is not only about traveling into our own darkness, but also the mystery of the universe. Both jaguars and leopards are solitary animals, and black panther spirit animal lends us the courage to venture into the unknown alone. The mystery of the universe is … the darkness of the womb, the place of pure potential creation… The void is a place beyond the five senses where we must venture on faith alone. The absence of moonlight makes black panther less visible and a superior huntress. The new moon is a time of both death and rebirth, when we stand at the threshold looking back at what was and looking ahead at what’s come. Neither are certain for this brief window in time. What was is no more and what’s to be is not yet born… The moon is strongly associated with the feminine as is the jungle and darkness, thus the black panther is said to carry the energy of the feminine principles of receptivity and intuition. Now is not the time for figuring things out or striking out, but for both turning inward to your soul and opening up to the Divine.”

The quote in the Oxen of the Sun episode complicates things further: “The black panther himself was the ghost of his own father.” Previous passages in which the phrase appears had clear references to Hamlet, and to Christ, whose father was referred to, sometimes indelicately, as the Holy Ghost. In Telemachus, however. Stephen hears his father’s voice as his own, for, as Mulligan has said, “he himself is the ghost of his own father.” This could infer that Stephen is either seen as another Irish victim, or, likelier (especially coming from Mulligan), a co-conspirator in Ireland’s destruction.

notes.title: She follows her mother with ungainly steps, a mare leading her fillyfoal. Twilight phantoms are they, yet moulded in prophetic grace of structure, slim shapely haunches, a supple tendonous neck, the meek apprehensive skull.
notes.html_source: This is how Bloom would compare his daughter Milly to her mother. Carol Loeb Schloss, in Lucia Joyce: To Dance in the Wake, however, asserts that Joyce thinks of Milly as “that once coveted, but impossible-to-possess student lover of days gone by. To herself she is ‘silly Milly’ [from Calypso episode], but to her father she is "Millicent, the young, the dear, the radiant [see next paragraph], who ‘follows her mother with ungainly steps, a mare leading her fillyfoal. Twilight phantoms are they yet moulded in prophetic grace and structure, … etc.’ From the mother Molly to the daughter Milly, from the mother mare to the daughter filly, the girl child in Ulysses is perceived to be a smaller, newer version of the older woman. This is so whether that woman is considered to be her actual mother or her more spiritually similar progenitor, the mystery lady from Trieste who gave her a flower. She is ‘the same thing [as her precursor] watered down,’ [from Hades episode] as if all women, in time, shared the same biological fate. ‘Destiny’ thinks Bloom. [from Calypso episode]. The pronoun "she” at the beginning of this passage references back to the “soul,” and in that context perhaps the message is that it is that entity that is affected in its “grace,” “shapeliness,” “suppleness,” and “meek apprehensiveness” by its precursors. Perhaps this is as true for Stephen as it is for Milly.

notes.title: They fade, sad phantoms: all is gone. Agendath is a waste land, a home of screechowls and the sandblind upupa. Netaim, the golden, is no more. And on the highway of the clouds they come, muttering thunder of rebellion, the ghosts of beasts.
notes.html_source:
The antecedent noun to the pronoun “they” could also be more “souls,” or it could be “stars.” “Twilight phantoms” above already seems to fall back on “stars,” but the mention of “structure, haunches, necks, and skulls points to the mare and her fillyfoal. That the pronoun "she” wants to point back to “soul,” especially inasmuch as the soul is used repeatedly in Ulysses, Portrait of the Artist, and in classical literature generally using the feminine gender, makes it hard to argue that we are not talking about a soul (of either gender) and its mother (or father if we’re using “feminine” as gender-neutral in reference to souls).

The section suggesting the style of De Quincy notwithstanding , to this point it seems to bear a strong, but satirical, correlation to Wordsworth’s Ode: Imitations of Immortality, notably, its fifth stanza, especially if we’re talking about souls here. To begin with, the stanza begins with the words “Our birth.” The birth process, Mrs. Purefoy giving birth as the chapter’s setting, the theme of the disinclination of Irish youth in contributing to the volume of Irish births, all leave a strong link. Wordsworth’s “Soul that rises with us,” he describes as, “our life’s Star points to a "scattered … perennial dew of stars here”. Forms of the word “cloud” are used three times in Joyce’s passage. Wordsworth claims that it is “trailing clouds of glory [that we do] come/From God, who is our home.” The Ode’s serene soul “cometh from afar,"lying on its cloud, forgetting and asleep. Joyce’s "souls” come on a misty highway “muttering thunder of rebellion, the ghosts of beasts.” It must be noted that De Quincy was very closely associated with Wordsworth, lived near him in the Lake District, and wrote a series of reminiscences of the great poet.

Agendath Nataim is a very important symbol in Ulysses; the reference appears thirteen separate times in the novel as a promised land, despite the disparagement it appears to receive in this instance – another reason I believe the insolence of the souls in the passage is also meant as irony. The ad he had seen earlier in the day calling on European Jews like himself to become part of the cultivation of Palestine, a restoration of Zion, and the poorly drafted, disjointed, contradiction-laden notice brings to Bloom’s mind the fecklessness of the Celtic revivalist movement in resolving the persistent problems of identity for Ireland. It is of Ireland and not Palestine of which Joyce is speaking here as “a waste land, a home of screechowls and the sandblind upupa,” (a weak-sighted bird that lines its nest with human excrement).

notes.title: See, thy fleece is drenched
notes.html_source:
In the book of Judges in the Bible, Gideon is called upon to lead a relatively small force of Israelites against a massive army of Middianites. Gideon wanted to make sure God was with him, so he proposed a test; “Behold, I will put a fleece of wool in the floor; and if the dew be on the fleece only, and it be dry upon the earth beside, this shall I know that thou wilt save Israel by my hand, as thou has said.” As indicated here, on the morrow the fleece was not just wet, it was drenched, and so Gideon was able to successfully lead a group that was whittled down to 300 men against the opposing army of 130,000, suggesting God’s abundant favor.

This entire passage honors Theodore Purefoy, and extols his virtues, having sired the newly born infant. Of course, the father’s role here is minimal, given without any thought of creating a new person. But, at least he is married, and he is not doing anything to prevent conception as he engages with his wife. This is high satire, in that it is the wife who faces the ordeal of nine months of pregnancy and the painful process of labor and delivery. As we have seen before, the references in the chapter, as throughout Ulysses, deal with the process of literary creation. Joyce implies, once again, that fatherhood is not as true a trope for that process as is motherhood, and that the course of creating superior literary art takes time and great and often painful effort.

notes.title: Tally ho
notes.html_source:
Annotating for etymology.

“Tally ho” was a cry raised during a fox-hunt when the quarry was sighted.

It dates from around 1772, and is probably derived from the French taïaut, a cry used to excite hounds when hunting deer.

Taïaut may have originated in the second half of the 13th century by the concatenation of a two-word war-cry: taille haut. “Taille” is the cutting edge of a sword and “haut” means high or ‘raised up’. So the original meaning might be something close to “Swords up!”.

notes.title: Red and green will-o’-the-wisps and danger signals.
notes.html_source:
A will-o'-the-wisp painted by Arnold Böcklin (1882), via Wikimedia Commons.

Will-o'-the-wisps are still-unexplained transient lights reported by old travelers—they form a big part of European folklore. They’re generally seen to be bad omens; some strains of myth depict them as souls rejected from Hell.

Don Gifford in Ulysses Annotated draws a connection with the will-o'-the-wisp in Goethe’s Faust:

In Goethe’s Faust (I.xxi), a will-o'-the-wisp lights the way up the “magic-mad” mountain as Faust and Mephistopheles make their way toward the Walpurgisnacht (Witches' Sabbath) assembly. (p.452)

PROPOSED SUGGESTION: It might be helpful to point out how appropriate it is to begin the episode with reference to the “danger signals” the will-o-the-wisps provide inasmuch as they light the way up the hill Ignis Fatuus in Faust describes as “magic-mad tonight.” “Magic-mad” fairly describes the phantasmagoric journey on which Joyce takes the reader in these pages.

notes.title: Grab wafers between which are wedged lumps of coal and copper snow
notes.html_source:
This whole episode is a wild and weird Witches Sabbath, and its phantasmagorical method makes it difficult to maneuver. The initial scene has us guessing at what it is we’re looking at when the narrator describes a cart owned by the “real” Antoni Rabaiotti dispensing ice cream, surrounded by squabbling “stunted” men and women, who greedily “grab wafers between which are wedged lumps of coal and copper snow.” They’re all “children,” the narrator explains. The immediately available choices for interpretation are, of course, many and diverse: Are the figures children who are “stunted” future adults? Are they merely callow adults acting immaturely? A deeper search by the reader will reveal that this first scene hearkens back to the Wandering Rocks episode, where children are eating ice cream by Rabaiotti’s ice cream cart when they encounter a one-legged sailor who “growls” at them. That he is a sailor is why the children order him to salute.

Of course, nothing has to make sense in this surreal setting, but, since Joyce is not one to “waste” his imagery, a carnival atmosphere such as this at the gateway to the carnal, when the root of “carnival” is carne vale, or “farewell to flesh,” with vale representing a Latin “good-bye” (literally “be strong” or “be well”), it is difficult not to see this as yet one more jab at Irish lechery-born paralysis, especially when, after clamoring for the ice cream, and having sucked on what turns out to be lumps of coal and copper snow, the children “scatter slowly” in apparent chagrin.

What we will encounter repeatedly in Circe are glimpses into past passages in the book that now take on completely different understandings – epiphanies. This chapter is about sudden enlightenment – epiphany (among other things).

Whistles call and answer.
 
 THE CALLS Wait, my love, and I’ll be with you.

notes.html_source: This exchange is mindful of the Sirens episode when Richie Goulding “cocked his lips apout,” and issued a “low incipient note sweet banshee murmured.” The whistle call of “Wait my love…” here in Circe echoes the word “wait” that appears in its sundry forms no less than fifty-five times in Sirens. The theme of waiting for love, subordinate to the greater theme in Ulysses of The Pain of Love, is brought center stage here in Circe’s stage-play setting when we recall the Siren episode’s narrator saying, “Time makes the tune.” It certainly makes the tune heard in THE CALLS' whistle here in Circe. Molly has only to wait through three more episodes (some four hours) and then Bloom “will be with [her]. In Sirens, "How sweet the answer.” How sweet THE ANSWERS of assent here in Circe.

notes.title: Jerks past, shaken in Saint Vitus’ dance.
notes.html_source:
He suffers from Sydenham chorea. Via Britannica:

Sydenham chorea, also called St. Vitus Dance, chorea minor, infectious chorea, or rheumatic chorea, a neurological disorder characterized by irregular and involuntary movements of muscle groups in various parts of the body that follow streptococcal infection. The name St. Vitus Dance derives from the late Middle Ages, when persons with the disease attended the chapels of St. Vitus, who was believed to have curative powers….Most often a manifestation of rheumatic fever, Sydenham chorea occurs most frequently between the ages of 5 and 15 years, and is more common in girls than boys. The disease may occur as an infrequent complication of pregnancy.

St. Vitus' dance is also the term for a medieval dancing mania, a bizarre social phenomenon in which:

…outbreaks seized groups of people who engaged in frenzied dancing that lasted intermittently for days or weeks. Social scientists typify victims as females who were maladjusted, deviant, irrational, or mentally disturbed. These activities were typically accompanied by symptoms similar to tarantism, including screaming, hallucinations, convulsive movements, chest pains, hyperventilation, crude sexual gestures and outright intercourse. Instead of spider bites as the cause, participants usually claimed that they were possessed by demons who had induced an uncontrollable urge to dance.

The causes are still not fully understood; however the Skeptical Inquirer argues that religious sects (not disease or “hysteria”) were probably responsible, and that many “facts” about the dancing manias (that they were spontaneous, mostly sustained by women, etc.) don’t hold up to scrutiny.

Medieval dance crazes: truly crazy.

notes.title: Fish and taters
notes.html_source:
Bloom here remembers that 17 JUN 1904 falls on a Friday, during which practising Catholics (at the time) were to abstain from meat. It is unlikely that he would be able to purchase anything to eat on a Friday in Catholic Dublin other than seafood and vegetables. He chooses in the next paragraph to purchase meat (at the last possible moment) for later consumption, thereby demonstrating his relaxed attitude toward Friday abstinence.

The Irish for “Friday” is “Aoine,” which translates literally as “fasting.”

Mercurous chloride (Hg2Cl2) is also known as calomel. Strangely, it was a white compound ! It was a popular drug from the 1800s onwards as it contained mercury, a chemical that was claimed to cure many illnesses. However, it slowly poisoned those who used it because mercury is toxic. academia.dk

notes.title: Nebrakada! Feminimum.
notes.html_source:
“Little heaven of blessed femininity.” This is a curious expression on a number of counts:

First, if (as it first appears) it is Molly angrily scolding the camel the expression makes no sense, which, in this episode, it doesn’t necessarily need to.

Second, the expression is part of a phrase Stephen reads in the Wandering Rocks episode, where he has picked up a book off a barrow in front of Clohissey’s bookshop on Bedford Row. The book purports to contain “Secrets of secrets,” including “How to win a woman’s love.” The full quote is “Se el yilo nebrakada femininum! Amor me solo! Sanktus! Amen,” or “[My] little heaven of blessed femininity, love only me. Holy! Amen.” So this is Bloom’s hallucination, wherein Molly says something neither she nor Bloom knows anything about.

Third, in spite of the fact that it was Molly who had betrayed Bloom earlier in the day, she is demanding, condescending, and angry. It is Bloom whose self-esteem is at low tide (for now). The ludicrous camel “fumbles to kneel” just as Bloom “stoops his back for leapfrog.” The camel is Bloom.

The opera Maritana by William Vincent Wallace contains a song “There is a Flower That Bloometh.” The title could not be more pertinent, either for the novel Ulysses or for the goings on at this point in Circe. The card Bloom has been carrying in his hat since morning, the card bearing the name “Henry Flower” he used as ID to get his letter from Martha Clifford that morning from the post office. This is the “Flower” that “Bloometh.” Now, as defendant in his “trial,” he appears, “holding a fullblown waterlily,” symbol of purity of heart. In the opera, Don Caesar has been tricked into marrying Maritana, and is unhappy, not knowing who she was, veiled as she had been for the ceremony. Maritana is now gone from his life, and he sings, “There is a flower that bloometh / When autumn leaves are shed. /… Oh, pluck it ere it wither, / ‘Tis the memory of the past// It wafted perfume o'er us, / Of sweet, though sad regret / For the true friends gone before us, / Whom none would e’re forget. / Let no heart brave its power, / By guilty thoughts o'ercast, / For then, a poison flow'r / Is – the memory of the past.”

If Bloom ever had true friends, there are none there to defend him. He was washed over in loneliness and the poison flower of guilty thoughts of his bad behavior, the memories of the past.

There is linkage between the Don Caesar/ Maritana couple and the Blooms. Leopold has not known who Molly is (nor, certainly, she him) and he has believed she is now is gone, at least, emotionally, from him forever. “All is lost,” the title to another aria from the opera Martha with deep significance to Ulysses.

This reference to the poem by that title by James Clarence Mangan, which, if the reader will study it, will reveal much of what haunted Joyce about his own life. There are so many parallels between this poem written long before Joyce’s birth and Joyce’s life as well as with much of the imagery in Ulysses, it is difficult to believe it was not studied by Joyce. notes.title: Timothy Harrington
notes.html_source:
Timothy Charles Harrington (1851 – 1910), born in Castletownbere, County Cork, was an Irish journalist, barrister, nationalist politician and Member of Parliament (MP) in the House of Commons of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland. As a member of the Irish Parliamentary Party he represented Westmeath from February 1883 to November 1885. In 1885 he was elected for the new constituency of Dublin Harbour, which he represented until his death in 1910. He served as Lord Mayor of Dublin three times from 1901–04.

notes.title: Was Jesus a Sun Myth?
notes.html_source:
There’s no direct proof, but it’s a plausible theory. The sun is often cast as a symbol of Christ, and Christian festivals tend to fall on at important points of the solar cycle: Christmas on the Winter Solstice and Easter on the Vernal Equinox.

Jesus also bears more than a slight resemblance to the Roman god Sol Invictus (“Unconquered Sun”), whose birth seems to have been celebrated on December 25. Some scholars have theorized that the date of Christmas Day was chosen to coincide with this, but the theory does not currently hold much sway.

A repoussé (metal relief) of Sol Invictus, from the 3rd century, found at Pessinus. Image via Wikimedia Commons.

notes.title: Bids the tide turn back
notes.html_source:
Viking King Canute had learned that his flattering courtiers claimed he was “So great, he could command the tides of the sea to go back”. Now Canute was not only a religious man, but also a clever politician. He knew his limitations – even if his courtiers did not – so he had his throne carried to the seashore and sat on it as the tide came in, commanding the waves to advance no further. When they didn’t, he had made his point that, though the deeds of kings might appear ‘great’ in the minds of men, they were as nothing in the face of God’s power.

notes.title: Artane orphans
notes.html_source:
The Artane Industrial school (Dublin) was set up in 1871 in Artane House by the Congregation of Christian Brothers. Industrial Schools were established to take in orphaned or abandoned boys or those who were involved in petty crime, and even such a minor offence as skipping school could be enough for a boy to be sent there. It has been said that about 5% of the children in Artane, indeed in all Industrial Schools, were actually orphans. Most of the incarcerated children were from families that had broken down and as separation was not allowed either, the children of these broken marriages were incarcerated and the religious institution in whose charge the children were put were paid one-third of a labourer’s wage to feed, educate and clothe each child.

notes.title: Who’s Ger Ger? Who’s dear Gerald
notes.html_source: Should read, “Who’s moth moth? Who’s dear Gerald? Dear Ger, that you? O dear, he is Gerald.” This points to the Italian philosopher Giordano Bruno who had an impact on Joyce. Bruno wrote extensively on the art of memory, a loosely organized group of mnemonic techniques and principles, and we see them mentioned in Virag Lipoti’s “testimony” at Bloom’s “trial” three times. But, much more importantly, are the hidden references to Bruno’s doctrine of the coincidence of contraries, by which he means: “Every power in nature or in spirit must evolve an opposite as the sole condition and means of its manifestation; and every opposite is, therefore, a tendency to reunion.” Joyce mentions this in an examination essay he took in Padua in which he adds that Bruno taught that these “contraries” create a power “without which man cannot fulfill himself.” So we see these opposites appearing in minor things such as the inverting of Virag’s name. Giordano Bruno was burned to death for his “heretical” views on February 17, 1600

notes.title: Masked with Matthew Arnold’s face
notes.html_source: Matthew Arnold was an Oxford don who argued for a renewed religious faith and an adoption of classical aesthetics and morals, particularly representative of mainstream Victorian intellectual concerns. A main theme Joyce borrows from his has to do with the effects of Hebraism and Hellenism. He writes: “At the bottom of both the Greek and the Hebrew notion is the desire, native in man, for reason and the will of God, the feeling after the universal order, — in a word, the love of God. But, while Hebraism seizes upon certain plain, capital intimations of the universal order, and rivets itself, one may say, with unequalled grandeur of earnestness and intensity on the study and observance of them, the bent of Hellenism is to follow, with flexible activity, the whole play of the universal order, to be apprehensive of missing any part of it, of sacrificing one part to another, to slip away from resting in this or that intimation of it, however capital.” The term “Hebraism” is used generally to infer the benefits and moral constraints of religion, while “Hellenism” refers to the “perfecting” effects of high culture. This is a significant and involved theme for Joyce, and to determine his intentions for its use is subject to discussion. Clearly drunkenness is not something Arnold would condone.

Bastinado is corporal punishment by hitting the bare soles of a person’s feet

notes.title: Die and be damned to you if you have any sense of decency or grace about you
notes.html_source: The character “Bello”, vile and indecent himself has just carried out a barrage of indecencies to humiliate Bloom. Joyce then has “him”, with fortified irony, rail against Bloom with “Die and be damned to you if you have any sense of decency or grace about you;” it is Bloom being consigned to the lowest point of Hell – it is he being condemned for immorality by the vilest of wretches. The scene’s counterpoint in The Odyssey is in Book 10 wherein Odysseus begs Circe to let him leave to continue his journey home. She gives him the bad news that, before he can return home he must visit the Land of the Dead – Hell. When Odysseus points out to her that no one has ever visited there and returned, she gives him directions for the trip and tells him of the sacrifices he must make for a successful journey. In fact, Joyce has already placed Bloom at Hell’s depths. Are there to be hints as to how he might find a safe return?

notes.title: Le distrait or absentminded beggar
notes.html_source:
This references back to the Scylla and Charybdis episode wherein Stephen is discussing Hamlet, “the distracted” or absentminded beggar. The allusion is to a Hamlet soliloquy in which he asks whether his own inaction is caused by “bestial oblivion,” or by a dull or cowardly thoughtlessness. Since both thought and action in this episode are bestial, “dull” and “cowardly” perhaps are better indictments of Stephen in the previous episode. Hamlet’s tendency to forget his purposes as avenger of his father’s murder, is similar to Stephen’s propensity toward distraction as to his purposes as literary creator, as demonstrated this evening through mind-numbing alcohol and sex, something paralyzing many young Irishmen, but is especially unfortunate with one, who, like Hamlet, has a supposedly unique role to play, requiring action, not degenerate inaction.

Much of Joyce’s great talent is due to a nearly encyclopedic memory and ability to focus, to avoid distraction. Something that becomes very apparent to the Ulysses reader is how critically needful those gifts are for himself.

notes.title: Broke his glasses
notes.html_source:
A reference to A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man (Chap 1):

During Father Arnall’s Latin lesson, Father Dolan, the prefect of studies, who wields the menacing pandybat in search of “lazy idle little loafers,” appears. Dolan notices that Fleming and Stephen are not doing their lessons. After disciplining Fleming, Dolan approaches Stephen, who explains that he has been excused temporarily from his assignments because he broke his glasses.

Refusing to believe that Stephen broke them accidentally, the cynical, sadistic Dolan commands the boy to put out his hands for “pandying.” This punishment, according to Dolan, is demanded for idleness and schoolboy tricks.

Hamlet advises the cast caution against overacting. “For anything so overdone is from [contrary to] the purpose of playing, whose end, both at the first and now, was and is, to hold, as ’t were, a mirror up to nature; to show virtue her own feature, scorn her own [nature’s] image and the very age and body of the time his form and pressure.” The scene just endured here in Circe is seemingly overwrought, and laden with inflated distaste so as to hold up a mirror to, and scorn, unconstrained nature, the image of that age in Ireland, the form of the times. We can conclude, then, that if what has been displayed in the scene is not exaggerated, but is intended as an accurate portrayal of contemporary Irish culture, then it is not, in fact, overacting.

notes.title: Pasiphae
notes.html_source:
PASIPHAE was an immortal daughter of the sun-god Helios. Like her siblings, Aeetes and Kirke (Circe), she was a skilled practitioner of witchcraft…As punishment for some offence against the gods–committed either by herself or her husband–she was cursed with lust for the king’s finest bull. The queen enlisted the help of the artisan Daidalos (Daedalus) who built her an animate, wooden cow wrapped in bovine-skin. Hidden inside the contraption she coupled with the bull and conceived a hybrid child–the bull-headed Minotauros (Minotaur).

notes.title: Frauenzimmer
notes.html_source:
Interesting German term. Literally “woman’s room”, it has come to be a derogatory or belittling term for a woman.

Etymology from wiktionary:
From Middle High German vrouwenzimmer; Frau (“woman”) +‎ -en- +‎ Zimmer (“room”). Originally (in the 15th century) denoting a woman’s room, then her things and (in the 16th century) her attendants, and then (in the 17th century) an individual woman, often one of low status, for which reason the term started to become derogatory. Compare Danish fruentimmer and Swedish fruntimmer.

notes.title: Their’s not to reason why
notes.html_source:
A famous line from Alfred, Lord Tennyson’s poem The Charge of the Light Brigade (1854).

  1. Half a league, half a league,
    ⁠Half a league onward,
    All in the valley of Death
    ⁠Rode the six hundred.
    “Charge,” was the captain’s cry;
    Their’s not to reason why,
    Their’s not to make reply,
    Their’s but to do and die,
    Into the valley of Death
    ⁠Rode the six hundred.

  2. Cannon to right of them,
    Cannon to left of them,
    Cannon in front of them
    ⁠Volley’d and thunder’d;
    Storm’d at with shot and shell,
    Boldly they rode and well;
    Into the jaws of Death,
    Into the mouth of Hell,
    ⁠Rode the six hundred.

  3. Flash’d all their sabres bare,
    Flash’d all at once in air,
    Sabring the gunners there,
    Charging an army, while
    ⁠All the world wonder’d:
    Plunged in the battery-smoke
    Fiercely the line they broke;
    Strong was the sabre-stroke;
    Making an army reel
    ⁠Shaken and sunder’d.
    Then they rode back, but not,
    ⁠Not the six hundred.

  4. Cannon to right of them,
    Cannon to left of them,
    Cannon behind them
    ⁠Volley’d and thunder’d;
    Storm’d at with shot and shell,
    They that had struck so well
    Rode thro' the jaws of Death,
    Half a league back again,
    Up from the mouth of Hell,
    All that was left of them,
    ⁠Left of six hundred.

Honour the brave and bold!
Long shall the tale be told,
Yea, when our babes are old—
⁠How they rode onward.

notes.title: Oblate orange
notes.html_source:
Oblate spheroid is the shape of a planet, so on one level Stephen means “upon this Earth”. However, ‘oblate’ also has a religious meaning:
“In Christianity, an oblate is a person who is specifically dedicated to God or to God’s service. Oblates are individuals, either laypersons or clergy, normally living in general society, who, while not professed monks or nuns, have individually affiliated themselves with a monastic community of their choice” (from Wikipedia).

Orange also has a special significance in Irish history, since it’s the colour of Unionism. Since Stephen’s altercation was with a pair of British soldiers, this is likely no accident.

notes.title: STEPHEN (Tries to move off.) Will some one tell me where I am least likely to meet these necessary evils?
notes.html_source:
Chapter 9, “Scylla and Charybdis”

—A father, Stephen said, battling against hopelessness, is a necessary evil.

Stephen considers himself under the oppression of two figurative fathers in addition to his biological father Simon: the imperial British rule and the Catholic Church. Earlier in “Circe,” Stephen drunkenly verbalizes his opposition to both:

(He taps his brow.) But in here it is I must kill the priest and the king.

notes.title: But by Saint Patrick
notes.html_source: This quick reference comes from the scene where Horatio reproves Hamlet: “These are but wild and whirling words, my Lord.” Hamlet responds: “I’m sorry they offend you…” Horatio: “There’s no offence, my Lord.” Hamlet: “Yes, by Saint Patrick, but there is.” Horatio: “And much offense, too.” This captures the essence of this entire chapter. There is much offence by Saint Patrick as symbol of Ireland, But there is much offence to Saint Patrick, as the spiritual symbol of Ireland.

notes.title: Cutty sarks
notes.html_source:
“Cutty sark)” is 18th-century Scots for “short chemise” or “short undergarment”.

Hyphenated, Cutty-sark was a nickname given to the witch Nannie Dee, a fictional character created by Robert Burns in his Tam o' Shanter, after the garment she wore. The figurehead of the tea clipper Cutty Sark is named after the character and a brand of Scotch whisky is named in turn for the ship.

For more elaborate etymology, see link, but essentially chemise -> witch -> ship -> whiskey

notes.title: Enoch Arden
notes.html_source:
Enoch Arden – The hero of Lord Tennyson’s eponymous poem is a fisherman turned merchant sailor Enoch Arden. He leaves his wife Annie and three children to go to sea with his old captain, who offers him work after he had lost his job due to an accident; in a manner that reflects the hero’s masculine view of personal toil and hardship to support his family, Enoch Arden left his family to better serve them as a husband and father. However during his voyage, Enoch Arden is shipwrecked on a desert island with two companions; both eventually die, leaving Arden alone there. This part of the story is reminiscent of Robinson Crusoe. Enoch Arden remains lost and missing for more than ten years.

He finds upon his return from the sea that, after his long absence, his wife, who believed him dead, is married happily to another man, his childhood friend Philip (Annie has known both men since her childhood, thus the rivalry), and has a child by him. Enoch’s life remains unfulfilled, with one of his children now dead, and his wife and remaining children now being cared for by his onetime rival.

Enoch never reveals to his wife and children that he is really alive, as he loves her too much to spoil her new happiness. Enoch dies of a broken heart.

notes.title: Rip van Winkle
notes.html_source:
The story of Rip Van Winkle is set in the years before and after the American Revolutionary War. In a pleasant village, at the foot of New York’s Catskill Mountains, lives kindly Rip Van Winkle, a Dutch villager. Van Winkle enjoys solitary activities in the wilderness, but he is also loved by all in town—especially the children to whom he tells stories and gives toys. However, he tends to shirk hard work, to his nagging wife’s dismay, which has caused his home and farm to fall into disarray.

One autumn day, to escape his wife’s nagging, Van Winkle wanders up the mountains with his dog, Wolf. Hearing his name called out, Rip sees a man wearing antiquated Dutch clothing; he is carrying a keg up the mountain and requires help. Together, they proceed to a hollow in which Rip discovers the source of thunderous noises: a group of ornately dressed, silent, bearded men who are playing nine-pins. Rip does not ask who they are or how they know his name. Instead, he begins to drink some of their moonshine and soon falls asleep.

He awakes to discover shocking changes. His musket is rotting and rusty, his beard is a foot long, and his dog is nowhere to be found. Van Winkle returns to his village where he recognizes no one. He discovers that his wife has died and that his close friends have fallen in a war or moved away. He gets into trouble when he proclaims himself a loyal subject of King George III, not aware that the American Revolution has taken place. King George’s portrait in the inn has been replaced with one of George Washington. Rip Van Winkle is also disturbed to find another man called Rip Van Winkle. It is his son, now grown up.

Rip Van Winkle learns that the men he met in the mountains are rumored to be the ghosts of Hendrick (Henry) Hudson’s crew, which had vanished long ago. Rip learns he has been away from the village for at least twenty years. However, an old resident recognizes him and Rip’s grown daughter takes him in. He resumes his usual idleness, and his strange tale is solemnly taken to heart by the Dutch settlers. Other henpecked men wish they could have shared in Rip’s good luck and had the luxury of sleeping through the hardships of the American Revolution.

The Land War (Irish: Cogadh na Talún) in Irish history was a period of agrarian agitation in rural Ireland in the 1870s, 1880s, and 1890s. The agitation was led by the Irish National Land League and was dedicated to bettering the position of tenant farmers and ultimately to a redistribution of land to tenants from landlords, especially absentee landlords. While there were many violent incidents and some deaths in this campaign, it was not actually a “war”, but rather a prolonged period of civil unrest.

notes.title: It’s in the blood, Mr Bloom acceded at once. All are washed in the blood of the sun
notes.html_source: There is a temptation to perhaps make more of these two sentences than Joyce intended. The immediate assumption is that Joyce is simply having Bloom state that Italian “impetuosity” is in the blood, and that “All are washed in the blood of the sun” is a pun on the Christian doctrine of redemption through the blood of the Son of God, or “blood of the Lamb” as the term is used in Lestrygonians. All three of the men are intensely emotional and romantic, in one form or another, Aquinas mostly in the chivalric sense. But it can be said that in each of the three flowed blood fired by religious conviction having been washed in the blood of the Son of God. Joyce often used Christian symbology and ritual as metaphor, and some argue that, regardless of his rejection of the Catholic Church per se, and his violation of Christian practice, in his more mature years, he realized that his faith was an inherent part of his identity, just as Bloom’s Jewishness was part of his, even while outwardly rejecting the tenets of Judaism. In this section in which the nature of souls, and their possible simplicity and the reconciliation between reason and belief is mentioned, it is highly unlikely that a reference to Aquinas is coincidental, despite the ironic word following “blood of the sun.”

notes.title: The Cornwall case
notes.html_source: This could refer to the case involving King Edward VII, who, before his coronation, was Duke of Cornwall and Prince of Wales, and who was called on to testify on the witness stand in divorce case. It is probably more likely, however, that, given the reference to the #16, a furtive reference to homosexuality, and also, considering the verbiage to appear shortly in the paragraph about something “under their veneer in a way scarcely intended by nature… except women chiefly, who were always fiddling more or less at one another… to acts of impropriety between the two…,” that this is probably attributable to a case in 1883 in which two officials in Dublin Castle, named Cornwall and French, were publically involved in an extensive homosexual circle.

notes.title: Is that first epistle to the Hebrews, he asked, as soon as his bottom jaw would let him, in? Text: open thy mouth and put thy foot in it.
notes.html_source: Gifford suggests “Stephen’s witticism implies that Mr. Deasy’s letter is addressed to a chosen people in a promised land,” which would certainly be consistent with the references to “mouth” and “foot”, considering the letter’s subject having to do with Foot and Mouth Disease. However, if one considers the text in Paul’s Epistle to the Hebrews (there is only one) there are other possibilities. Stephen could be reacting to Bloom’s preaching at him as saying what is written in verse five, “And again, I will be to him [Stephen] a Father, and he shall be to me a Son.” Verse nine contains words that Bloom might suggest apply to Stephen and his talents: “God, hath anointed thee… above thy fellows.” As for opening one’s mouth and putting one’s foot therein, in this context, it could be an indication of Stephen’s doubts over either assertion.

notes.html_source: Presabbath is friday, the day before the Jewish Sabbath, is considered an unlucky day because it is traditionally supposed to be the day on which Adam and Eve fell and were expelled from the Garden of Eden. notes.html_source: A possible interpretation: At birth, an infant is perceived generically. Throughout life, though a person may be perceived as interacting with others in no extraordinary manner, by the time he reaches death, he would be perceived by all in a way that was, in actuality, as none perceived. No one would understand the true nature of the person, not even those closest to him.

notes.html_source: As Milly grew up, and especially after she left home, Bloom had to concentrate on a domestic problem that had always plagued him – what to do with our wives? He tried many things from games to music. He decided to shore up her deficient education but without success. He found, finally, that he could manage her only by indirect suggestion implying self-interest.

notes.title: Sesquipedalian
notes.html_source:
An adjective meaning “big words” or a person who is given to using big words.

Literally, from Latin for “a foot and a half long”; from Latin sesqui (“one and a half”); + pedal, from Latin pedis, form of pes (“foot”), + adjective suffix -alis; + adjective suffix -ian. Cognate to French sesquipédal.

First used by the Latin poet Horace in his Ars Poetica, line 97 “sesquipedalia verba”, “words a foot and a half long”, referring to poets using excessively long words.

notes.title: YES
notes.html_source:
Yes begins and ends “Penelope,” a series of eight long, unpunctuated sentences. The formless stream resists categorisation. The non-style differentiates it from the rest of the chapters, facilitating the complex characterisation of Molly and indicating that we are to take her revelations as read. The chapter has contributed to feminist critical theories.

PROPOSED SUGGESTION: Molly thinks ‘yes’ scores of times throughout this chapter. Usually she uses the word to affirm something she is thinking. What is she affirming here? What is the antecedent to ‘Yes’?

We can usually understand what Molly is thinking once we identify the person involved. But there are several instances where short passages seem to just pop in out of the blue and defy interpretation with the context of the surrounding thought stream. See below for examples.

notes.html_source: A miser, coming from the Latin word miser, meaning “unhappy” (note the presence of the word in “miserly”), in Modern English and other languages has come to refer to someone who is afraid of spending money and prefers to save it, no matter how little the cost is. When Molly calls Leopold the “greatest miser” here, she means that he was even afraid to spend 4d, or 4 pence, which has always been a small amount of money in Britain. There are 100 pence to the British pound. As of the time of writing this in 2024, 4 pence is roughly 5¢, and 4 pence from 1924 is worth about $3.92 (£3.05).

notes.html_source: As Molly is thinking about sex with a priest and reminiscing about Boylan, there are two lines that seem to refer to Bloom’s grief over his father’s death: ‘his eyes were red when his father died’ and a few lines later ‘I suppose he was thinking of his father’; however, Rudolph died in 1886 when Bloom was 18, two years before he began courting Molly; this implies that they had known each other for at least a couple of years before becoming romantically involved. The second line occurs in the midst of Molly’s recollection of her and Boylan’s post-coital snack and slumber. notes.html_source: Molly muses over Josie, a former interest of Bloom’s, who was mentioned earlier in the text too. In this perspective however, we see how Molly views Josie from a female perspective, in the role of a fellow wife. The morals here seem skewed, considering Molly’s own infidelity and the subtle hint of irritation and concern over Josie and Bloom’s interactions. It is also interesting to note how Molly still values her relationship with Bloom, considering herself lucky to be paired with her husband, and needed by him, while Josie is stuck with a “dotty husband” who wears her down. Most importantly, it is fascinating to read this text from a “female’s perspective” because its bluntness seems authentic, and her internal struggle to pretend there is a contentedness with Bloom as a means to excuse, or distance her jealous emotions towards Josie. She attempts to act in denial of her own feelings here to some degree, and yet she reverts back to her dissatisfaction soon enough, showing the realistic innerworkings of Molly. Joyce manages to capture a unique perspective whilst preserving the character development by simply ending the text with Molly ruminating once more on a memory of Bloom’s proposal to her, similar to how he ends this sentence with her preference and relief to be with Bloom, rather than with a potentially worse man such as Josie’s husband.

notes.title: Cameron highlander
notes.html_source:
We learn that two soldiers (from the Queen’s Own Cameron Highlanders) have exposed themselves to Molly. One behind the meat market, and one behind a tree where “the statue of the fish used to be”.

According to Don Gifford, the Cameron Highlanders were stationed in Gibraltar and the statue was in Alameda Gardens in Gibraltar. So, Molly has flashed back to growing up in Gibraltar.

The Highlanders were relieved by the Surreys in 1882. So, Molly must have been under the age of twelve when the men exposed themselves to her.

Also, Gifford says that the statue was removed from the park in 1884, so Molly must have been very young when this happened.

notes.title: Lips were taittering
notes.html_source:
“Taittering of the lips,” apparently, was Irish vernacular for quivering of the vulva. Joyce seems to have found the expression in Havelock Ellis, Studies in the Psychology of Sex:

Even in the absence of sexual excitement there is a vague affection, occurring in both married and unmarried women, and not, it would seem, necessarily hysterical, characterized by quivering or twitching of the vulva; I am told that this is popularly termed “flackering of the shape” in Yorkshire and “taittering of the lips” in Ireland.

It’s unclear whether Molly invokes this meaning on purpose or if Joyce is having his own fun at Molly’s expense.

http://www.jjon.org/joyce-s-words/taittering

From the first line of Keats' Endymion (1818):

notes.title: It was leapyear like now
notes.html_source: In Ireland, it’s tradition that every leap year on the 29th of February, women propose to men and the men are obligated to say yes. Despite this, Molly is the one repeating “yes” as this passage continues and she was the one who said yes to the proposal as well. With the roles reversed, this suggests that Molly has more of a traditionally “masculine” role in her marriage and was forced by traditional relationship conventions to say yes to a marriage she knew would leave her unfulfilled.

notes.html_source: This passage shows how Molly responds to Bloom’s marriage proposal and her agreeing to get married to him. It also shows how much she has always valued physical intimacy, immediately affirming her decision and letting him know that she is serious by inviting him to touch her body. The passage brings to light how Molly’s love language is physical touch, and how she often acts based on her sexual desires, perhaps also suggesting that her acceptance of Bloom’s proposal might have to do with what she expects physically from a marriage with him.

notes.title: Yes I said yes I will Yes.
notes.html_source:
The chapter ends with “Yes,” as it began. Here the “Yes” comes as a memory of sexual consent (during Molly’s first meeting with Leopold) and an affirmation of life, femininity, and sexuality. Joyce’s associations with “yes” were very specific: he called it “the female word,” “the least forceful word I could possibly find” to end the book, and wrote that it “denotes acquiescence, self-abandon, relaxation, the end of all resistance.”

In the Linati schema, Joyce has the hour as none and the 8 sentences of the “Penelope” chapter represent infinity, i.e. the 8 on its side–or as Joyce biographer Richard Ellmann wrote eloquently:

The time is no o’clock, or as he said in an Italian schema of the book, it is the time indicated mathematically by the lemniscate or figure eight lying on its side—∞—the number of infinity and eternity. It might be more exact to say that the ruins of time and space coexist with the mansions of eternity and infinity, at least until the very end.
